Inequality in intern pay is distorting the Swiss job market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
11:30:47 UTC
20:30:47 KST

Inequality in intern pay is distorting the Swiss job market
The disparity in pay and perks offered for company and NGO internships is vast in Switzerland. Some interns receive CHF3,500 ($4,360) per month while others work without salary or allowances at certain NGOs.
In an increasingly competitive job market, internships are becoming the norm at entry level, sometimes to the detriment of young people. An entire generation’s relationship to work is being defined by the lottery of either landing a lucrative position or ending up in precarious employment.
Some organisations pamper interns. Thomas Villaman is training in medical communication at a multinational pharmaceutical company based in Meyrin, near to Geneva. His monthly salary ranges from CHF2,000 to CHF3,000, plus the benefits of free meals, tea and coffee, and even access to a gym.
More
Minimum wage: Swiss cantons push on despite national setback
“I have a supervisor and a project to work on. I’m going to write a report, a short thesis for my master’s degree,” he said. His position isn’t meant to replace a permanent job, but to provide additional support.
Undelivered promises
At another organisation, the situation is radically different. Nina* is doing a six-month, unpaid internship at a Geneva-based NGO. For her, the experience quickly turned into a nightmare.
“I’m working in a place where there are no employees. All the work is done by interns. And the manager is completely absent,” she said. She finds herself shouldering a heavy workload and accumulating overtime.
She was promised training, but it never materialised. She has chosen to break the silence to “stop normalising these unpaid internships.”
Such disparities are possible because there is no federal law that regulates the remuneration of interns. Regulations are primarily defined by individual cantons or by collective labour agreements.
Job market disruption
This lack of a national pay framework puts students in a vulnerable position. In Lausanne, the Federation of Student Associations is sounding the alarm. Faced with a wave of applications that far outweighs the number of internship on offer, “employers can set whatever criteria they want,” explained a representative.
This risks creating a wage war that undermines the principle of equal opportunities. To accept a full-time, unpaid internship, students must rely on personal savings or financial support from their families.
For some observers, the problem goes beyond financial considerations. Sociologist Dominique Glaymann, an emeritus professor at the University of Évry Val d’Essonne in France, fears a “staging”, or artificial manipulation, of the job market.
According to Glaymann, the proliferation of these short-term, low-cost contracts is profoundly altering access to employment. Positions once reserved for junior employees are now systematically filled by interns.
This is a significant paradox for a measure intended to facilitate the integration of young people into the workforce.
More
A broke intern’s guide to enjoying Geneva
The effectiveness of this process is also questionable. No statistical data proves that completing a series of internships increases the chances of obtaining a permanent contract.
Yet, for some start-ups, this workforce has become a cornerstone of survival. This is the case for a natural cosmetics start-up in Neuchâtel, where two interns work alongside seven employees.
The boss stands by this choice, dictated by budgetary constraints. “An intern costs on average two and a half times less than a junior employee,” said director, Paul Liurette.
Some cantons, such as the French-speaking Geneva, Neuchâtel, and Jura, have adopted laws introducing a minimum wage.
However, these laws allow for exceptions. In Geneva, for example, working for free for an international organisation remains perfectly legal.
Other cantons, such as Valais and Fribourg, have no guidelines. The canton of Vaud, however, has just accepted the principle of a minimum wage. Its specifics for internships remain to be defined.

Artist says giving up artworks to cover fraud loss hurts less than giving up studios

Artist says giving up artworks to cover fraud loss hurts less than giving up studios
In May, the Estonian Artists' Association (EKL) was defrauded of nearly €700,000. To cover part of the financial loss, works from the association's collection and newly donated pieces will be auctioned. EKL board member Jaanus Samma said it is less painful to give up artworks than the studios that belong to the association.
In addition to donated works, pieces from the association's collection will go under the hammer from October 8 to 10. They were mostly acquired from spring and fall exhibitions featuring well‑known Estonian artists.
"We decided to put part of the collection up for sale. Certainly not everything, and a very important part will remain. But when faced with the choice of selling a studio where artists work or a painting, it is less painful to give up the painting," Samma, a member of the art infrastructure council and the EKL board, said.
Rethinking the collection
"Our plan is not to enter the auction market. This will definitely be very different from classic fall auctions. We wanted the diversity of our association to be reflected in the auction. That is why all techniques and mediums are represented," Samma added.
"These decisions had to be made. In every bad situation, you have to look for something positive. On the positive side, this gave us a chance to rethink our collection. To understand what the focus is and what it could be in the future. That also made our choices easier, because we decided to keep all works that depict artistic life or where artists portray each other, their work, their studios," he said.
Graphic works with duplicate prints will also be sold. "We will sell one and keep the other. That does not hurt us as much. Fresh works donated by artists also play a major role. Even before the decision to hold an auction, some artists contacted us and wanted to donate. That is how the idea grew. There are well‑known names from different generations," Samma said.
Sales potential considered
The association does not yet dare to estimate how much money the auction will bring in. "We certainly do not expect to cover the entire lost amount. But even part of it would be a big help. When making the selection, we naturally thought about what might have sales potential, let's put it that way. What might be popular in a good sense, what fits the market context and what is collected," he explained.
On September 18, an exhibition will open in the ARS building in Tallinn for a couple of weeks, where people can view the works headed for auction. "I recommend coming not only to those who plan to buy something, because it will be a very diverse exhibition full of good art. The auction itself will take place online and bids can be made from home. In real life, these works are still quite different."
Samma said that in some ways the crisis has already passed. "All bills have been paid, life goes on, exhibitions are happening. The first shock is over and life has normalized. At the same time, the ax is still hanging overhead, because the association has taken out a loan and that loan must be repaid. In that sense, the crisis is still ongoing."
--

Bringing the Bible back: i24NEWS travels to the Elah Valley to uncover the ancient Judean fortress of Azekah
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
11:23:04 UTC
20:23:04 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel
- Archaeology
- Bringing the Bible back: i24NEWS travels to the Elah Valley to uncover the ancient Judean fortress of Azekah
Bringing the Bible back: i24NEWS travels to the Elah Valley to uncover the ancient Judean fortress of Azekah
Even as war continues to test the excavation team, the researchers at Tel Azekah have returned to the biblical fortress every season for 16 years, determined to keep uncovering its Judean past
For 16 years, the Lautenschläger Azekah Expedition has excavated the ancient stronghold of Azekah in central Israel's Elah Valley, working to uncover one of the Kingdom of Judah's key fortresses. i24NEWS traveled to the site and spoke with the team’s directors to learn how their work persists, and in some cases thrives, amid the ongoing conflicts around the world.
Prof. Oded Lipschits, who directs the excavation and serves as dean of the Faculty of Humanities at Tel Aviv University, said the site's importance lies in its location on the border between the Judeans and the Philistines, and later between Judah and Israel to the north. "Anyone who wants to conquer Judah had to cross through this place," he said.
Tel Azekah is over 3,000 years old, and the team continues to make discoveries from across the millennia, including stamp impressions, weights, jewelry, game boxes, weapons, and other finds which Lipschits says tie the site directly to biblical history. It’s not just what’s above ground either. Tel Azekah maintains its own subterranean world. Underneath the large mound is a system full of caves and installations, which will be part of the team’s focus for coming excavation seasons.
"This is a really exciting thing because it's bringing the Bible back; it's bringing the Judean history of the site," Lipchits exclaimed.
A stronghold recorded in biblical and Assyrian texts
Azekah's occupation spans roughly 3,500 years, beginning in the Early Bronze Age, when the site was first settled. It became a strongly fortified, urban city during the Middle Bronze Age (2000-1550 BCE) before its destruction at the end of the Late Bronze Age. After a period of abandonment, it was resettled during the Iron II period (1000-586 BCE) and flourished as a Judean town.
The fortress’s history stretches into some of the best-known narratives of the Hebrew Bible. The book of Joshua lists the city among the towns allotted to the tribe of Judah in the western foothills, naming it alongside Eshtaol, Zorah and Jarmuth as one of "fourteen towns and their villages" (Joshua 15:33-36).
First Samuel 17 places Azekah at the staging ground for the battle between David and Goliath: "Now the Philistines gathered their forces for war and assembled at Sokoh in Judah. They pitched camp at Ephes Dammim, between Sokoh and Azekah” (1 Samuel 17:1).
Suggested articles
- Excavations in Jerusalem's City of David uncover royal seal inscriptions from Judah's final days | i24NEWS, Henry Kirshner
- The Babylonian destruction: Archaeologists discover charred beams from First Temple Period elite building | i24NEWS, Henry Kirshner
- US returns two smuggled ancient coins to Israel after joint trafficking probe | i24NEWS, Henry Kirshner
The fortress also appears in Assyrian records. In 701 BC, King Sennacherib of Assyria recorded his campaign through Judah on the Taylor Prism after King Hezekiah refused to submit to Assyrian rule; one of the cities he claims to have destroyed was Azekah. The City was described as being “Situated upon a mountain peak. Like the blades of daggers without number, they rise high into the heavens... were well fortified and rival high mountains."
Azekah's destruction under Sennacherib was not the end of the city. Jeremiah 34:7 describes Azekah and Lachish as the only fortified cities of Judah. The city would go on to be repopulated by Greeks, Romans, Persians, and the Byzantines before it was forgotten.
Finding the forgotten fortress
The site was left forgotten until the excavations of British archaeologists F.J. Bliss and R.A.S. Macalister on behalf of the Palestine Exploration Fund between 1898 and 1899. Lipschits described their approach as "a very destructive method of archaeology" that damaged other sites they worked at, including Maresha and Gezer, and said it was long believed Azekah had suffered the same fate.
Time constraints forced the pair to abandon the project and backfill it, and for more than a century afterward, most archaeologists believed the site had been fully excavated.
Renewed excavations began in 2012 under Lipschits, Yuval Gadot and Heidelberg University's Manfred Oeming. Dr. Sabine Kleiman, who joined the project as a field director after three seasons as assistant supervisor at the nearby Ramat Rahel excavation, said the depth of prior work at Azekah makes it possible to date material from ceramics and even small potsherds in ways other sites do not allow.
"I can't do this on other sites. It's a big opportunity," Sabine said.
The project has since grown to include archaeologists, historians, scientists and students from Germany, the Czech Republic, Italy, Malta, the United Kingdom, Spain, China, Indonesia, Australia, Canada and the United States.
Fighting the learning amid war and uncertainty
But the dig has not been immune to the region's conflicts. Kleiman said the team has continued excavating every year, including during the COVID pandemic and the wars with Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran that followed October 7, though it has been difficult.
"We were not able to really get a hold on good grants, which we usually would go for from abroad," Kleiman explained, noting the excavation now operates with far fewer volunteers than in past seasons.
"Usually we would have in this area 20 volunteers working," she said, describing a crew that has shrunk to two. She said she does not yet feel the strain but expects to "in the long run."
Looking toward the future
Despite the war's toll on funding and staffing, Kleiman said Azekah already draws busloads of school visitors to its lookout point to hear the story of David and Goliath, though she said they currently arrive, hear the story and leave. She said she hopes visitors will eventually be able to buy refreshments on site.
Lipschits said his dream is for visitors within about four years to walk through the citadel's high walls and inner structures and along the street surrounding the fortress, calling it a future "pearl" among Israel's archaeological sites.

UN and Red Cross step up call for international rules on ‘killer robot’ weapons systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
11:23:02 UTC
20:23:02 KST

UN and Red Cross step up call for international rules on ‘killer robot’ weapons systems
GENEVA (AP) — The United Nations and the International Committee of the Red Cross on Tuesday ratcheted up a joint call for countries to adopt bans and restrictions on use of autonomous weapons systems — often known as “killer robots” — warning that “the risks have intensified.”
Building on an initial appeal three years ago and international talks on the issue for years, the appeal stops short of calling for a blanket ban, but notes that such weapons systems are being developed — though the U.N. and Red Cross haven’t confirmed their use on the battlefield.
The organizations said, however, that civilians need to be protected for when that day may come.
“We are now dangerously close to crossing a moral red line: The autonomous targeting of humans by machines,” said U.N. Geneva spokesperson Alessandra Vellucci, reading a joint statement by U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres and ICRC President Mirjana Spoljaric.
“Today, we renew this call with even greater urgency,” the statement said. “The fundamental concerns remain unchanged, but the risks have intensified.”
The two international organizations say the development of weapons technology at “record speed” has strained the international rules system, and widened the gap between technological capacities and regulatory constraints.
“Autonomous weapons systems are not part of a distant future — a race toward greater autonomy in weapons systems is already well underway,” the joint statement said.
The call comes as negotiators are set to meet in Geneva in November on ways of strengthening the existing Convention on Conventional Weapons, with the U.N. and ICRC saying the conference “offers the clearest path available” to move toward binding legal rules on the use of such autonomous systems.
The yearslong effort to rein in the use of autonomous weapons systems has struggled to produce limits. The new push comes against the backdrop of drones and other technologies used in conflicts as diverse as the Russia-Ukraine war, the Middle East, Sudan and others.
Ground robotic vehicles have so far been used on the Ukrainian battlefield primarily to ferry supplies to infantry and carry out evacuations, because of Ukraine’s need to preserve manpower amid the growing prevalence of drones.
Kyiv is now seeking to scale up armed robotic systems to reduce the pressure on increasingly outnumbered infantry by equipping them with firing power, but those efforts have been limited so far.
“Scientists and engineers developing these systems have themselves raised the alarm,” the organizations said. “When the architects of this technology are calling for limits, states cannot afford to remain passive.”
“This year must mark a turning point,” the statement said.

Trump floats renaming Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’ as trade war with Canada escalates
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Tuesday that he is considering changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” as the trade war between the United States and Canada intensifies.
Such a change would be reminiscent of the Republican president’s unilateral action last year by executive order to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.
The United States and Canada are locked in a trade dispute, with Canada expected to announce retaliatory measures Tuesday. That’s in response to the Trump administration enacting 50% tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian goods over the weekend after talks between the countries broke down.
“The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don’t expect to doing much business with Ontario any longer,” Trump said Tuesday on social media.
Ontario is Canada’s most populous province and is home to the country’s auto industry.
The rhetoric between the two countries is escalating, with Trump telling Canadian leaders Monday to “fall in line” or face consequences “far WORSE” than existing tariffs. Prime Minister Mark Carney has accused Washington of trying to subordinate Canada.
Trump also threatened new 50% tariffs on Canadian vehicles, auto parts and steel, while Carney said U.S. trade demands showed that Washington wanted to “destroy our major industries,” including autos, steel and aluminum.
Canada and the United States share one of the world’s largest trading relationships, with deeply integrated supply chains across autos, energy, agriculture and manufacturing, making a prolonged trade fight potentially costly for businesses and workers on both sides of the border.
Businesses and consumers are caught in the middle, facing uncertainty about how much prices may increase.
Michael Howard II, owner of a furniture business in Warren, Michigan, outside Detroit, said the tariffs will hamper the “ability for us to put food on the table for our family, but also impacts the ability for us to give back to our community.”
Howard and his wife started their business a decade ago. They make and sell everything from dining room tables to bookcases.
“To say that we don’t need Canada is just disingenuous,” he said. “It’s dishonest. And it’s just absolutely not truthful. We need our neighbor, but also they need us.”
Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne and three other Cabinet ministers are also expected Tuesday morning to share details of support for workers affected by tariffs. Carney said earlier Monday that Canada may need to move away from matching U.S. tariffs dollar for dollar and instead use more targeted retaliation aimed at protecting Canadian workers and businesses.
“An attitude at the negotiation table that Canada is a subsidiary of the United States” is “not something we’re going to accept,” Carney said.
Carney was even more blunt in French.
“We learned during the negotiations that the Americans want to destroy our major industries, including autos, steel and aluminum,” Carney said. “That was one of the main reasons we said no. It was a bad deal.”
Carney said Monday U.S. negotiators had raised the discoverability of French-language content on streaming platforms, along with French-language labeling rules, as trade irritants. He rejected the idea that those protections were negotiable, saying in French: “For the Americans, questions about the French language, Quebec culture, francophone culture and Canadian culture are irritants. Here in Quebec, here in Canada, they are rights.”
In a social media post early Tuesday, Trump wrote “I would never interfere with Canadians speaking French! In fact, I have never even thought of doing such a stupid thing. This lie was made up by a weak and ineffective Prime Minister in an attempt to gain political support, which he has totally lost, from the people of Quebec. I love French Canadians!”

Rob Gillies reported from Ontario. Associated Press writers Seung Min Kim contributed from Washington and Mike Householder from Warren, Michigan

Stara Zagora Opera invites audiences to “On the Shores of Ancient Seuthopolis”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
11:15:32 UTC
20:15:32 KST

News
Stara Zagora Opera invites audiences to “On the Shores of Ancient Seuthopolis”
Tuesday 25 August 2026 12:26
Tuesday, 25 August 2026, 12:26
PHOTO Stara Zagora State Opera
Font size
Beneath the tranquil surface of the Koprinka Reservoir, the ancient city of Seuthopolis, the capital of Thracian ruler Seuthes III, continues to live on. From August 27 to 30, 2026, for the sixth time, one of Bulgaria’s most spectacular open-air stages will bring music, theatre and dance to the shores of the submerged city.
PHOTO Stara Zagora State Opera
The “On the Shores of Ancient Seuthopolis” festival was launched by the Stara Zagora State Opera in 2021, with the support of Kazanlak Municipality, as part of the traditional “Festivals in the Valley of the Thracian Kings”.
In previous years, audiences have applauded some of the most impressive productions by the Stara Zagora Opera, including Turandot, Carmen, Attila, The Pearl Fishers, Tsar Kaloyan and Nabucco, as well as the ballets Nestinarka and Ghetto, the operetta La Belle Hélène, the musicals Esmeralda, Notre Dame de Paris and Romeo and Juliet, the musical-theatrical fairy tale Beautiful Green Bird, and a series of symphonic and opera concerts.
Today, the festival has established a distinctive identity of its own, combining a diverse, multi-genre repertoire and spectacular productions with a unique sense of the millennia-old history of the site.
PHOTO Stara Zagora State Opera
Each edition adds a new dimension to Kazanlak’s cultural map, transforming the shores of the Koprinka Reservoir into a stage with its own artistic identity. This year, “On the Shores of Ancient Seuthopolis” offers an intriguing programme featuring Bulgarian opera classics, a celebrated European operetta and a contemporary concert.
PHOTO Stara Zagora State Opera
On August 27, audiences will be treated to The Madman (Lud Gidiya) by Bulgarian composer Parashkev Hadzhiev, inspired by the poem of the same name by Pencho Slaveykov. With its vivid characters, gripping plot and rich musical language, the work, which literally embodies the Bulgarian national spirit, is a natural choice for the shores of ancient Seuthopolis, where the legends and spirit of the Bulgarian land live on.
The production is conducted by Vladimir Boshnakov and directed by Alexander Moutafchievski. The leading roles of Iliya and Zornitsa are performed by Stoyan Buyukliev and Emilia Terzieva. Alongside the soloists, chorus and orchestra of the Stara Zagora State Opera, the production also features the Zagore Municipal Folklore Ensemble.
On August 29, the stage by the Koprinka Reservoir will welcome the elegant humour, beautiful melodies and festive spirit of Johann Strauss II’s sparkling operetta masterpiece Die Fledermaus, again conducted by Vladimir Boshnakov.
Conductor Vladimir Boshnakov focuses on young musicians and Bulgarian classics
PHOTO Stara Zagora State Opera
The festival will conclude on August 30 with the concert Rock Swings, featuring Vasil Petrov, the orchestra of the Stara Zagora State Opera and guest performers, under the baton of Tsvetomir Vasilev.
The “Festivals in the Valley of the Thracian Kings” are among the most significant cultural events organised by Kazanlak Municipality. Every year, they bring together traditional and contemporary forms of various arts to promote the cultural heritage of the ancient Thracians.

Almost €600 million in advance payments already disbursed to farmers in Italy
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
13:15:07 CEST
20:15:07 KST

Almost €600 million in CAP advance
payments have already been disbursed to Italian farmers, around
three months ahead of the 16 October deadline.
                                    
                                       
				In particular, Agea, the Agency for Agricultural Payments, began
authorising payments as early as 26 July, with €577,835,632.03
already disbursed. Under EU rules, the first tranche of direct
aid in the form of advance payments was originally due to start
on 16 October.
                                    
                                       
				"We worked on the timing. In the past, receiving funding on time
was an ordeal. We also activated the anti-fraud service to
ensure that these were lawful payments, and we put the entire
process for disbursing EU funding under pressure. As a result,
we were the first European country to make the advance
payments," Agea Director Fabio Vitale said during ANSAIncontra,
commenting on the results. "We started making payments on 27
July," he explained. "This was an option granted to Member
States which the government deemed necessary and essential to
implement. As the technical body, we were ready because already
in June we had collected 700,000 applications nationwide,
processed them in five days and, by 6 July, we were already
ready to make payments before the EU regulation had even been
approved. We have paid €577 million to date and will pay €680
million through Agea and €621 million through regional paying
agencies by the end of August, for a total of €1.3 billion."
Agea's objective, Vitale said, "is to have disbursed €1.6
billion by 15 October, the day before the European financial
campaign formally opens, and to reach around €2.5 billion by 30
November, when the advance-payment campaign closes". Since 1
January, the total amount disbursed through various forms of
payment has reached €2.2 billion.
                                    
                                       
				In addition to the timing of payments, implementation procedures
for the tax credit on diesel fuel have also changed, with the
relevant measures issued within just 48 hours instead of 48
days. Agea is also active on the legality front through
Agecontrol, as part of the steering committee established by the
Italian Ministry of Agriculture. "Using risk indicators," Vitale
said, "we inspected farms in Basilicata and Calabria, and all of
them were found to be non-compliant for various reasons, with
some employing workers irregularly."
On the fight against illegal labour recruitment, Vitale proposed
"having a body appointed by a public institution collect these
workers and take them to their workplaces, but to do this they
must have formal employment contracts". In essence, he
explained, this would mean "institutionalising the process of
integrating these people into areas where work is available",
with the support of local authorities, agricultural associations
and municipalities. This would provide "an additional tool to
drive criminal organisations and illegal labour recruiters out
of the system".

Denis Manturov
                    
                    MINSK, 25 August (BelTA) - A prototype of the Osvey aircraft will be ready in 2027, with certification expected to be completed by the end of 2029, Russian First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov told the media following a meeting with Belarusian President Aleksandr Lukashenko in Minsk on 25 August, BelTA has learned.
 
  
“Belarusian aviation industry enterprises are participating in the production of Russian aircraft and components, including painting in Minsk, for which good facilities have been provided,” the first deputy prime minister said.
 
 
 
  
 
                    
                    
                                        
                                    
                                                        
                
                
            He specifically mentioned the new Osvey aircraft project, in which Belarus is also involved. “We are moving according to the adjusted schedule. Next year we will have a prototype that will begin flight testing. We expect certification to be completed by the end of 2029, and the aircraft will receive a green light for operation on the Belarusian and Russian markets. We also plan to supply it to third countries,” Denis Manturov said.
The Russian first deputy prime minister noted that the list of joint projects and areas of cooperation between Belarus and Russia is very broad, covering many sectors. Importantly, the emphasis is on developing industrial cooperation. Last year, industrial products accounted for 65% of Belarusian-Russian trade. Overall, trade continues to grow while maintaining a balance between exports and imports.
“This is the result of systematic work. The personal involvement and engagement of the Belarusian head of state in every project and every area yields positive results. Understanding the essence of the issues and making timely management decisions,” Denis Manturov said.
He noted the intensification of cooperation in mechanical engineering in general and automotive manufacturing in particular. There are good prospects on the Russian market and steady demand for Belarusian BELGEE vehicles. The level of localization in the production of these cars is increasing, including with the participation of Russian companies, which deepens cross-border industrialization, Denis Manturov added.
He also mentioned cooperation with BelAZ: Russian mining enterprises regularly purchase equipment from this manufacturer. But it is not just trade that matters - Russian companies’ participation in manufacturing components and mechanisms for BelAZ vehicles is equally important, the first deputy prime minister said. For example, some types of engines are produced by Kolomna’s Transmashholding and Sinara Group.
“A new project with BelAZ is now on the agenda - developing specialized equipment for Nornickel, specifically mining machinery that is currently mostly of Western origin. We will use Belarusian technologies. This is good synergy,” Denis Manturov said.
In addition, cooperation in electronics and electronic engineering is also on the bilateral agenda.
“We will continue to develop all these areas with the same intensity,” the Russian first deputy prime minister added.

El Nino drives up corn futures to highest in 3 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
11:13:13 UTC
20:13:13 KST

Burhan Sansarlioglu, Emir Yildirim
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
Corn prices rose to $5.2425 per bushel in global markets, reaching their highest level in three years amid the El Nino weather event, dry conditions and geopolitical risks due to the Russia-Ukraine war.  
Price movements in grains came to the fore due to El Nino, with sharp hikes in corn prices.
Corn previously reached $5.2450 on July 31, 2023.
Corn rose more than 11% compared with the end of July and increased more than 17% compared with the end of December 2025.
The bushel price of corn later stabilized at around $5.18.
Growing concerns over crop yields in the US fuel expectations of tighter supplies and drive up corn prices, while rising US corn exports contribute to the price increase.
Hot and dry weather in some corn-producing regions of the US, adverse weather in Europe and ongoing grain shipment disruptions in Ukraine fuel concerns over the global corn supply.
The corn harvest in the American Midwest came in lower than expected, while Russian and Ukrainian attacks on each other's shipping routes halted grain exports.
While weather conditions threaten production, geopolitical disruptions pose risks to crop deliveries, and given the already high energy and fertilizer costs, the margin for offsetting additional supply shocks narrows.
Waning expectations of Fed rate hikes and falling demand for the US dollar also continue to drive up commodity prices.
Zafer Ergezen, a futures and commodities expert, told Anadolu that El Nino’s effects began to be seen in June, especially in South America, Southeast Asia and Australia, and to a somewhat lesser extent in the US and Europe.
“We’re seeing a serious impact of the weather phenomenon in West Africa,” he said. “There were concerns over a decline in corn yields, especially in Brazil, the US, and Southeast Asia.”
Ergezen stated that oil prices also contributed to the rise in corn prices as demand for corn used in biodiesel production climbs when oil prices rise, while around 60% of the corn produced across the globe is used for industrial purposes.
The combined effects of El Nino and high oil prices were instrumental in raising corn prices.
“El Nino will continue until the beginning of next year, and if oil remains at these levels, we may see even more upward movements in corn,” he said.
“As long as oil prices don’t decline and there isn’t a lasting peace deal between the US and Iran, I don’t expect a deep pullback in corn prices,” he added.

The 4 Best Car Phone Mounts I’ve Tried (2026): Belkin, Andery, Andobil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
11:08:00 UTC
20:08:00 KST

A car phone mount is no longer an option—it's a necessity. Nearly every US state restricts cell phone use while driving (we see you, Montana!), and most require full hands-free operation. The best car phone mounts offer an easy view of your phone's screen without blocking your view of the road, hold your phone securely, and keep vibration to a minimum.
I've spent weeks and hundreds of miles testing car phone holders for iPhones and Android alike, on busy freeways and on potholed city roads. What I found is that the best car phone mounts aren't necessarily expensive or name brands: They're just smartly designed.
The best car phone mount for an iPhone is almost always a secure MagSafe mount. The one I keep in my car when I'm not testing other mounts is a sturdy, compact Andery suction mount ($36) that holds preternaturally fast to both my phone and dash but can also be mounted to a window. My favorite mechanical car phone holder for Android phones is a sturdy, versatile, ball-joint mount from Andobil ($30) that affixes tightly to a car's dash, windshield, or air vents.
Here are the best car phone mounts for each car and phone type. See also WIRED's guides to the Best USB Car Chargers, Best Portable Jump Starters, Best iPhone Cases and Accessories, Best MagSafe Accessories, and Best Wireless Phone Chargers.
Best Car Phone Mount for iPhones and Qi2 Phones
The world is full of bulky phone mounts that block your view of the road, inflexible phone mounts that only allow for horizontal or vertical mounting, weak suction cups, and kinda mid MagSafe attachments. And then there's this innovatively designed, wonderfully compact dash and window mount from Andery.
On flat surfaces, the nano-gel suction cup holds fast like Hodor at the door. The 22-magnet MagSafe ring allows airflow to avoid overheating, but it also holds stronger than most comparable Qi2 magnets. And unlike bulky plastic mounts, the Andery's aluminum-arm, stainless steel ring keeps a low profile and interferes minimally with one's line of sight. In fact, when affixed to my dash, this device doesn't block my view of the road at all. The ring rotates 360 degrees. The two-joint arm can either fold tightly to the mount or extend outward. No other mount I've tested combines all of these virtues.
But note you'll need a relatively flat surface to get a good bond with the suction cup. I've also seen some reports that the suction cup can lose adhesion over time if repeatedly re-mounted (and it's cussedly difficult to remove in the first place, though it leaves no residue when you do). Non-Qi2-compatible Android phones will need a MagSafe case to be compatible with this car phone holder. But if your phone has a magnet or a magnetic case, this is the simplest and most effective car phone mount I know, and it performs leagues better than other similarly designed car mounts like this one from Acer.
Note also that Andery offers a Qi2-compatible phone charger version at the expense of airflow. I haven't tested this variant yet.
Best Universal Car Phone Mount
Mechanical mounts like this one from Andobil—with holders that can be slid in sideways to securely grip the phone—are flexible for a broad range of phones and don't require MagSafe technology. But they're also mostly bulky, making them a less preferred option as a windshield or dashboard mount because this will block your field of vision.
Among all similar devices I've tested, this one from newer Chinese company Andobil is the most compact I've tested when not in use, while still offering a lot of flexibility. The nanogel suction cup on its dash mount is one of the most stable I've tested (almost aggressively stuck on, to be honest). And the extendable arm, while plastic, feels less cheap and breakable than other models. The kit also comes with an air vent mount, whose three-point design makes it among the most stable vent mounts I've tested and allows you to maneuver the phone so it does not block the vent.
This mechanical car phone holder is hard to call aesthetic. It's essentially a pad with a gripper on the side. But the grips extend to accommodate even larger phones and are able to keep the phone in place even during vigorous shaking. (If you're wondering whether I place phones in these phone mounts, and then come at them like they're a shake weight? I do.) The release button's a little awkwardly placed, and Andobil's marketing about “military standards” is a little silly on a low-cost device made with thermoplastics. But after I watched other suction cups wilt in summer heat, this Andobil's still going strong.
★ A Great, Low-Cost Air Vent Mount: If you're mounting only to your air vent, the Vanva air vent phone mount ($13) is among the cheapest mounts of any kind that I've tested, while ranking among the most secure mechanical mounts. (Actually, I like the mechanical phone holder a bit better than Andobil's.) The lockable clamp affixes easily and securely to most vertical or horizontal-slatted vents—and unlike hook-based vent mounts, it's easy to install and remove. The multi-joint ball arm can be maneuvered so you don't lose airflow from the vent, and the adjustable grips that lock in your phone can be released with a simple button press. This Vanva is a relatively flimsy plastic device, so I don't rule out that it might break someday. But its inexpensive replacement cost makes this an acceptable risk.
Best Car Phone Mount With Charger
Look, I'll be honest: I have mixed feelings about chargers on car phone mounts. The mount will have to be plugged into a car charger anyway—and at that point, I might as well just plug in the phone directly, which will usually lead to faster charging.
But convenience is in the eye of the beholder, and many people prefer to just leave the car mount plugged permanently into a car charger so they never have to worry about their phone draining while navigating on a mapping app. For y'all, here's the car mount from ESR, which offers decently fast 15-watt charging and a cooling fan to mitigate phone overheating.
The suction was effective when attached to both my window and dash, and the device is compact enough to not much hinder my field of view. Charging speed is merely moderate, enough to charge an older iPhone in a couple of hours. ESR also offers a faster-charging Qi2.2 device for twice the money, though I have not tested it.
★ A Good, Stylish Vent Charging Mount: Most vent chargers plant themselves directly into the airflow of your vent. But not all of them do. WIRED editor Julian Chokkattu recommends the Peak Design Car Vent Mount ($100). The mount stays secure on the vent, but an arm allows the charger a little distance from the vent. It's also a little bit stylish, a rarity for vent mounts. If you're using a Pixel or Samsung phone, we also like Peak Design's MagSafe phone cases.
Best Minimalist Car Phone Mount
Most people don't overwhelmingly want their car vent mount to be a defining feature in their car's interior. This Belkin takes this notion to the extreme. This silver and black air vent mount is minimalist, svelte, and—dare I say—almost classy. It grips phones surprisingly securely for a phone mount without feet to support the phone's bottom, according to WIRED reviewer Simon Hill, and you can rotate easily from portrait to landscape. There's also a handy rubber clip to hold charging cables in place. Just note that this will not be the best option for larger or heavier phones.
★ For larger phones: The Kenu Airframe Pro ($30) has a similar design but is built to accommodate thicker cases and larger phones, noted WIRED tester Simon Hill. The ball-and-socket joint allows 360-degree rotation and also lets you angle your phone for better viewing. It's a bit less sleek, however.
How I Test and Select Car Phone Mounts
Car phone mounts are and are not a sensitive technology. Bulky mounts can block your field of view while driving. And it's a genuine safety hazard if your car mount, or your phone, falls on the floor while you're driving down the freeway.
Every phone mount I and other WIRED testers recommend has been road-tested against this possibility, driven for hours on the road, and on long road trips, over sometimes bumpy roads. Often, I kept as many as eight devices at a time glued to my dash, windshield, and vents so that my car looked like a dollar-store communications center. For the most recent round of testing, this included multiple days of relatively humid, 90-degree Fahrenheit heat.
I pulled suction cups off of dashboards and windshields, over and over, to see if suction cups wore out the first time you had to move a device—or if the cups left residue on the windshield. I tested using multiple models of iPhone, a long folding Motorola Razr, and a large-model Nokia, onto each mount to see how it held up—with or without bulky cases.
I clamped each phone in and out repeatedly, to see how easy it is to remove a phone from the mount. I also turned each mount upside down and shook vigorously to see how violent I had to be to shake the phone loose from its mooring.
Where chargers were involved, I tested the charging capacity with ammeters and phone apps, as well as simply by marking how long it took to charge my phone compared to other chargers. I also tested the MagSafe charging speed vs. the speed if I'd just plugged the phone directly into my preferred USB car charger. (The USB always wins, for multiple reasons.)
For the most recent round of testing, I tested a dozen phone mounts during a sticky summer, selecting both best-selling and best-recommended mounts from both well-known brands and a new breed of hyper-specialized brands like Andobil and Andery that have made their name only on car phone mounts. My colleague Simon Hill likewise tested a dozen mounts in a previous round of testing.
Can Android Phones Use MagSafe and Qi2-Compatible Mounts?
MagSafe is a great technology for the more than half of cell phone owners in the US who use Apple products. The best phone mounts, with the fewest compromises, are pretty much all magnetic mounts.
But alas, most makers of Android phones have been more resistant to adding magnetic mounting capability. The Google Pixel 10 is an exception and offers built-in magnets and native Qi2-compatible charging support. Other phone makers, like Samsung, offer MagSafe-compatible cases for newer models like the Galaxy S26 series.
Some makers of MagSafe mounts offer little stick-on devices meant to affix to your non-magnetic phone. Don't bother with these; they don't work that well and don't stay affixed for long. If you'd like the convenience of a magnetic mount, you're going to have to get a MagSafe-compatible case for your phone. And for this, I refer you to WIRED's guide to the Best MagSafe Accessories.
Honorable Mentions
Belkin 15W MagSafe Mount for $80: This Belkin MagSafe charger and vent mount is an older device we've recommended previously as a top pick—with a secure magnet pad that offers 15-watt Qi2 charging. The mount positions itself in the air vent and blocks airflow a bit, but on summer days with the air-conditioner running, this positioning can help cool your phone while it charges. It's also a little bit sleek but also a bit on the spendy side for what it offers.
Andobil MagSafe Air Vent Mount for $37: This vent-mounted MagSafe device looks like a charger but isn't. The mount's broad, flat surface does stabilize the phone a bit. But in trade, it blocks airflow both to the phone and from the air vent. For these reasons, it's not really my favorite design. But the magnet is strong enough to hold the phone in place, and the vent mount is also stable.
iOttie iTap 3 Air Vent Holder for $16: This compact vent mount from iOttie is low-cost, and the MagSafe mount is strong enough. I can hold this thing upside down and shake it without dislodging my phone. But there's very little range of motion, and the phone can only be mounted where it'll block airflow from the vent. I also tend not to favor mounting mechanisms that use hooks, because it can make the mounts more difficult to remove when needed—though for unusual air vent geometries, the hook might be the only style of vent mount that works.
iOttie One Touch Dash and Windshield Mount for $28: This dash and windshield mount from iOttie was a favorite of WIRED tester Simon Hill when he tested it two years ago. But there's been a design update and some reports of durability issues, so until we test the newest model, I'm leaving this in the honorable mentions.
Vanmass Car Phone Holder for $40: Similar to the Andobil I recommend as a top pick, this Vanmass is a ball-socket mount with options for air vent or dashboard/windshield mounting. But it's a bit bulkier than the Andobil, and the air vent mount is a hook-based mount—which I tend to find more difficult to remove. The suction cup on the dash/windshield mount is ridiculously strong and is unllikely to dislodge even on hot days—and didn't leave residue when I removed it. But while Vanmass advertises “military-grade” tech, whatever this means for a phone mount, the plastic felt a bit flimsy, especially on a vacuum locking mechanism for the suction cup.
Bokilino Car Cup Mount for $16: This is a different sort of phone mount than most I tested: It affixes to a standard cup holder and holds up your phone like a liberty torch from atop a bendable gooseneck stem. This is all well and good when you're driving solo, notes WIRED reviewer Kat Merck, but during longer trips with family, it takes up a much-needed cup holder, and the stem can get in the way. In most cars, you'll have to look a bit too far away from the road to see the screen.
Not Recommended

Danube ports, rail and road can carry 4.5 mln tonnes of exports out of 6 mln that went by sea – infrastructure ministry
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
14:05:33 EEST
20:05:33 KST

Alternative routes covering Danube ports, rail and road logistics make it possible to export about 4.5 million tonnes of cargo per month out of the 6 million tonnes that Ukraine's maritime corridor could handle, First Deputy Minister for Reconstruction, Infrastructure and Transport Serhiy Derkach has told Interfax-Ukraine.
"This figure (4.5 million tonnes) allows us to export… Reports that we have a collapse in exports are not true," Derkach stressed.
He noted that of the total 6 million tonnes of cargo transported via the maritime corridor, about 4 million tonnes consisted of grain, while another 2 million tonnes were mostly various types of metals and iron ore.
According to him, among the alternative routes being developed by the ministry, the Danube ports play an important role — they have already begun operating in an enhanced mode and can handle up to 3 million tonnes of cargo per month.
The first deputy minister confirmed that Russia has intensified attacks on these ports as well, but noted that the ministry is taking additional measures to ensure their continued operation, and that over the past month the Danube ports have already tripled their cargo handling volumes.
The situation could be further improved by restoring round-the-clock operation of Romanian pilots on the Sulina maritime canal, which currently operates only during the day. Talks on this issue are underway with the European Commission and Romania.
The infrastructure ministry is also working with Romania to train Ukrainian pilots who, once certified, will be able to guide vessels through the canal, Derkach added.
He said rail routes can handle the transport of a further 1-1.5 million tonnes of cargo per month, while road transport can handle around 200,000-300,000 tonnes, bringing the total to 4.5 million tonnes.
To increase cross-border road transport, work continues on expanding checkpoints. In particular, a bridge is being built between Ukraine and Moldova in the town of Yampil (Vinnytsia region). There are also plans to open the Yampil-Cuseuti checkpoint as a full-fledged crossing point with a bridge, the first deputy minister said.
He recalled that four lanes for freight transport have already been built at the Porubne-Siret checkpoint on the border with Romania. Once Romania completes matching infrastructure on its side, this will double freight capacity, with an estimated 150 trucks per day able to cross this checkpoint for export.
Overall, the ministry expects to increase capacity along the entire border by 15-20% over the year through the expansion of checkpoint lanes, the first deputy minister said.
Derkach separately noted that this is important not only for exports but also for imports, since road transport accounts for more than 30% of all imports into Ukraine.
At the same time, the first deputy minister acknowledged that alternative routes increase logistics costs.
"If we're talking about oilseeds, for example, this increase in costs isn't as critical for them. For grain, it's unprofitable, because [exporters] will lose money. On the other hand, if you absolutely need to get at least some working capital and move the grain out, then it's possible," Derkach said, describing the situation.
He stressed that the transport situation this year is objectively more difficult than in 2022 and previous years, because Russia has significantly intensified its strikes, deliberately targeting every link in logistics chains — warehouses, ports, bridges, checkpoints, locomotives and even individual vehicles.
According to the Ukrainian Sea Ports Authority (USPA), 185 attacks on ports in Odesa region, 92 attacks on vessels in ports, and 69 attacks on vessels outside ports were recorded from Jan 1 to Aug 24 this year.
Regarding attacks on the railway, according to Ukrzaliznytsia, while the enemy carried out 6,100 attacks over the entire course of the war, more than 1,500 of those took place between Jan 1 and Aug 20 this year alone.

Is Mojtaba Khamenei Dead?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
11:01:56 UTC
20:01:56 KST

Is Mojtaba Khamenei Dead?
The office of Iran’s supreme leader has fallen quiet, fueling uncertainty in a country with decisions to make.
Last Tuesday, Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei hosted a wake for his father and predecessor, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Among the thousands who thronged Tehran’s biggest mosque were the country’s most prominent political figures and several of the elder Khamenei’s sons. One person was notably absent: Mojtaba, the event’s official host.
Almost six months since his anointment, Iran’s supreme leader has been entirely obscured from the public eye. Not a single contemporaneous picture, video, or audio recording of him has been released. Many of the country’s top political leaders admit that they haven’t seen him—among them Abbas Araghchi, Iran’s foreign minister and a member of the National Security Council. IranWire, a London-based opposition outlet, reports that not a single cabinet member has met with Mojtaba since he became supreme leader.
Not even Mojtaba’s close friends and relatives have seen him. Fewer than five people have met with Mojtaba since his ascent to power, Mohammad Hossein Khoshvaght, a former official and a relative of Mojataba’s told me, “due to security precautions.”
The rationale is not implausible. Mojtaba would be a likely target for an Israeli or U.S. air strike, such as the one that killed his father. Direct communication from him could supply Iran’s enemies with clues to his whereabouts. He is also said to have sustained injuries in the February strike on his family that have made public speeches and appearances difficult.
But the totality of Mojtaba’s invisibility and a recent decline in statements from his office have set Tehran abuzz with new rumors of his death. Some sources inside and close to the government speculated to me that Mojtaba recently died from the injuries that he had sustained in February. And irrespective of his actual status, the uncertainty might have major implications for Iran.
“I believe Mojtaba has either passed away or is brain-dead,” a staffer at a government institution in Tehran told me, citing the tailing off of even indirect communication from the leader to the outside world. At least two other government officials told me the same. One said that he believed Mojtaba died or became brain-dead earlier this month.
Two sources in the Iranian government recently told IranWire that word had spread among those at the “highest level of the regime” that Mojtaba was doing very poorly and could die at any moment. About two weeks ago, a public appeal went out on a domestic messaging service, asking Iranians to pray for Mojtaba’s health and sacrifice sheep to bless him, as is customary in Islam. Mojtaba’s life was “under threat,” and some “clerics” had warned that he might be killed, the appeal said.
Since he was appointed, Mojtaba has ruled by decrees disseminated by his office. Iran’s supreme leader is a religious authority in addition to being the head of state, and on July 27, Mojtaba’s office published a list of his answers to practical questions posed by the devout. One correspondent had requested guidance on eating with bleeding gums, because blood is haram—forbidden—in Islam. Any food contaminated with blood, including from one’s own gums, must be thrown out, Mojtaba ruled. If his office is to be believed, then the leader was well enough to ponder Islamic law and issue relevant rulings as recently as a month ago.
The office’s most recent statement came on August 9 and reported that Mojtaba had met with President Masoud Pezeshkian. It didn’t say when the meeting had taken place but noted that it was on the occasion of the president’s third year in office, which puts it on or after July 28. Pezeshkian confirmed to the Iranian media that he spent seven hours with Mojtaba discussing the war and the country’s beleaguered economy. (According to Khoshvaght, Pezeshkian was taken to that meeting “without knowing where it was,” which suggests that he was transported blindfolded, mafia-style.) Also on August 9, Mojtaba issued a slew of decrees, appointing several generals to top military positions and swapping out one of his representatives on the National Security Council. Since then, the office has been silent.
Khoshvaght assured me that Mojtaba is definitely alive. The rumors about the leader’s death are “part of a psychological war hoping to demoralize Iran’s officials and its people, for them to give up to the pressures and threats of America,” he said. He added that the rumors also aim to embolden Iranians opposed to the regime, giving them “courage to come to the streets so that the plans of the U.S. and Israel can be realized.” Abdolreza Davari, a former adviser to the interior ministry and a vocal supporter of Mojtaba’s, told me that the leader is “in full health” and will soon be revealed to the public. But the two weeks with no communication, the public appeal for sheep sacrifice, and the rumors emanating from government circles have led many Iranians to doubt such assurances.
Whether Mojtaba is dead or alive, his public absence creates problems for the Iranian regime. The supreme leader holds most of the constitutional power in the Islamic Republic and has in the past served as the final arbiter among the system’s warring factions and institutions. Mojtaba appears to be sitting these conflicts out, at a moment when their outcome could be particularly consequential.
The country’s 13-person National Security Council is effectively running the country as a collective. It is chaired by Pezeshkian, a reformist who favors an end to the war with America, and includes Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the powerful parliamentary speaker who led the talks with the United States. But it also includes General Ahmad Vahidi, the head of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, and other military leaders.
Back in June, 12 of the council’s 13 members voted in favor of the memorandum of understanding that Iran reached with the United States in Islamabad. Mojtaba sent a message endorsing the deal but also noting that he had initially opposed such an agreement “in principle.” Hard-line critics of diplomacy seized on this to claim that Ghalibaf had usurped power and forced the memorandum on the leader. A news outlet linked to a faction in the IRGC even issued a documentary called Ghalibaf’s Coup.
Mojtaba neither endorsed this view nor put it to rest. Rather, he has remained mum as various factions have purported to speak for him. Pezeshkian has told reporters that in his meeting with Mojtaba, the leader stressed that regime officials should “keep unity and cohesion” and avoid infighting.
But the infighting goes on. In June, a statement signed by 63 of the 88 members of the Assembly of Experts, a clerical body tasked with supervising the supreme leader, admonished regime officials that none of them was authorized to act against Mojtaba’s “definite opinion.” At the same time, the statement called on any Muslim “who could gain access” to kill Donald Trump—not quite the message of Iran’s negotiators, but rather more consonant with Mojtaba’s statements promising “blood revenge.”
The Iranian regime has existential choices to make as it decides between diplomacy and conflict. Iran’s constitution is clear about who has the authority to set the country’s course. But no one seems able to say for sure whether that person is alive or dead. And without a firm hand at the top, indecision can become a purgatory without a foreseeable end.

India faces criticism from UN discrimination watchdog
The UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination says India urgently needs to tackle hate crimes against Bengali-speaking Muslims and increase protections for other groups.
A United Nations watchdog has said India must step up protections for tribal peoples and disadvantaged castes facing extrajudicial killings, torture and other violence by law enforcement.
The UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) also said that the world’s most populous nation urgently needs to tackle hate crimes against Bengali-speaking Muslims.

“The committee was gravely concerned about reports of large-scale violations perpetrated by law enforcement officials against ethnic and ethno-religious groups, Indigenous and Tribal Peoples, including Scheduled Tribes, Scheduled Castes, particularly Dalits, and non-citizens,” it stated in a release on its findings on Tuesday.
“These included racially motivated violence, excessive use of force, extrajudicial killings, arbitrary and prolonged detention without due process, torture, ill-treatment and sexual violence.”
The committee urged India to investigate all such claims and bring those responsible to justice.
Caste remains a major determinant of social status in India, dictating access to resources, education and opportunity. The system, rooted in historic social hierarchical structures, separates Hindus by function and social standing.
CERD is a panel of 18 independent rights experts that monitors compliance with the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination by the 182 countries that are party to it.
Under the convention, which entered into force in 1969, countries must eliminate racial discrimination, eradicate practices of segregation and ensure equality before the law.
India appeared for review before CERD earlier this month, for the first time since 2007, with Solicitor General Tushar Mehta leading its delegation.
The committee pointed to an increase in law enforcement operations targeting Rohingya, Bengali-speaking Muslims, migrants and asylum seekers.
It said police stops and identity checks involving racial profiling had reportedly led to arbitrary arrest and detention without due process, as well as torture and mistreatment.
The committee also expressed concerns about deportations and forced returns of individuals requiring international protection.
It urged India to “urgently address discrimination, hate speech and hate crimes” against these groups, protect their rights and refrain from collective expulsions.
CERD’s opinions and recommendations are non-binding but hold significant reputational weight.
In a statement, India’s mission said that, during the review, its delegation “highlighted our pluralism; diversity; scale and complexity; constitutional and legal framework and safeguards … as we continue our journey towards ensuring equality, dignity and opportunity for all Indians”.

Hong Kong’s Chinese Medicine Hospital to start 24-hour inpatient services in December

The Chinese Medicine Hospital of Hong Kong will launch 24-hour inpatient services in December, the first of its kind in the city, and charge patients HK$980 (US$125) per day for subsidised care, more than three times the fee at public hospitals.
The city’s first dedicated traditional Chinese medicine hospital will also launch 10 additional special disease programmes within this year to help treat conditions such as eczema and Parkinson’s disease.
The hospital, which was opened last December in Tseung Kwan O, aims to provide services for more complex cases under a model that features Chinese medicine as the primary approach, integrated with Western medicine.
The expansion of services, announced on Tuesday, includes the provision of 24-hour inpatient services from December 11.
The hospital will provide 93 inpatient beds – consisting of 60 government-subsidised and 33 non-subsidised ones – as well as 20 beds under its clinical trial and research centre and two high-dependency beds in the first phase. The number of beds is expected to reach 400 by the end of 2030.
The subsidised inpatient option will cost HK$980 a day – a fixed, overall package price that covers all treatment-related services, such as room fee, visits by registered practitioners, Chinese medicine interventions, tests and medication.

Neuroscientists map how early-life scent memories evolve and move through the brain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
11:00:10 UTC
20:00:10 KST

The scent of a particular perfume or a childhood home can often bring back vivid, emotionally charged memories from a person’s earliest years. A recent study on mice suggests that these early-life scent memories are initially stored by specific neurons that develop just after birth, but as time passes and the scent is encountered again, the memory trace relocates to broader networks in the brain. The research, published in PLOS Biology, provides evidence for how the brain encodes, sustains, and eventually reorganizes our most cherished childhood memories.
Scent-triggered memories are a well-documented psychological phenomenon, famously described by Marcel Proust as a flood of vivid nostalgic feelings brought on by the smell of a madeleine cake. In humans, autobiographical memories linked to scents tend to originate from the first decade of life. These memories also tend to carry a much stronger, more positive emotional tone than memories triggered by sights or sounds.
Supporting this idea, a 2016 review indicated that scents tied to positive personal memories have a uniquely powerful impact on a person’s mood, often increasing positive emotions and reducing physiological signs of stress. Despite this well-known emotional potency, the exact ways the brain creates and stores these long-lasting scent memories have remained somewhat mysterious.
When a person or animal smells something, the information first enters the olfactory bulb, a small structure at the front of the brain. Within this structure, specific neurons called granule cells help process the scent. In rodents, a massive wave of these granule cells is born on the very first day of life. Because these neonatal neurons are highly active during childhood and tend to survive for a long time, scientists suspected they might be ideal candidates for storing early-life scent memories.
Memory researchers also know that the brain’s storage systems do not remain static. According to a framework discussed in a 2018 review, memories often shift between different brain areas as time passes. A memory might initially rely on specific regions, like the hippocampus, before being reorganized and transferred to broader networks in the brain’s outer layers.
“I have been interested in odor perception and in the mechanisms of brain plasticity underlying olfactory learning since my PhD in Lyon, and later during my postdoctoral research at Cornell University,” said study author Nathalie Mandairon, a director of research at the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) based at the Lyon Neuroscience Research Center. “This study therefore follows naturally from my previous research.”
“The question that particularly intrigued me was this: during childhood, we are exposed to a multitude of odors,” Mandairon continued. “Why do some of them remain embedded in our memory for decades, while others disappear? And what brain mechanisms allow these very early olfactory memories to persist or resurface later in life?”
To find out, the research team began by surveying 647 adults about their earliest scent-based memories. “We found that this memory generally dated back to childhood, before the age of 10,” Mandairon explained. “They were most often associated with a pleasant odor, but also with a particularly positive, sometimes joyful, context.”
“In most cases, the experience had also been repeated several times during childhood,” she added. “Based on these observations, we developed a mouse model to investigate the brain mechanisms involved in the formation and long-term maintenance of this early olfactory memory.”
During the mouse equivalent of childhood, the researchers placed the animals in a large, enriched cage filled with toys, tunnels, and opportunities for social interaction. They paired this playful environment with a specific attractive odorant over five separate sessions. Microphones recorded the mice emitting a higher number and frequency of high-pitched squeaks, known as ultrasonic vocalizations, which indicates a positive emotional state.
When the mice reached young adulthood, at two months of age, the researchers tested their reactions to the childhood odorant. The mice that had experienced the scent in the playful environment spent more time investigating it compared to a control group that had smelled the same scent in a standard, non-playful cage.
To understand what was happening in the brain at this two-month mark, the researchers looked at granule cells born on the mice’s first day of life. “Our results revealed an important role for neurons in the olfactory bulb that are generated at birth,” Mandairon said. “These neurons are highly plastic and, together with the brain’s reward system, contribute to the memory of an odor learned very early in life.”
To test whether these neurons were strictly necessary for the memory, the scientists used optogenetics, a technique that allows researchers to turn specific brain cells on or off using light. When they used light to temporarily silence these early-born granule cells, the mice no longer showed a preference for the childhood scent.
The researchers also examined broader brain activity in the young adult mice. They found that smelling the childhood odorant triggered highly synchronized activity between the brain’s reward centers and memory systems. This network included areas like the dorsal hippocampus, which is involved in detailed memories, and the medial prefrontal cortex, which handles complex decision-making.
Next, the team investigated how this memory held up as the mice aged into later adulthood, at six months old. “We also found that, later in life, mice retained the memory of this odor only if they had been occasionally re-exposed to it during adulthood,” Mandairon told PsyPost. “Without such re-exposure, their preference for that particular odor disappeared.”
However, if the researchers briefly re-exposed the mice to the scent every three weeks, the positive memory persisted at six months of age. Surprisingly, this long-lasting memory no longer relied on the neonatal granule cells in the olfactory bulb. The light-based silencing technique that worked at two months had no effect at six months.
The researchers had expected a brain structure so directly involved in processing odors to continue playing a central role in olfactory memory. “Instead, over time, other brain circuits, particularly those associated with emotions, seem to take over,” Mandairon said.
“What is particularly interesting is that the brain circuits supporting the memory appear to change over time,” she explained. “In adulthood, the contribution of the olfactory bulb and the reward system decreases, while regions of the limbic system, which is strongly involved in emotions, become more important. In other words, the memory can persist, but the brain mechanisms supporting it seem to evolve throughout life.”
These network shifts are in line with a study covered by PsyPost in 2016, which found that early-life memories in young rats persist into adulthood as latent traces that can be reactivated by later reminder cues. The findings also align with another 2016 study covered by PsyPost, which found that worms form lifelong olfactory memories using specialized neural circuits. It is worth noting, however, that both of those previous studies examined the formation of aversive memories in response to threats, whereas the current study measured the development of positive odor associations in mice.
One detail to keep in mind is that modeling human autobiographical memory in rodents comes with inherent limitations. “Although the anatomical and functional organization of the olfactory system shares many similarities between mice and humans, the study was conducted using a mouse model,” Mandairon cautioned. “Our study primarily allows us to identify general principles and brain mechanisms that can then be investigated further in humans.”
Moving forward, the research team hopes to uncover the specific conditions that make some scent associations permanent while others fade. “We would like to determine whether there is a common ‘recipe’ that allows an odor encountered during childhood to become a memory that stays with us for a lifetime: what the odor was, the context in which it was encountered, who we were with, the emotions we experienced,” Mandairon said.
The study, “Positive early-life olfactory memory is rooted in the olfactory bulb and triggers large-scale changes beyond the olfactory system,” was authored by Jules Dejou, Anna Athanassi, Théo Brunel, Marc Thevenet, Anne Didier, and Nathalie Mandairon.
