A second chance: The uncertainty &amp; struggle behind India's organ transplant boom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:38:58 UTC
19:38:58 KST

India’s transplant system has grown rapidly, from 4,990 transplants in 2013 to 20,138 in 2025. But for a patient, a transplant is far more than a surgical procedure. It is a journey through medical tests, clearances, documentation, waiting, uncertainty, organ matching and, eventually, surgery and lifelong follow-up.Transplant hospitals and coordinators are at the centre of this system, working within the wider network of the National Organ and Tissue Transplant Organisation (NOTTO), Regional Organ and Tissue Transplant Organisations (ROTTOs) and State Organ and Tissue Transplant Organisations (SOTTOs).Yet statistics and institutional structures can obscure what the process actually feels like for the person waiting for an organ. For recipients such as Hemant Kumar Thakur and Shrishti Sinha, the reality is one of uncertainty, exhaustion and fear — followed by the possibility of a second chance at life.
India's organ transplant system works through a three-tier hierarchical network coordinated by NOTTO, ROTTO, and SOTTO
The journey begins before surgery
A patient with advanced organ failure is first evaluated at a registered transplant centre. The assessment can involve blood tests, imaging, organ-specific investigations and evaluation by a multidisciplinary team. If found medically suitable, the patient is registered in the relevant transplant system.
Being on a waiting list, however, does not simply mean waiting in chronological order. Allocation depends on the organ and applicable rules, including factors such as medical urgency, compatibility and, for some organs, time spent on the list. NOTTO’s framework also provides for urgent and super-urgent categories. For kidney patients, for instance, time on dialysis is among the factors considered.
Live Kidneys lead India’s transplant numbers.
NOTTO coordinates the system nationally, while ROTTOs and SOTTOs connect regional and state-level transplant activity. The State Appropriate Authority separately oversees regulatory compliance, including the registration of transplant centres and adherence to legal and ethical requirements.For recipients, however, the elaborate network can feel much simpler: a long wait, a stream of tests and paperwork, and the constant question of what happens next.
“The process is not smooth”
Hemant Kumar Thakur, from Jamshedpur, Jharkhand, underwent a kidney transplant at Apollo Hospitals in Kolkata, with his wife, Kanchan Mala, donating a kidney. For him, the hardest part was not the operation but navigating the process beforehand.Because he lived in Jharkhand while the transplant took place in West Bengal, Hemant had to deal with inter-state approvals and paperwork.“Because the procedure involved two different states — Jharkhand and West Bengal — I had to obtain No Objection Certificates (NOCs) from both states before the transplant could proceed,” he said.
The transplant journey begins long before the operating room, with a long road of tests, paperwork and waiting.
Despite the difficulties, Hemant was fortunate to have a compatible donor within his family.“The process is not smooth; it is quite challenging. I was lucky that the match was found within my own family, with my wife,” he said.His experience also made him aware of the uncertainty faced by patients without a matching family donor. He recalled seeing patients who had found donors and completed much of the paperwork, only for the donor to later withdraw.“After going through the entire process, they were back where they had started — back to square one,” he said.
Consent can change the course
India’s transplant framework is governed by the Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act, 1994 (THOTA) and related rules. Organ donation must be voluntary and free from commercial dealings, while transplantation is permitted only through authorised institutions.Dr Ankur Garg, GI Surgeon and Liver Transplant Specialist at Paras Health in Gurugram, says legitimate organisations and transplant coordinators play an important role in educating patients, facilitating listing and supporting families when brain-stem death is declared.But he warns that patients can also be targeted by unscrupulous intermediaries.“There will always be unsocial elements, touts, agents in society luring needy patients and families and giving false hopes and promises of early organ allocation, lesser waiting times and so much extra,” he said.Consent can also change during the donation process. Dr Garg explains that once brain-stem death has been declared and the family consents to donation, the process of identifying eligible recipients begins. But consent can still be withdrawn before organ retrieval.“Before wheeling into the operation theatre where organ harvesting happens, anyone can withdraw consent, and the whole process will stop,” he said.For recipients, that possibility can mean losing an organ they had been preparing to receive and returning to the uncertainty of the waiting list.
Once an organ is allocated, the recipient is prepared for surgery and then closely monitored for complications and organ function
Living donation: another route, but not a simple one
Not every patient has to depend on a deceased donor. Certain organs, particularly kidneys and part of the liver, can be donated by living donors after medical, legal and ethical evaluation.The donor’s compatibility and health are assessed, while the legal process depends partly on the relationship between donor and recipient. Near-relative donations follow the applicable framework, while other living-donor relationships may require scrutiny by an Authorisation Committee.Dr Garg says a patient cannot simply register at multiple centres and wait for whichever offers an organ first.“As per the rule, any patient is allowed to register at one place only. Under NOTTO guidelines and Indian transplant regulations, a patient cannot be registered on a deceased donor waiting list at multiple hospitals or centres simultaneously,” he said.He said the listing process requires a medical summary, blood group, relevant reports and valid Aadhaar or national identification.
Following the surgery, transplant centres also continue monitoring recipient information and clinical status.
The surgery is only the beginning
Once an organ is allocated, the recipient is prepared for surgery and then closely monitored for complications and organ function. But leaving the hospital does not mean leaving the transplant journey behind.Recipients must take prescribed immunosuppressive medicines consistently, attend follow-up appointments and undergo regular investigations. Transplant centres also continue monitoring recipient information and clinical status.Hemant said his own transplant was comparatively smooth once the approvals and paperwork were completed, but the financial and medical commitments continued.He spent approximately Rs 15–20 lakh on the transplant and related treatment in 2020.“I do not have any additional complications. I just go for routine check-ups every six months and have to take medication for the rest of my life,” he said.He currently spends around Rs 7,000–8,000 a month on medicines, although he noted that aftercare and medication costs vary between patients.Hemant also contrasted the long-term experience of the recipient with that of his living donor, his wife.“The donor has to take medicines for about three months after the transplant and can lead a normal life,” he said.
The emotional toll of transplantation
Shrishti Sinha, an engineer who now works as a freelancer in Delhi, describes her transplant journey through a different lens: uncertainty, gratitude, fear and the possibility of rebuilding a future.
“There are many moments of uncertainty. There are medical tests, clearances, waiting for updates and constantly wondering what comes next,” she says.Even hope was fragile.“Not completely. As if one moment hope was rising, the next it was gone. There were cases more severe than mine, or someone who had a higher percentage of surviving,” she recalls.Shrishti underwent treatment at R&R Hospital in Delhi and remembers her doctors as a source of encouragement.“It was R&R Hospital, Delhi, and the doctors were positive and kept trying to cheer me up,” she says.When she finally realised she would receive an organ, her response was deeply personal.“I was crying and feeling grateful that I was going to live, that I would get to spend more time with my husband and create a future,” she recalls.
Recovery brings a new set of challenges
The transplant did not instantly restore normal life. Shrishti found recovery difficult, from eating and drinking to physiotherapy.“Recovery was not straightforward. There were challenges with eating, drinking and physiotherapy. Seeing the scar for the first time was scary,” she says.There were unexpected experiences, too.“The weirdest thing was having strange cravings that I never used to have,” she recalls.Five years later, however, she says the biggest change is her ability to think beyond her illness.“The biggest change is that I can think about the future again. Before the transplant, so much of my life revolved around my health and whether my condition would deteriorate further.”
She now marks the day of her operation as something more than a medical milestone.“Five years later, I have started treating my operation day as my second birthday, a chance to live,” she says.
Behind every transplant statistic is a patient who has waited, a donor who has made an extraordinary decision, and a family navigating a system in which every clearance, consent and organ offer can change the course of a life.
Beyond the numbers
India’s transplant system may be measured in hospitals, registries, waiting lists and annual numbers. But for the person inside it, transplantation is much more intimate: months of paperwork, uncertainty and waiting, followed by surgery and the lifelong responsibility of protecting the new organ.Behind every transplant statistic is a patient who has waited, a donor who has made an extraordinary decision, and a family navigating a system in which every clearance, consent and organ offer can change the course of a life.For recipients like Hemant and Shrishti, the transplant is ultimately not just about surviving. It is about being able to imagine tomorrow again.
Subhadra Srivastava is a journalist with The Times of India, covering geopolitics, international and national affairs. With over three years of experience, she focuses on national and global developments, conflict, diplomacy and their impact on India. Her work combines breaking news with in-depth analysis, offering readers context and clarity on the stories shaping the world.

Hansen to farmers: 'Difficult summer amid heat and drought, EU stands by you'
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
12:38:39 CEST
19:38:39 KST

"This summer is particularly
difficult for farmers in the European Union, and especially in
Italy, with more extreme and frequent heat and drought and
increasingly frequent wildfires in several regions.
                                    
                                       
				I know how much these events are putting farmers to the test,
and in these difficult times, the European Commission stands by
them." This was the message from EU Agriculture Commissioner
Christophe Hansen, in a statement paying "tribute to farmers who
continue to work in these difficult conditions, despite the
uncertainty affecting their crops and production".
                                    
                                       
				The Luxembourgish politician recalled that the Common
Agricultural Policy "is already mobilising billions of euros to
support farmers in adapting to and mitigating the effects of
climate change. We will continue these efforts," he assured. He
also pointed out that when extreme weather conditions, such as
drought, "affect their crops or livestock", Member States "can
recognise such situations as cases of force majeure", allowing
farmers to receive the CAP payments to which they are entitled
even when they are unable to meet certain requirements due to
exceptional circumstances. The Commissioner also recalled that
Member States can "reallocate funds within their CAP plans to
help restore agricultural production potential in areas affected
by wildfires".

EU agri-food exports to US plunge 13% between January and May
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
12:35:42 CEST
19:35:42 KST

Between January and May, the EU
recorded a sharp contraction in agri-food exports to the United
States, down 13% (€1.6 billion) compared with the same period in
2025.
                                    
                                       
				The figure comes from the European Commission's regular
monitoring report on agri-food trade. Brussels notes that the
decline in exports follows "high levels" of exports in the first
months of 2025, when companies sought to bring shipments forward
ahead of the US tariffs that had been announced. The most
significant declines were recorded in beverages, olive oil and
cocoa products.
                                    
                                       
				Overall, in May the EU exported €19.3 billion worth of agri-food
products, down 5% compared with the previous month and 4%
compared with the same period last year. Since January,
cumulative exports have reached €96.9 billion, 3% below last
year's level (-€3.0 billion). Cumulative imports also fell by
5%, reaching €77.5 billion, compared with the same period of the
previous year. Despite the contraction in both imports and
exports, the report shows that in the first five months of the
year, the EU agri-food trade surplus reached €19.4 billion, €1
billion more than in the previous year.

US troops a liability for some Kuwaitis amid Iran fury: ‘we’re paying the price’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:35:33 UTC
19:35:33 KST

US troops a liability for some Kuwaitis amid Iran fury: ‘we’re paying the price’
‘Targeting locations where the Americans are stationed has created fear and anxiety among residents,’ a Kuwaiti national says
Like many Kuwaitis, Ghanim Alsulaimani still vividly remembers Iraqi tanks rolling through his hometown when his small Gulf state faced extinction had US troops not liberated it from invasion.
Now, decades later and six months into the US-Iran war, some are seeing those same American troops as more of a liability than an asset, as their presence has put Kuwait in Tehran’s line of fire.
Since the Middle East conflict first erupted in late February with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, the Islamic Republic and its allies have hammered Kuwait with recurrent barrages.
They have targeted civilian infrastructure, including water desalination plants and energy installations, along with bases hosting American troops.
Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz has put Kuwait, which is locked into the waterway and relies on oil exports for revenue, in a difficult economic position.
Yet Alsulaimani continues to stand by the United States, even as talks to end the war have stalled, weighing on Gulf economies.

In Poland, eight men beat three Ukrainians; the attacker wanted to give a &quot;lecture on Volhynia&quot; — media
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
13:33:54 EEST
19:33:54 KST

In Poland, eight men beat three Ukrainians; the attacker wanted to give a "lecture on Volhynia" — media
Kyiv • UNN
In Radom, eight men attacked three Ukrainians, who suffered head and facial injuries. One of the attackers faces up to five years in prison.
In Poland, eight people attacked three Ukrainians; the attacker wanted to give them a "lecture on Volhynia," reports Onet Wiadomości, writes UNN.
Details
According to reports, a drunk 34-year-old man attacked three 20-year-old Ukrainians in Radom and began asking them about their origins and the Volhynia tragedy. Seven more men then joined the Pole, and together they carried out the attack, the publication writes.
The incident occurred on August 2 between 5 and 6 a.m. on Malczewskiego Street in Radom, but the media reported it only several days later.
"Tomasz G., a 34-year-old resident of Lublin, came to Radom for a wedding, but after it ended, he began wandering around the city. He met three young Ukrainians on Malczewskiego Street. He started a conversation with them, asking where they were from. An exchange of remarks followed. However, he did not like their answer. They, in turn, reported that he wanted to give them a lecture on Volhynia. A verbal misunderstanding arose, and at that moment [...] the resident of Lublin called over three or four young men who were crossing the street and told them that they were Ukrainians. They reacted very energetically to this, and the attack began," prosecutor Cezary Ołtarzewski from the local prosecutor's office told MójRadom.
As the publication notes, "several more attackers later joined in beating the Ukrainians, bringing the total number of attackers to eight."
"The Ukrainians sustained injuries, mainly to their heads and faces. Forensic medical experts thoroughly examined them," the publication states.
In an interview with Gazeta Wyborcza, the prosecutor added that after the incident Tomasz G. "ordered a taxi and left as if nothing had happened."
According to reports, the police managed to establish the identity of the main attacker. He has already been taken to the prosecutor's office and charged with using violence or making unlawful threats for discriminatory reasons, as well as participating in a brawl or assault. He pleaded guilty and provided detailed explanations. Among other things, he stated that he had been under the influence of alcohol. He was placed under police supervision. He faces up to five years in prison.
The search for the other participants in the brawl is ongoing. Police are examining city surveillance footage. The situation is reportedly complicated by the fact that the detainee did not know the other attackers.

Washington Post ordered to rehire fired columnist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:33:10 UTC
19:33:10 KST

This file photo shows former Washington Post columnist Karen Attiah. (AP photo)
The Washington Post was ordered on Aug. 24 to reinstate columnist Karen Attiah, who was fired over social media posts she wrote in the aftermath of right-wing influencer Charlie Kirk’s assassination.
Kirk was shot dead last September on a Utah college campus, sparking a wave of grief among conservatives and threats of a clampdown on the “radical left” from President Donald Trump.
Attiah wrote on social media afterward that she would not display sadness for Kirk’s killing and shared the activist’s past racist comments about Black women.
She was later fired, with the Post accusing her of “gross misconduct” and of violating its social media policies, according to the paper’s own reporting.
An arbitrator ordered the Post on Aug. 24 to rehire Attiah and compensate her with back pay, writing in the decision that the Post “did not have good and sufficient cause” for her dismissal.
Attiah wrote on X that she was “happy” at the decision, saying she had been forced out for “speaking the truth.”
The Post said it respected the arbitration process but declined to comment further.
Attiah had worked at the publication for 11 years and noted that she was the “last remaining Black full-time opinion columnist at the Post” at the time of her firing.
In her posts about Kirk, she shared his racist claims that Black women lack “brain processing power” and therefore require help from diversity programs.

Optoma GT2400HDR Review: Ace Projector for Golf Simulation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:32:00 UTC
19:32:00 KST

This Optoma laser projector is great for setting up a golf simulator in your living room, but mediocre video quality makes it less appealing for home entertainment.
Great for golf simulation. Continuous operation. Light and portable. Affordable. Easy to configure using the remote.
TIRED
No built-in smart TV OS. Outdated HDMI ports. Passable performance for home entertainment and gaming. Confusing remote for everything but the initial setup.
Indoor golf simulators aren't easy to set up, and they aren't inexpensive. It starts with a home cinema projector, but you also need a wide, open space for swinging clubs, a backdrop with netting, and a gaming laptop or desktop to run the software. I was on a mission to see if I could do this much more cheaply with an affordable projector.
I accomplished my goal successfully by building around the Optoma GT2400HDR short-throw projector. I skipped the most expensive components, like the backdrop and the clubs. Instead, I used a gaming laptop and controller I already owned, and played EA Sports PGA Tour, which is included with my PC Game Pass Ultimate account. While the projector isn’t a bad option for playing golf at home on the cheap, it’s not ideal for watching movies and TV shows. It also struggles with high-octane games, and it doesn’t even include a smart TV platform.
Made for Indoor Driving Ranges
Optoma describes the GT2400HDR as a laser-based short-throw projector designed for gaming, entertainment, and golf simulation (the latter being my main intention). It can project a screen size from 30 to 300 inches at Full HD 1080p (1920 x 1080) resolution. My goal in creating an indoor driving range was to keep costs as low as possible, so I planned to use my Xbox controller with a gaming laptop and play on a 100-inch screen while still feeling like I was out on the links. For a golf game, you can get by with a midrange computer or even use a golf sim app on your iPad. (To do that, you’ll need to cast to a device that supports AirPlay or connect through HDMI via an adapter.)
Photograph: John Brandon
For less than $1,300, the GT2400HDR is a reasonable option, especially since it works well as a basic golf sim and costs far less than 4K models that can run $5,000 or more. The GT2400HDR also has some interesting perks that make it ideal for long golfing sessions.
For starters, it’s rated for 24/7 continuous operation. That’s because the laser light source doesn’t need to cool down after a few hours and can last 30,000 hours total. (Optoma does recommend powering the unit off when not in use, though.) The laser light source does not use a bulb, so there is nothing to replace. Heat dissipation is amazingly good, as the projector tends to run cool, unlike some high-end models. The GT2400HDR has an IP6X dust rating, so it’s sealed better than some massive home theater projectors that cost $4,000—ironic, considering that if you’re spending that much, you would expect better dust protection.
The projector's light weight (just under 7 pounds) and portability make it a good match for golf simulation. I found it easy to position the projector on the floor and then use it on a table or even in another room without lugging it around like a massive brick.
I first had to figure out where to place it for the golf sim, though. As a short-throw projector, it should normally sit about 4 feet away from the screen. Since I wouldn’t be using actual golf clubs, I could set it on the floor in my windowless testing room; otherwise, I would have to mount it on the ceiling, away from swinging clubs. The projected image looked big enough that, when I started playing EA Sports PGA Tour, the players looked about as tall as they are in real life.
Photograph: John Brandon
I noticed Optoma offers an app to help with initial setup, but it’s a hassle to use. You have to install the app and sync over Bluetooth, but I found it was easier to just do the keystone adjustment with the included remote. (Also, Optoma did not include the required Bluetooth dongle even though it is normally part of the package.)
Fortunately, keystoning was easy with the remote because, during setup, you can just position the four corners of the image. I ran one HDMI cable for my laptop and one for an AV receiver for surround sound (I used a Yamaha RX300A). In less than 30 minutes, I had the projector running, and I was swinging with the pros at Augusta.
I will say, I had an absolute blast with the setup. I loved the massive screen for golf, and I was pleased I didn’t have to bother with golf clubs, a backdrop screen, netting, or anything else to replicate the experience. If you want to use real clubs and balls, there are quite a few golf sim apps like SkyTrak for both PC and tablets that scan your motion and render a virtual player, although the total cost can add up quickly, including the backdrop and other gear.
Even though I was using a controller to play a video game, I still felt like I was on the links because of the massive size, bright 4,200-lumen rating, and colorful picture.
Photograph: John Brandon
The GT2400HDR only runs at 1080p resolution, but it does so at low latency (only 8.4 milliseconds at 120 Hz). I wasn’t expecting home cinema quality at this price, and golf simulations don’t require subtle color variations like a theatrical movie, which might have scenes that take place at night. You need accurate greens and blues, and the GT2400HDR handled that well.
There are two HDMI ports, which is fairly common, but the projector does not support the latest HDMI 2.1 standard for eARC passthrough audio. That means no Dolby Vision, and if you connect an AV receiver, you could run into compatibility issues. For example, I tried using my Onkyo receiver and had some minor audio glitches.
The projector also doesn’t support Wi-Fi unless you add a streaming device like a Google TV or an Amazon Fire TV. It has a legacy VGA port if your device is still in the dark ages (e.g., an extremely old computer, but in reality it is still widely used for signage, in schools, and as a fail-safe port), both a 3.5-mm input and output, and (in another unusual twist) a 3D Sync port for connecting 3D glasses (which I didn’t test).
Photograph: John Brandon
The remote has one of the most confusing layouts of any projector I have used. It seems like it was designed for a bygone A/V era. There are way too many buttons, and they're very small. There are so many buttons that it all seemed like overkill, especially since you may only use those buttons occasionally. Indeed, once everything is running, I didn’t find the need to use the remote that often.
Performance off Course
Outside of golf simulation, the GT2400HDR was just average in just about every other way. I ran a few typical benchmarks, and the skin tone tests all looked bland and grayed out, as though every face looked the same. There just wasn’t enough dynamic tonal range. In a demo video, mist over a mountain scene blended into the white background and did not look distinct. In a scene involving a fence with green grass in the background—one of the best ways to test color quality—the GT2400HDR made everything look way too brown.
For movies, I watched a scene in The Batman with flares that look shockingly red on higher-end projectors like the Xgimi Titan Noir Max. Here, the reds were too dark, lacked shadow detail, and blended too much into the dark background. In a scene from the 4K Ultra Blu-ray version of Blade Runner 2049, where the main character arrives at a protein farm, several buildings should have rendered in distinct yellows and blues. Instead, the scene looked too grayed out, like a thin veneer covered the entire screen. Of course, it didn’t help that the 4K movie had to be downgraded to 1080p resolution.
Photograph: John Brandon
I won’t harp on these detriments too much, because the GT2400HDR is not meant to compete with a movie theater. I switched to a few more games and found that Red Dead Redemption 2 on an Xbox Series X looked pretty good, if a little too atmospheric. That’s a kind way of saying the contrast is not great. At times, it seemed like the projected image had more in common with an LCD computer monitor than a home cinema projector.
The GT2400HDR disappointed in its handling of what should be impressive updated graphics in Halo: Campaign Evolved. Instead of rich, vibrant-looking trees, they looked too bland, with flat, dull greens. In Assassin’s Creed: Black Flag Resynced, the colors in a level that takes place in Havana should pop when you walk through the town, but the blue tunics, yellow fruit, and green trees lacked vibrancy.
A news broadcast looked dull and bland, as did a World Cup match I rewatched. There’s a theme here: bland and dull colors. However, I was surprised that a dark scene of a character riding a bike in the movie Awake didn’t look terrible. I could make out faces and some colors, which is saying a lot since this scene is hard to render. An entire moonlit scene in House of the Dragon, via the HBO app on a Google TV Streamer, looked completely washed out until I switched to the Vivid picture mode, which helped a bit. It was all par for the course, no pun intended.
I then watched scenes from Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 and noticed that Cinema picture mode did help punch up the colors a bit. Super Mario Galaxy lacked the color vibrancy and clarity that it normally has and looked like it was playing on a cheap computer monitor (e.g., poor contrast and less-than-vivid colors). When I switched to The Ark on YouTube TV, the colors looked much better because the show features bright, well-lit interior shots in almost every scene.
In the end, everything I tested and benchmarked on the GT2400HDR looked just OK, but I liked how well this projector works as a golf simulator. It can run all day long for multiple rounds, has low latency to make sure your controller nudges translate to accurate drives, and looks massive and bright on a large projector screen in a dark room. Sure, just about everything else is average, but if you are into golf, this is a good low-cost entry-level option.

Vande Mataram row: Is Congress taking a calculated gamble or walking into BJP's trap?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:27:32 UTC
19:27:32 KST

Vande Mataram row: Is Congress taking a calculated gamble or walking into BJP's trap?
Kunal Varma / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 25, 2026, 16:06 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Mallikarjun Kharge, Sonia Gandhi and Rahul at Congress headquarters on Independence Day.
NEW DELHI: Is the Congress trying to send out a subtle message signalling “soft minority appeasement”? Or has the party played to BJP’s strength by lapping up a controversy that may push it into a corner?The Congress's decision to sing only two stanzas of Vande Mataram at party events signalled a rare hardening of stance on an issue that the party knows could make it vulnerable to attacks over both minority appeasement and nationalism.As expected, the Congress decision, which cited a 1937 resolution, triggered sharp reactions from the BJP, with Union home minister Amit Shah accusing the Congress of repeating "politics of appeasement."
Union Minister JP Nadda also slammed the Congress, alleging that the party's 1937 resolution was driven by "appeasement politics" and contributed to the circumstances that led to the Partition. In a post on X, Nadda said the Congress' decision in 1937 to divide 'Vande Mataram' into two parts fuelled the two-nation theory and ultimately led to the partition of the country.'This was followed by attacks questioning Congress’s commitment to nationalism and patriotism.Union Minister Giriraj Singh accused the Congress leadership of disrespecting the legacy of India's freedom fighters and operating under ideological pressure. "This is not just opposition to Vande Mataram but against our revolutionaries," Singh said, adding, "Now, the Congress has become the Muslim League. This is not Gandhi ji's Congress but Sonia Gandhi and Rahul Gandhi's Congress," the BJP leader said.
BJP MP Dinesh Sharma also accused the opposition leadership of harbouring "Muslim League-like thinking." He equated senior Congress leaders with Muhammad Ali Jinnah, the founder of Pakistan who spearheaded the Two-Nation Theory, to criticise the Congress party's approach toward national symbols.Later, the BJP passed a resolution condemning the Congress Working Committee's decision to sing only the first two stanzas of 'Vande Mataram' and announced a nationwide campaign to raise awareness about the history and significance of the National Song.No surprises here. All these attacks were on expected lines. Surely, the Congress would have anticipated these high-pitched narratives questioning its nationalism and accusing it of appeasement.
Congress fights back
Congress leaders defended the party's stand, saying 'Vande Mataram' was associated with the freedom struggle and held emotional significance for the Congress. They accused the BJP of politicising the issue and diverting attention from the issue of Ram Mandir donation theft."BJP was not a part of the freedom struggle. Vande Mataram was a part of the freedom struggle; it is emotional for us, but political for them (BJP)," Venugopal said, adding, "We have been reciting Vande Mataram since 1937, more than 90 years. What is new for us?"The Congress leaders alleged that political rivals led by the BJP were deliberately stoking nationalist narratives to cover up their failures. What the Congress perhaps did not realise, or chose to ignore, was that the BJP had already set the stage for bringing Vande Mataram to the centrestage of its politics.Why the 1937 reference created more problems than it solvedBankim Chandra Chatterjee wrote ‘Bande Mataram’ in the late 19th century in Sanskritised Bengali. The original version consisted of six stanzas. The song was first inserted into the pages of his novel, Anandamath, set during the late 18th century when famine and rebellion tore through Bengal.In 1950, alongside ‘Jana Gana Mana’ as the national anthem, Vande Mataram received the honour of a national song following a decision of the Constituent Assembly, under the guidance of Rajendra Prasad, considering the historic role it played in India’s freedom struggle.However, only the first two stanzas of the song were adopted as the national song.The Congress Working Committee (CWC), in a resolution of October 29, 1937, decided that only the first two stanzas of Vande Mataram would be sung at national and public gatherings.This had followed advice from Rabindranath Tagore, who was the first to set Vande Mataram to music and publicly sing it at the 1896 Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress. In a letter to Jawaharlal Nehru, he suggested that only the first two stanzas of the song be used for public and national gatherings.Tagore then noted that the later verses — which invoked Hindu deities like Durga within the context of Bankim Chandra Chatterjee's novel Anandamath—could alienate non-Hindu communities.The fact that the Muslim League and M A Jinnah were among the most vociferous critics of the song made the Congress’s 1937 resolution vulnerable to Muslim appeasement attacks ever since.
BJP’s Vande Mataram push
BJP’s Vande Mataram push began in May this year when the Union Cabinet approved a proposal to amend the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act and put the National Song, Vande Mataram, composed by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee, on the same footing as the National Anthem, Jana Gana Mana.It was during the special discussion of Parliament on “150th Year of Vande Mataram” in December last year that defence minister Rajnath Singh had strongly advocated for elevating the status of Vande Mataram to match the National Anthem. Rajnath had then accused the Congress of historically communalising the song and sidelining it due to appeasement politics.Earlier in January this year the Union home ministry had outlined appropriate conduct and protocols concerning Vande Mataram. The ministry had issued an order that all six stanzas of the official version must be rendered first whenever the National Song and the National Anthem are performed together. It said that the full six-stanza version was to be sung or played on key state occasions.These proposals became law in the just-concluded Monsoon session after Parliament amended the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971, giving Vande Mataram equal legal standing to the National Anthem. The government is also midway through a year-long commemoration of Vande Mataram's 150th anniversary.The amended Act mandates Vande Mataram shall be honoured equally with ‘Jana-Gana-Mana’ and shall have equal status with it, and whoever intentionally prevents the singing of the Indian National Anthem or causes disturbance to any assembly engaged in such singing shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or both.
Could Congress have avoided this row
Clearly, given the BJP moves, the Congress would have been aware of the political fallout of its Vande Mataram decision. Minority appeasement has been one of the biggest weapons, which the BJP has used very effectively to attack and corner the Congress.In the last 12 years, we have seen the Congress suffer politically over allegations of minority appeasement. The Congress leadership has tried to fight back with a calculated push for soft Hindutva. Rahul Gandhi and other top Congress leaders have visited temples to counter BJP’s attacks on minority appeasement.In the 1980s, the Congress faced a Shah Bano moment, which is still used to target and corner the party over allegations of minority appeasement. The then Congress government led by Rajiv Gandhi enacted a law in Parliament to limit a Muslim husband's maintenance obligation to the three-month iddat period, neutralizing a Supreme Court maintenance order under Section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC).Minorities, especially Muslims, for a very long time were part of Congress’s core vote bank and supported the party electorally. However, as the Congress lost political heft, the minorities gradually shifted to other regional parties. The same happened with other social groups like the SCs, STs and the OBCs. For the last many years, the Congress has been forced to align with the regional parties that weaned away its core voters. Now, as it tries to script its revival, it is trying to win back these communities into the party fold.We have seen Rahul Gandhi aggressively woo the SCs, STs and the OBCs by repeatedly taking up issues that impact them. The Congress leader’s sustained pitch for caste census was an open move to reach out to these core voters. But when it comes to wooing back the minority voters, the Congress perhaps wants to play it safe. And it’s not just the Muslim appeasement attack that the Congress wants to avoid, it perhaps also does not want to antagonize its ally in Uttar Pradesh - the Samajwadi Party.
Interestingly, Rahul and Akhilesh Yadav appeal to the same social support base and hence the alliance chemistry is always overshadowed by competing interests.It is in this context that one is left wondering: Has the Congress taken a calculated gamble?

Chinese ship caught with banned shark fins in Pacific Ocean in operation involving U.S. Coast Guard
Kiribati, a tiny Pacific neighbor to Hawaii that has grown ties with Beijing, detained a Chinese vessel this month for illegally harvesting shark fins, its maritime police told AFP.
The practice of cutting fins off live sharks and throwing the carcasses back into the sea is banned in much of the Pacific Ocean, but persists due to demand in East and Southeast Asia.
The Chinese ship was among four vessels detained in a surveillance crackdown by 11 Pacific island nations between Aug. 3 to Aug. 14, assisted by the U.S. Coast Guard in some areas and an Australian military aircraft. Kiribati, however, operates its own patrol boat.
The vessel was licensed to travel through Kiribati's waters but was detained by the maritime police after inspectors found shark fins on board, commander Tom Redfern told AFP.
"It was escorted back to Christmas Island for further investigation," he said, referring to a large atoll belonging to Kiribati and located south of Hawaii.
Kiribati has an exclusive economic zone spanning 1.4 million square miles of ocean, and has drawn interest from Chinese state companies since switching diplomatic ties from Taiwan in 2019.
It also hosts Chinese police, a decision the United States has said risks fueling regional tensions.
"A Kiribati Police maritime boarding officer, not under a shiprider agreement, boarded and inspected it, finding that the vessel was breaching its condition of license by keeping and retaining shark fins onboard," said Redfern.
Kiribati has recently strengthened cooperation with France, with French military personnel due to arrive next month on Christmas Island to rebuild local police stations.
The practice of removing shark fins is banned across the region.
The cruelty behind the shark fin trade is well-documented. Shark finning often involves slicing fins off live sharks and discarding the mutilated animals back into the ocean, where they die from blood loss, suffocation or predation.
"Hard to detect"
Andrew Chin, a fisheries researcher at Australia's James Cook University, said finning had led to "massive declines" in shark numbers, prompting stringent controls in the Pacific.
"Because it is now illegal, if people are doing it, it is going to be hidden and really hard to detect," he said.
Research on the DNA of thousands of shark fins sold in Hong Kong markets pointed to its origins in the region.
"We have seen evidence of illegal trade from the western and eastern sides of the Pacific," Demian Chapman, who conducted the research as director of the Sharks and Rays Conservation Research Program at Mote Marine Laboratory in Florida, said.
There have been other cases of Chinese vessels violating the finning ban, he told AFP.
Reduced demand in China for shark fin soup, including a ban on serving it at government functions, had contributed to a fall in the amount of fins being traded in Hong Kong, he added.
Last November, U.S. authorities assisted the Peruvian government in seizing an estimated 10,000 shark fins destined for China. The bust, at an industrial port outside of Lima, led to the arrest of three men tied to a transnational criminal network involved in illegal fishing and wildlife smuggling, officials said.
In 2020, wildlife inspectors at a port in Miami discovered 1,400 pounds of dried shark fins.

How to reset your child’s sleep schedule for back-to-school season
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:23:02 UTC
19:23:02 KST

How to reset your child’s sleep schedule for back-to-school season
NEW YORK (AP) — After a summer of vacations and late nights, it’s time to set those back-to-school alarms.
A good night’s sleep helps students stay focused and attentive in class. Experts say it’s worth easing kids back into a routine with the start of a new school year.
“We don’t say ‘ get good sleep ’ just because,” said pediatrician Dr. Gabrina Dixon with Children’s National Hospital. “It really helps kids learn and it helps them function throughout the day.”
The amount of sleep kids need changes as they age. Preschoolers should get up to 13 hours of sleep. Tweens need between nine and 12 hours. Teenagers do best with eight to 10 hours of shut-eye.
Set an earlier bedtime
Early bedtimes can slip through the cracks over the summer as kids stay up for sleepovers, movie marathons and long plane flights. To get back on track, experts recommend setting earlier bedtimes a week or two before the first day of school or gradually going to bed 15 to 30 minutes earlier each night.
This article is part of AP’s Be Well coverage, focusing on wellness, fitness, diet and mental health. Read more Be Well.
Don’t serve a heavy meal before bed and avoid TV or screen time two hours before sleep. Instead, work on relaxing activities to slow down, like showering and reading a story.
“You’re trying to take the cognitive load off your mind,” said Dr. Nitun Verma, a spokesperson for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. “It would be like if you’re driving, you’re slowly letting go of the gas pedal.”
Parents can adjust their back-to-school plans based on what works best for their child. Nikkya Hargrove moves her twin daughters’ bedtimes up by 30 minutes the week before school starts.
Sometimes, her kids will negotiate for a few extra minutes to stay up and read. Hargrove said those conversations are important as her children get older and advocate for themselves. If they stay up too late and don’t have the best morning, Hargrove said that can be a learning experience too.
“If they’re groggy and they don’t like how they feel, then they know, ‘OK, I have to go to bed earlier,’” said Hargrove, an author and independent bookstore owner from Connecticut.
In the morning, soaking in some daylight by sitting at a window or going outside can help train the brain to power up, Verma said.
Squash back-to-school sleep anxiety
Sleep quality matters just as much as duration. First-day jitters can make it hard to fall asleep no matter how early the bedtime.
Dixon says parents can talk to their kids to find out what is making them anxious. Is it the first day at a new school? Is it a fear of making new friends? Then they might try a test run of stressful activities before school starts to make those tasks feel less scary — for example, by visiting the school or meeting classmates at an open house.
The weeks leading up to school can be jam-packed and it’s not always possible to prep a routine in advance. But kids will adjust eventually, so sleep experts say parents should do what they can. After all, their kids aren’t the only ones adjusting to a new routine.
“I always say, ‘Take a deep breath, it’ll be OK,’” Dixon said. “And just start that schedule.”

Hungary files a criminal complaint over $965M COVID-19 ventilator deal, citing possible fraud

Hungary files a criminal complaint over $965M COVID-19 ventilator deal, citing possible fraud
BUDAPEST, Hungary (AP) — Hungary’s foreign ministry has filed a criminal complaint with prosecutors over what it says was possible fraud related to the previous government’s purchase of ventilators worth some $965 million during the COVID-19 pandemic, Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said Tuesday.
Hungary’s previous government under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán purchased the roughly 17,000 ventilators from China in March and April 2020, drawing criticism at the time that it was buying far more units than could be realistically deployed and paying much more per unit than other European countries.
In a video posted to Facebook on Tuesday, Foreign Minister Orbán, who is not related to the former prime minister, said the results of a ministry investigation into the purchase “raises suspicions of breach of fiduciary duty causing particularly substantial financial loss and other criminal offenses.”
She didn’t detail specific allegations, but noted that the investigation involved tens of thousands of documents — some of which had to be recovered using digital tools “after unsuccessful attempts to delete them” — and raised further questions “about the responsibility of the ministry’s former senior leadership.”
A statement released on the Hungarian government’s website on Tuesday pointed to other suspected irregularities related to the ventilator procurement, including that most of the units were purchased through intermediary companies that saw their revenues rise exponentially due to the transaction.
Some of the ventilators were defective, and a significant proportion of them was never deployed, the statement reads, adding that storage costs for the unused devices ran into the millions of dollars.
Hungary’s former foreign minister Péter Szijjártó cultivated close ties with China during his nearly 12 years in office, and oversaw the purchase of the ventilators as well as the procurement of 5 million doses of the China-produced Sinopharm COVID-19 vaccine.
Last month, Szijjártó resigned his seat in Parliament to take an executive position with Chinese automaker BYD, prompting accusations of a conflict of interest due to his role in facilitating substantial government subsidies given to the company while in office.
Hungary’s government later launched an investigation into large investments into Hungary made by BYD during Szijjártó’s tenure.

Putin issues decree opening door to state control of key sites after deep Ukrainian drone strikes

Putin decree lets Russia take control of infrastructure damaged in Ukrainian drone attacks
Russian President Vladimir Putin has decreed that the state can temporarily seize control of critical infrastructure facilities if private owners fail to protect them from Ukrainian drone attacks or rebuild them after the strikes.
The move came Monday amid growing economic pressure and public frustration being felt in Russia after months of escalating Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries and e-commerce hubs that have caused nationwide disruptions.
Ukraine also is reeling from relentless aerial attacks that have smashed its power grid ahead of winter and heavily damaged homes as Russia’s invasion stretches into its fifth year.
The decree may pressure owners to undertake repairs
The Kremlin’s exact intentions with the decree are unclear. However, it applies to various sectors, including energy infrastructure, as well as industrial, communications, transportation and logistics facilities.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Tuesday that “often business owners do not pay enough attention to taking measures to ensure safety, anti-drone safety.”
Given the threat to vital economic infrastructure, “we must take measures, we must ensure our own safety,” he said.
Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov said in a statement the decree doesn’t imply the nationalization of companies or a change of ownership — only “involvement of the state in the management of an enterprise to solve specific security problems.”
He added that the decree “doesn’t imply widespread use,” and that “targeted, carefully considered decisions will be made at the highest level.”
Russian political analyst Abbas Gallyamov said the measure might be a “tactical” step designed to force the owners of repeatedly damaged oil refineries into making repairs.
“Given the fact that the same refinery has already been hit three to five times, it’s safe to assume that the owners are now reluctant to invest in restoring what’s been destroyed,” he said on the Telegram messaging app.
“Why spend billions if they’re going to get hit again tomorrow?” said Gallyamov, a former speechwriter for Putin.
He said the government is giving companies an ultimatum: “If you don’t finance the restoration of the refineries, we’ll take them away from you.”
Ukraine says it hit more Russian refineries
In the latest attacks, Ukraine’s General Staff said Tuesday its forces struck facilities at Russia’s Afipsky oil refinery in the Krasnodar region overnight, causing a fire. Krasnodar Gov. Veniamin Kondratyev said a fire broke out at an oil refinery in the town of Afipsky.
A Ukrainian attack also damaged the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery in southern Russia’s Rostov region overnight and halted operations, Rostov Gov. Yuri Slyusar said, without elaborating.
It was the eighth time in a year that Ukrainian drones have targeted the Afipsky refinery and the fourth time in the past year they have aimed at Novoshakhtinsk, according to data from Ukraine’s General Staff.
Russian businesses face fundamental economic challenges as the costly war drags on. The government has raised taxes and increased domestic borrowing to keep its budget deficit under control, and taking over major companies could potentially bring in revenue.
At the same time, seizing damaged assets could bring another financial burden. The Kremlin may intend the measure as a way to pressure companies to shoulder more responsibility for air defense, as Russia’s vast territory is hard to protect.
Russia also is offering more help for its biggest online retailer, Wildberries, and businesses selling goods through it. The company and thousands of sellers working with it have been hit hard by repeated Ukrainian strikes on warehouses. The Finance Ministry proposed Monday extending deadlines for tax and insurance payments to give Wildberries and its sellers some financial breathing space.
On Saturday, Putin told state television that Russia “must and will improve the air defense system and enhance its capabilities.”
“We need to streamline coordination between defense, law enforcement and civilian agencies at all levels, and to leverage the capabilities of state‑run enterprises and private businesses,” he said.
In May, following deep strikes that unsettled Moscow, Russian lawmakers approved a bill that allowed the Central Bank, state-controlled Sberbank and other financial services to fend off drone attacks by installing air defenses on their premises.
News outlet RBC, citing anonymous sources in and close to the Defense Ministry, reported that month that a mechanism had been established for businesses to procure weapons and equipment to protect themselves from drone attacks, something Russian officials and lawmakers have said companies should do.

What do we know about the Syria and Israel meeting in Jordan?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:22:59 UTC

Breadcrumb
What do we know about the Syria and Israel meeting in Jordan, and efforts to revive negotiations?
The meeting that brought Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani and Israeli Mossad chief Roman Gofman together in Jordan on Sunday, 23 August, raised questions about the possibility of reviving Syria-Israel negotiations after months of deadlock and rising tensions on the ground.
The meeting was mediated by the United States and hosted by Jordan, with the participation of security and military officials from both sides, according to Damascus, at a time when contacts between the two sides had stopped following the Israeli airstrike on Abu al-Duhur airbase in the Idlib countryside on 18 August.
The meeting, which brought the Syrian foreign minister together with the head of the Israeli foreign intelligence service, was the highest-level publicly announced direct contact since the start of the security track between the two sides.
Gofman held a phone call with al-Shaibani on 14 Aug. before tensions escalated and led to the bombing of Abu al-Duhur.
The far-right Netanyahu-led government claimed that the Israeli army had repeatedly recommended attacking the airport, located in the eastern Idlib countryside, based on intelligence that allegedly indicated Turkey intended to carry out activities inside the airport that would threaten "Israel's security".
Damascus says the meeting focused on de-escalation and halting Israeli attacks, arrests and targeting operations, as well as discussing the revival of Syria-Israel negotiations to reach a security agreement that could later form the basis for a more comprehensive agreement.
It also stressed that any arrangements must respect Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity and its right to rebuild its army and determine its alliances.
Al-Shaibani had said in an interview with Reuters on Saturday that Damascus expected security negotiations with Israel to resume soon, despite the lack of trust between the two sides.
He added that Syria's priority was to stop Israeli attacks, with the security agreement ultimately leading to an Israeli withdrawal from all Syrian territory seized after the fall of Bashar al-Assad's regime at the end of 2024.
The Syrian minister said Damascus was extending its hand for diplomacy, understanding and peace, but needed Israeli steps in return to build trust.
He said contacts had been cut off after the bombing of Abu al-Duhur but considered communication necessary with a party that Damascus views as a direct threat to its security.
Damascus says the proposed agreement discussed in earlier stages had come close to completion.
It included the establishment of security zones in southern Syria, including a buffer zone where the United Nations would be the only presence, as well as other areas where Syrian forces would be deployed to varying degrees.
But al-Shaibani accused Israel of failing to show the necessary willingness to implement what had been agreed, while stressing that his country would not abandon Turkey's support for rebuilding the Syrian army. This issue has become one of the main sources of tension between Israel and Turkey in Syria.
Syria-Israel negotiations: Five rounds without an agreement
Jordan announced on Monday, 24 August, that it had hosted a meeting on Sunday to discuss de-escalation between Syria and Israel.
The Jordan News Agency quoted an official source saying, "The meeting was held at the request of our brothers in Syria and discussed de-escalation and achieving calm after the Israeli bombing of Syrian territory last week."
"Jordan affirms the Kingdom's absolute support for the Syrian government in its efforts to protect its security, stability and territorial integrity," the source added. "We stress the need to immediately halt the brutal Israeli attacks on Syria, for Israel to withdraw from occupied Syrian territory and to respect the 1974 disengagement agreement."
Meanwhile, the Syrian state news agency SANA quoted a diplomatic source at the Syrian Foreign Ministry on Sunday, 23 August, as saying that the meeting came following the latest Israeli bombing of Syrian territory and escalating tensions in the south of the country.
Discussions focused on establishing practical mechanisms to halt Israeli attacks, arrests and targeting operations and reviving the negotiating track to reach a security agreement that could form the basis of a future, more comprehensive agreement.
According to the source, the Syrian side stressed during the meeting that Syria is a sovereign state with the full right to rebuild and develop its national army and to determine its alliances and partnerships in line with its national interests.
Syrian officials also reiterated "its firm position that the occupied Golan is Syrian territory", noting that "discussion of its final status and the path leading to that remains premature at the current stage and that the immediate priority is the withdrawal of Israeli forces to the lines that existed before 8 Dec. 2024 and the reactivation and full implementation of the 1974 disengagement agreement."
The discussions also addressed the importance of supporting stability in Syria and maintaining regional security, including efforts aimed at bringing Turkey's and Israel's positions closer together and ensuring that the existing tensions between the two countries do not spill over into Syrian territory.
According to the source, the meeting was mainly focused on taking practical steps to de-escalate while exploring ways to return to the negotiating track, with Syria stressing that any security arrangements must respect its sovereignty, territorial integrity and sovereign rights.
The negotiations between al-Shaibani and Gofman did not start from scratch.
The two sides had held five previous rounds of negotiations, the latest in Paris in January, which ended with an agreement to increase the frequency of meetings and take confidence-building measures, in addition to establishing a channel for exchanging intelligence.
But these understandings did not prevent Israel from continuing its attacks inside Syrian territory, prompting Damascus to say that Israel had not practically adhered to what had been agreed.
The latest developments reveal the extent of the gap between the two sides.
The Israeli airstrike on Abu al-Duhur airbase, which targeted runways and facilities at the base, was followed by another Israeli strike in southern Syria on 22 Aug.
Israel, meanwhile, claims that its operations are linked to security concerns and preventing potential threats to its forces.
In this context, Syrian-Israeli relations expert Khaled Khalil told The New Arab that the latest contact represents the highest point in the negotiating track so far.
He noted that Syria-Israel negotiations in earlier stages had been conducted through an Israeli political and diplomatic team led by former Strategic Affairs Minister Ron Dermer.
He considered the shift in communication to the level of the Mossad chief a reflection of the increased importance of the security issue but ruled out a rapid breakthrough because of the crisis of trust and the big differences in the two sides' views.
Withdrawal for 'security'
The first sticking point in Syria-Israel negotiations concerns the fate of the sites seized by Israel in southern Syria after the fall of the Assad regime.
Damascus is demanding the withdrawal of Israeli forces to the lines that existed before Dec. 8, 2024, and the reactivation and full implementation of the 1974 disengagement agreement.
It also maintains that the Golan is occupied Syrian territory but considers discussion of its final status premature at the current stage.
But Israel does not appear prepared simply to return to the situation that existed before the fall of the previous regime.
The information circulating indicates that Israel wants security arrangements broader than those stipulated in the 1974 agreement, including restrictions on the size, armament and deployment of Syrian forces in the south.
Here, a fundamental dilemma emerges: Damascus wants negotiations to serve as a gateway to restoring sovereignty and an Israeli withdrawal, while Tel Aviv wants the new security arrangements to provide a long-term guarantee against any threat from Syrian territory.
Thus, the core dispute is no longer only over the principle of withdrawal, but also over the line to which Israel will withdraw and which of the sites it seized on the ground it will retain.
Southern Syria under attack
Southern Syria represents the most complicated sticking point in Syria-Israel negotiations and any potential agreement between them.
Israel desire a largely "demilitarised" south, with restrictions on the deployment of heavy weapons, missiles and drones near the Golan.
It also seeks guarantees preventing the return of Iranian influence or the activity of groups linked to Lebanon's "Hezbollah" in the area, alongside more effective mechanisms for monitoring the border.
On the other hand, Damascus rejects any formula that undermines its sovereign right to build its army and develop its capabilities. It explicitly said during the Jordan meeting that Syria is a sovereign state and has the right to rebuild and develop its army and determine its alliances and partnerships in line with its national interests.
Thus, negotiations over the south will not be merely technical but will concern the very concept of sovereignty: to what extent can Syria deploy its military within its own territory, and to what extent will Israel retain what it calls the right to intervene if it considers there to be a "threat" to its security?
There was no discussion regarding Israel's military capabilities, including its nuclear arsenal.
Turkey: The third party
The Turkish factor has emerged in recent weeks as one of the most sensitive issues in Israeli calculations.
Israel says any Turkish military deployment or the establishment of Turkish air defence infrastructure inside Syria could pose a threat to it, particularly because it could limit the freedom of action of the Israeli air force in Syrian and regional airspace.
The Mossad chief discussed Israeli concerns over the growing Turkish military presence in Syria with al-Shaibani during the phone call on 14 August, days before the bombing of Abu al-Duhur.
Damascus and Ankara deny plans to establish a Turkish base that threatens Israel, while US special envoy to Syria Tom Barrack recently described the Israeli strike as unnecessary escalation and pushed for a mechanism to prevent friction between Israel, Turkey and Syria.
Thus, Syria-Israel negotiations could become part of a broader regional negotiating track, involving not only relations between Damascus and Tel Aviv but also the future of Turkey's role in Syria.
Political analyst Ahmad al-Mousa remarked to TNA that Damascus took part in the Jordan meeting with clear sovereign demands, most notably an end to airstrikes and attacks, an Israeli withdrawal from the territories seized after the fall of the previous regime, a reduction in Israeli-Turkish tensions, and preservation of Syria's right to build its capabilities and establish its alliances.
Al-Mousa considers the negotiations at this stage not to represent normalisation, but rather security communication to manage the conflict and prevent a slide into open confrontation.
Political analyst Ghazi Dahman, meanwhile, believes that Israeli policy towards Syria has gone beyond the concept of security and defensive measures to an attempt to impose a long-term reality on the Syrian state.
He told TNA that continued strikes and incursions aim to keep Damascus weak and unstable.
Regardless of the differing assessments, the continuation of Israeli military operations alongside Syria-Israel negotiations represents one of the biggest problems facing the current track and leaves each round of negotiations vulnerable to collapse at the first escalation on the ground.
Little chance of sixth round succeeding
If Syria-Israel negotiations resume soon, the next round will face a more difficult test than previous rounds because the two sides will enter it with a record of mistrust and new realities on the ground.
In this context, Khaled Khalil believes that Israeli intransigence, along with domestic political considerations in Israel, makes rapid progress in Syria-Israel negotiations unlikely.
He believes the Israeli government may resort to escalation when facing political or regional pressure.
For its part, Damascus faces a different equation.
It wants to assert its sovereignty and recover the territories it lost control of, but at the same time it does not currently have the military capability to impose its conditions by force.
Therefore, negotiations appear to Damascus to be a tool for managing a transitional phase rather than a ready path to comprehensive peace.
Damascus says the security agreement could serve as a prelude to a broader agreement, but this possibility appears remote in the near term.
Even if the two sides succeed in agreeing on an end to attacks, a withdrawal and arrangements for the south, the ongoing Israeli occupation of Golan will remain postponed, along with questions of normalisation, diplomatic relations and the future of the borders.
Damascus maintains that the Golan is occupied Syrian territory while currently prioritising an end to attacks, an Israeli withdrawal from the recently occupied territories and the reactivation of the 1974 agreement.
At the same time, Israel is focused on security guarantees concerning southern Syria, limiting Turkey's military role and maintaining its freedom of action in Syrian airspace.
For this reason, a resumption of negotiations, if it happens, will not necessarily mean that a final agreement is near.
The next phase is more likely to begin with an attempt to establish a limited security understanding to prevent escalation before moving to more complicated political issues.
The key question remains: Can Washington turn the current de-escalation into an agreement that can be implemented, or will the negotiations remain hostage to changing military and political realities?

Can Pakistan’s Asim Munir convince Iran military chiefs to return to talks?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:22:00 UTC
19:22:00 KST

Can Pakistan’s Asim Munir convince Iran military chiefs to return to talks?
Pakistan says progress was made in Tehran, but Iran’s security establishment remains wary of Washington.
Islamabad, Pakistan — Pakistani Field Marshal Asim Munir spent Monday moving through the power corridors of Tehran: the presidency, parliament, the Supreme National Security Council, and the foreign and interior ministries.
He met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, as well as Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who is Tehran’s chief negotiator in talks with the United States to end their now six-month-long war.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Pakistan’s army chief back in Iran: Can he break peace talks deadlock?
- list 2 of 4US launches ‘Operation Economic Outcast’ to cut Iran’s economic lifeline
- list 3 of 4Yemen’s Houthis report attack on Saudi ship
- list 4 of 4How US sanctions on Iran ripple through global markets and consumers
But amid a deadlock in those peace negotiations, many analysts say that Munir’s true test as mediator will lie in his ability to use his position as an influential military leader to convince his Iranian counterparts in olive uniforms to agree to a return to talks with Washington.
Days before Munir’s visit, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told a gathering of doctors in Tehran that it was time to end the war while Iran held the advantage, a message aimed as much at Tehran’s own security establishment as at Washington.
“It is better that we bring the war to an end now as we are in a position of power and dignity,” he said, adding that “the whole world acknowledges our victory”.
Hours later, on August 21, the chief of the general staff of Iran’s armed forces, Major-General Ali Abdollahi, promised “revolutionary, crushing, regret-inducing and devastating” responses to any American miscalculation.
It was a sharp illustration of the gap between Iran’s president and the men now running its military — one that Munir will need to also navigate, analysts say.
And that’s why Munir’s most significant meeting on Monday might have been with General Mohsen Rezaei, a representative of Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei and the newly appointed secretary of the Supreme National Security Council. Rezaei is essentially the bridge between the military and Khamenei.
State of the war
Munir’s visit to Tehran came on a day when the region and the world were bracing for US President Donald Trump’s threatened “economic D-Day” sanctions against Iran, accompanied by a threatened punishment for all countries that continue to trade with Tehran.
Later in the day, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveiled “Operation Economic Outcast“, a sweeping sanctions campaign targeting Iran’s digital assets, gold, aviation, technology and shipping networks.
But while warning other countries to sever trade ties with Iran, he held back from actually announcing any penalties for those nations, acknowledging that such a step would “blow up the global financial system”.
Meanwhile, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, speaking the same day, kept the option of renewed strikes open.
“If we need to use kinetic strikes, we’ll use them. If Iran is foolish enough to overplay their hand or mess with the American military, we’ll do what we need to do,” he said.
It’s unclear whether Munir’s visit helped stave off broader US action against Iran and its trading partners.
But the timing was significant, analysts point out. Munir travelled to Tehran days after taking a phone call from United States President Donald Trump, who reportedly asked Islamabad to use its influence to bring Iran back to the table.
Pakistan’s Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said the one-day visit had produced “comprehensive discussions” on reopening the Strait of Hormuz and ending the war.
Iranian officials, the ISPR added, “appreciated Pakistan’s constructive role and sincere efforts”.
Pakistan’s Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, who travelled with Munir, went further, calling the talks “very positive and productive” and saying “significant progress was made”.
A reshuffled Iranian military
This was his fourth visit to Tehran this year, but his first since Iran’s military hierarchy changed earlier this month.
On August 10, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei installed Abdollahi as chief of the general staff and moved Rezaei into the Supreme National Security Council. Ahmad Vahidi, commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), has held his post since March, when his predecessor was killed in the war’s opening strikes.
It is these military men that analysts say are now shaping Iran’s war moves, potentially giving a fellow man in uniform an edge over traditional diplomats in convincing Tehran to get back to talks.
“It is increasingly the IRGC and the wider security establishment driving decisions on war and peace during this crisis,” Ahmed Saeed, a former vice admiral in Pakistan’s navy and a defence analyst, told Al Jazeera.
Naqvi, the interior minister, has travelled to Tehran eight times since April without those visits producing a substantial breakthrough.
But unlike him, Munir is not a politician. He’s a general who appears to enjoy the trust of both the Iranian leadership and, crucially, Trump — who has described the Pakistani army chief as his “favourite field marshal”.
“The call [to Munir a few days ago] was initiated by Trump himself, requesting Pakistani leadership use its influence to bring Iran back to the table,” Saeed said.
Warm words, no movement
What Iranian officials actually told Munir, in accounts carried by Iranian state media, differed little from what they have been telling their own broadcasters all week.
“We distrust America, and it must change its behaviour,” Rezaei told Munir, according to IRNA.
Ghalibaf, Iran’s parliament speaker, was blunter.
“We are pursuing the implementation of the terms of the Memorandum of Understanding, and it is America that must adhere to its commitments based on the Memorandum of Understanding,” he told Munir, according to IRNA.
Pezeshkian, meanwhile, pressed Munir to tell Washington to “correct its tone and approach”, warning that “relying on force and bullying will only complicate the process”, according to Tasnim, another Iranian outlet.
Two tracks, one strait
Oman’s Foreign Minister Badr bin Hamad Albusaidi is also expected in Tehran today for a separate round of talks focused specifically on the Strait of Hormuz, a track that has run alongside Pakistan’s mediation for months.
Oman’s involvement is not new. Albusaidi has held recurring talks with Tehran on the strait’s navigation rules.
Ejaz Haider, a Lahore-based defence analyst, said the Omani and Pakistani diplomatic tracks complement each other.
“Oman and Islamabad channels complement, because clause 5 of the Islamabad MoU stresses a bilateral understanding on the strait [between Oman and Iran],” he told Al Jazeera. The Strait of Hormuz passes through the territorial waters of Iran and Oman.
“This [a deal between Iran and Oman to jointly manage the strait] is not in the interest of the US, which is why Trump has threatened to bomb Oman,” Haider said, referring to remarks Trump made on August 17, when he told Fox News he would bomb Oman if it “gets in the way” of reopening the strait, the second time he had threatened the US ally over Hormuz.
Where Islamabad’s advantage as a mediator lay was in its “direct access to Vahidi, Abdollahi and Rezaei, the actual architects of Iran’s decision-making”, Saeed, the former naval official, said.
An Iranian official close to the negotiations, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Albusaidi would be in Tehran “primarily to hear what Iran has decided and what it has discussed with its Pakistani mediator”.
Who holds the leverage?
Andreas Krieg, an associate professor of defence studies at King’s College London, said the differences that had emerged between the Iranian military and civilian leaderships demonstrate a gulf between their understanding of where the war stood.
Pezeshkian and Ghalibaf, Krieg said, were “essentially warning that Iran cannot live indefinitely in this condition”, while “parts of the IRGC believe the opposite and think time is working against Washington”.
But ultimately, he said, “Mohsen Rezaei, Ahmad Vahidi and the IRGC are central to whether any political understanding [to end the war] can be implemented”, referring to Iran’s top military leadership.
“[Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas] Araghchi can negotiate something, and Qatar can broker it, but none of that matters if the security apparatus does not accept the operational consequences.”
For now, Munir appears to be the candidate mediators believe has the best shot at getting Iranian generals from their war room to the board room.

5 injured as fire breaks out at Russia's Amur petrochemical facility
