UN chief, Red Cross renew call for rules on lethal autonomous weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:16:00 UTC
19:16:00 KST

UN chief, Red Cross renew call for rules on lethal autonomous weapons
Amid unconfirmed reports that fully autonomous and AI-guided drones are now being used on the battlefield, UN chief António Guterres and the President of the Red Cross on Tuesday renewed their urgent call for stricter global controls, before it is too late.
Key points
- Controls call for two types of autonomous weapons: those whose actions are "unpredictable" and those that target human beings
- AI advances could reduce human control over use of lethal force
- States urged to start negotiating on legally binding agreement
The timing of the appeal reflects growing concerns that increasingly sophisticated weapons are being made and deployed at ever greater speed and scale, boosted by increasingly powerful AI technology. Disarmament experts say that even arms manufacturers want clarity on the legal issues at stake.
“We are now dangerously close to crossing a moral red line: the autonomous targeting of humans by machines,” UN Secretary-General Guterres said, in a joint appeal with International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) head Mirjana Spoljaric Egger.
Targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure in conflict is already strictly prohibited under international humanitarian law, but understanding who non-combatants are in a conflict zone is often extremely difficult. The concern is that life-and-death decisions will be taken by machines unable to tell the difference in changing conditions.
Legal and ethical principle
Echoing those concerns in Geneva, head of disarmament affairs at UN Geneva, Mélanie Régimbal, stressed that the UN chief’s long-held position that systems that select or engage targets and take human lives without human control and judgement “are politically unacceptable, morally repugnant and should be prohibited under international law”.
Also in Geneva, ICRC’s Laurent Gisel described how conflict “is not a story of precision, distinction and restraints. It is a story of civilians killed, families displaced, hospitals, schools and homes destroyed at ever greater speed and scale."
In such a setting, “things can change very rapidly”, explained Mr. Gisel, Head of Arms and Conduct of Hostilities Unit at ICRC. “A combatant can surrender or be wounded and therefore be protected from attack; civilians can enter the area of operations of the autonomous weapons systems; the weapons may encounter a situation that would not have been anticipated.”
In the appeal, Mr. Guterres and Ms. Egger noted that autonomous weapons were “not part of a distant future”, as the race towards greater autonomy is already underway. Scientists and engineers developing such systems had also raised concerns about their risks, they noted.
States urged to act
The UN and ICRC are now urging governments to move beyond discussions and begin negotiations on a legally binding instrument establishing clear prohibitions and restrictions.
“States must show political courage and move beyond incremental discussions towards decisive action,” they said, warning that failure to act could leave future generations with a world where accountability for lethal decisions becomes increasingly difficult to establish.
The appeal comes ahead of the seventh Review Conference of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW), due to take place in November in Geneva. The leaders of the UN and Red Cross described the meeting as the “clearest path available” for States to agree to move towards negotiations on a legally binding instrument.
Important groundwork for an agreement has already been laid through discussions at the UN General Assembly and the CCW’s Group of Governmental Experts, they said, including progress towards defining the human judgement and control needed to ensure compliance with international humanitarian law.
The UN and ICRC first issued their joint appeal in 2023, calling on States to negotiate a legally binding instrument by 2026. Their initial statement stressed that human control must be retained over life-and-death decisions and that machines capable of taking lives without human involvement should be prohibited under international law.
Tuesday’s appeal renews that deadline-driven push, stressing that the painstaking work of recent years must now lead to action.
“We urge States to seize this moment,” the leaders said. “Innovation must serve humanity – not endanger it.”
The joint appeal is for two types of autonomous weapons to be prohibited:
- Unpredictable autonomous weapons; those that either by design or during use, the operator cannot predict or anticipate the outcome of force being used. “If it's not possible to predict it, then how is it possible to limit it?” asked ICRC’s Mr. Gisel.
- Anti-personnel weapons: although "all States" have acknowledged that autonomous weapons in general raise ethical questions because there is less control on the use of force, concerns are highest over those that deliberately target a human being "because that reduce human life to data, algorithm, sensor and machine operations", the ICRC expert stressed.

Palestinian artist Sliman Mansour, giant of resistance art, dies aged 79
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:11:46 UTC
19:11:46 KST

In Pictures
Palestinian artist Sliman Mansour, giant of resistance art, dies aged 79
Sliman Mansour’s art captured the essence of Palestine, blending ancient traditions with modern themes of resistance.
Celebrated artist Sliman Mansour, one of the founding figures of contemporary Palestinian art, has died at the age of 79 after a long illness, his family announced on Monday.
Born in Birzeit, near Ramallah, in 1947, Mansour rose to prominence in the 1970s as part of a generation of Palestinian artists, writers and poets seeking to rebuild a threatened identity through symbols rooted in land and memory. Over more than five decades, his paintings came to embody the story of Palestine: the farmer clinging to his soil, the stone house on a hill, the embroidered thobe and the smile of a young girl carrying the hope of return.
Mansour studied art in Beirut and Washington and went on to exhibit extensively, both in solo shows and group exhibitions across the Arab world and internationally. His works are held in museums and private collections worldwide, and he received numerous awards in recognition of his contribution to Arab and Palestinian culture.
His visual language drew deeply from the region’s ancient civilisations – Canaanite, Pharaonic and Assyrian – as well as Islamic and Arab art, particularly calligraphy and geometric motifs. At the same time, his upbringing in Birzeit anchored his work in the everyday life of Palestinian villages: the landscape, peasants, traditional homes and clothing. Mansour also absorbed influences from global art that carried messages of freedom and resistance, blending local forms with a universal appeal.
During the first Intifada, he helped found the New Vision group with fellow artists, turning to mud, straw, wood, leather, henna and natural dyes after Palestinian artists boycotted Israeli-made supplies. This shift, he later said, forged a vital link between post-Nakba art and the work of younger generations.
For many Palestinians, Mansour’s canvases were more than images; they were a visual archive of the cause itself. His brush, critics and admirers agree, carried the homeland.
Al Jazeera looks at some of his famous paintings.

Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:09:15 UTC
19:09:15 KST

Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
A new atomic-scale catalyst could transform stubborn plant waste into valuable chemicals now commonly made from petroleum.
- Date:
- August 25, 2026
- Source:
- University of Manchester
- Summary:
- Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.
- Share:
Lignin gives plants much of their structural strength and represents the largest renewable source of aromatic chemicals found in nature. It can make up a substantial share (up to 35%) of waste biomass from agriculture and forestry. Yet lignin's complicated molecular structure makes it notoriously difficult to break apart efficiently, which has limited its potential use in sustainable manufacturing.
In a study published in ACS Catalysis, an international team that included Dr. Christopher Parlett, Xinyue Zhou, and Yutao Jiang from the Department of Chemical Engineering developed a highly efficient "single-atom catalyst." The researchers also determined, at the molecular level, how the catalyst breaks the strong chemical bonds that help hold lignin together.
The catalyst contains individual ruthenium atoms embedded within a nitrogen-doped carbon material. By keeping the ruthenium atoms isolated, the design can deliver strong catalytic performance while requiring only very small amounts of metal, improving efficiency compared with conventional systems.
Revealing How the Catalyst Breaks Down Lignin
One persistent obstacle in lignin research has been identifying exactly which parts of a catalyst are responsible for breaking the material's unusually strong chemical bonds. Without that information, researchers have had limited guidance for designing more effective catalysts.
The team found that a particular atomic arrangement known as a "Ru-N4 site" is especially important. These sites activate oxygen molecules and help trigger the breaking of both carbon-oxygen and carbon-carbon bonds within lignin.
Using a combination of laboratory experiments and computational modeling, the researchers were able to reconstruct the process in greater detail. The catalyst first activates oxygen, producing highly reactive species. Those species then attack the lignin structure and split it into smaller molecules.
High Conversion With Milder Conditions
When tested under optimized conditions, the catalyst converted nearly all of the model lignin compounds and generated high yields of valuable chemical products, including phenol.
The process also works under relatively mild conditions and does not require harsh chemicals. That combination could make the approach useful for developing more sustainable methods of chemical manufacturing.
The researchers went beyond simplified model compounds and tested the catalyst on real lignin collected from several biomass sources. It successfully converted those samples into useful aromatic compounds that could potentially become building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.
A Potential Path Toward Biomass-Based Chemicals
The findings provide a more detailed picture of how single-atom catalysts operate during biomass conversion. That understanding could serve as a guide for developing more efficient catalytic systems in the future.
"Understanding exactly how these catalysts work at the atomic level allows us to design better materials for converting renewable resources into valuable chemicals," said Dr. Christopher Parlett, Lecturer in Chemical Engineering.
By making it easier to upgrade lignin and convert it into higher-value products, the research could support a broader shift away from traditional linear petroleum-derived chemical production and toward a more circular, biomass-based economy.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Manchester. Original written by Enna Bartlett. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Peru to welcome Pope Leo with hymn honoring slain nun
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:09:06 UTC
19:09:06 KST

Peru to welcome Pope Leo with hymn honoring slain nun
LIMA, Aug 25 - Peru will welcome Pope Leo XIV in November with a hymn in honor of a Catholic nun killed by Maoist insurgents, celebrating the pontiff's return to the country where he worked for decades as a missionary.
The song, featuring Andean rhythms and titled "Leon, Hermano del Camino" or "Leo, Brother on the Journey", will be performed by members of the Aguchita youth choir, named after Peruvian missionary Maria Agustina Rivas.
Rivas was killed by Shining Path rebels in 1990 while carrying out humanitarian work in Peru's remote Amazon jungle region.
Known as "Aguchita," she was beatified by the Vatican in 2022 under Pope Francis after the Church ruled she had been killed out of hatred for the Catholic faith.
Keverly Escobar, 27, one of the lead singers, told Reuters she was proud to be part of the choir honoring a Peruvian saint who gave "her life for the most humble."
The song's composer and musician, Jaime Montoya, said he was inspired to write the hymn because he saw a common thread —sacrifice — that unites the missionary and Pope Leo.
"The song came about partly while looking back on the life of our then-bishop, Robert Prevost," when the now-pontiff was a missionary in Peru, Montoya added.
Peru endured a brutal conflict between security forces and Shining Path, a guerrilla movement that sought to establish a communist state.
The violence left roughly 69,000 people dead or missing between 1980 and 2000, mostly in Peru's poorer indigenous and Amazon communities, according to official estimates.
"Aguchita knew she was confronting Shining Path, which at that time had the government under pressure and wanted to force all communities to join its cause," said Monsignor Pedro Castro of the Apostolic Vicariate of San Ramon, where the missionary served.
Pope Leo's visit comes soon after President Keiko Fujimori took office in July, pledging to unite the country following years of political turmoil.
Fujimori, the daughter of former President Alberto Fujimori, has praised her father's role in defeating the Shining Path insurgency in the 1990s, though his legacy remains divisive because of corruption and human rights abuses committed during his rule.
The hymn won a national competition to find a song symbolizing unity ahead of the Pope's November 11 to 16 visit to Peru, part of a South American tour that will include Argentina and Uruguay.
Pope Leo, the first U.S.-born pontiff, first arrived in Peru in 1985 and became a Peruvian citizen in 2015 after being appointed bishop of Chiclayo, where he stayed until 2023. REUTERS

Licence to grill (partially) reinstated in canton Lucerne
In the Swiss canton of Lucerne, fires in designated fire pits and in charcoal barbecues have been permitted again since Tuesday lunchtime. However, the ban on fires in and near woodland remains in force, even following the rainfall of the past few days.
The risk of forest fires varies from place to place, the State Chancellery announced on Tuesday. It has now been downgraded from “very high” to “high”. However, there has been no prolonged rainfall that would significantly reduce the risk of forest fires.
In open areas, however, the situation has eased following thunderstorms and lower temperatures. Consequently, the fire ban no longer applies across the board, but only within woodland and within a 50-metre radius of the woodland.
More
How to prevent wildfires in Switzerland and Europe
Barbecuing on unpaved fire pits and with disposable barbecues remains prohibited, it was further stated. This is due to the risk posed by flying sparks. Setting off fireworks and releasing so-called “sky lanterns” also remain prohibited.
The relaxation of the fire ban was carried out in consultation with the cantons of Central Switzerland and the Fire Service Inspectorate, the State Chancellery wrote. The absolute fire ban had been in force in Lucerne since August 6. Canton Zug had imposed it on August 12 and also relaxed it last Friday.

With six months of war, 20 dead in 68 incidents near Hormuz: IMO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:08:32 UTC
19:08:32 KST

Breadcrumb
After six months of US-Israeli war on Iran, 20 dead in 68 incidents near Hormuz: International Maritime Organisation
The Strait of Hormuz has been the main focus of the six-month war by the US and Israel against Iran, with many commercial vessels targeted in the vital conduit for oil and gas shipments.
In total, 68 incidents have been confirmed by the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) in the Gulf and neighbouring bodies of water, the equivalent of one every 2.6 days.
Across all incidents, at least 20 seafarers or port workers were reported killed, 35 wounded and one missing, the UN maritime agency said.
About half of the incidents have involved tankers, 20 percent container ships and 15 percent bulk carriers.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) classified 47 of the incidents as attacks.
Liberia-flagged vessels have been most affected, being involved in 13 incidents, followed by 10 vessels each from Panama and the Marshall Islands.
Iran-flagged vessels were reported as being involved in four incidents.
The rate of incidents has ebbed and flowed during the various phases of the US-Israeli war.
From the outbreak of war at the end of February until an agreement establishing a framework for peace talks was struck in mid-June, an incident was reported on average once every 2.3 days.
Incidents during this period accounted for 16 of the deaths and 19 of the injuries, and were recorded throughout the Gulf—both east and west of Hormuz, and off the coasts of Iraq, Iran, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Oman and the United Arab Emirates.
As peace talks continued, until around July 7, that rate halved to one incident every 4.6 days, on average.
No seafarers or other workers were reported killed, missing or injured during this period.
Four of the five incidents during this period were clustered off the Omani coast around the strait's narrowest point, along a route not authorised by Iranian authorities.
Iran, which hopes to retain control of the Hormuz after the war and charge fees for passage, had warned vessels against taking the alternative route.
Since talks collapsed, the rate has climbed almost back to pre-talks levels, with an incident recorded on average every 2.8 days.
Four seafarers or workers have been killed, 16 injured and one reported missing as a result.

Taiwan procures more than 7 million flu vaccine doses

19:04:27 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan has procured more than 7 million publicly funded flu vaccine doses for the 2026–2027 flu season, along with 2.4 million COVID-19 vaccine doses, the Centers for Disease Control said Tuesday.
The CDC said the publicly funded flu vaccination program will continue to cover 11 categories of people, with the first phase beginning Oct. 1. Eligible groups include people 65 and older, health care and disease-prevention personnel, young children, pregnant women, people with certain chronic illnesses, parents and caregivers of infants younger than 6 months, child care workers, and students, per a press release.
The agency is encouraging eligible people to receive flu and COVID-19 vaccines at the same time as part of its “left flu, right COVID” campaign, which promotes co-vaccination against both diseases. Adults aged 50 to 64 without high-risk chronic conditions will become eligible in the second phase beginning Nov. 2.
For the first time, Taiwan will introduce high-dose and adjuvanted flu vaccines as part of its publicly funded program. About 200,000 doses have been procured from two manufacturers, with the initial supply prioritized for people 65 and older living in long-term care and welfare institutions.
The remainder of Taiwan’s publicly funded flu vaccines will be trivalent inactivated vaccines containing two influenza A strains, H1N1 and H3N2, and one influenza B strain from the Victoria lineage, in line with recommendations from the World Health Organization and Taiwan’s immunization advisory committee.
For COVID-19, the CDC said 1.9 million single-dose vaccines for people 12 and older have been upgraded to a new-generation formulation. The vaccine contains one-fifth the antigen dose of the previous generation, while clinical and real-world data indicate lower rates of fever and local adverse reactions.
According to the CDC, clinical studies found that the new-generation vaccine produced nearly twice the antibody response of the previous formulation and the previous formulation and increased protection against severe COVID-19 by about 36%. The XFG COVID-19 vaccine will be the priority formulation for Taiwan’s fall and winter vaccination program as the virus continues to evolve.
The CDC is also preparing to launch its “Health Coin” program in October to encourage preventive health measures. Adults 18 and older who receive a COVID-19 or influenza vaccine, whether publicly funded or self-paid, will receive health coins that can later be exchanged for health-related rewards at participating convenience stores and supermarkets.
The agency urged eligible people to receive their shots as soon as the seasonal program begins, particularly older adults and others at higher risk of severe illness. The CDC said annual vaccination helps update protection against evolving flu and COVID-19 strains.

Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Lin Jian’s Regular Press Conference on August 25, 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
18:02:12 CST

Beijing Daily: Last week, Beijing hosted the 2026 World Robot Conference and the second World Humanoid Robot Games opened at the National Speed Skating Oval (the “Ice Ribbon”). Chinese humanoid robots broke multiple human records, including the 100-meter sprint and the men’s high jump, which sparked heated discussion worldwide. Meanwhile, some commentators suggest that the outlook for the industrial deployment and commercialization is uncertain. They also contend that China faces headwinds in sharing opportunities with the world, given the preventive and restrictive measures imposed by certain countries on its high-tech industries. What’s your comment?
Lin Jian: There has been extensive coverage of these events. Beyond the sporting events, what is more noteworthy is that humanoid robots are rapidly moving out of labs into real-world industries. They sort packages and assemble parts on factory floors, assist with elderly care and early childhood education in communities, and play ping-pong or fold clothes with dexterity. Behind these advances are OEMs, core part makers and algorithm developers working in concert, backed by China’s consistent policy support, robust innovation capabilities and diverse application scenarios.
At its core, China’s pursuit of new quality productive forces and technological innovation is about open cooperation and mutual benefit, not about setting up restrictions or seeking exclusive control. China stands ready to work with all other countries to continue dialogue and cooperation on artificial intelligence, embodied intelligence and other frontier areas, so that “innovation in China” and “intelligent manufacturing in China” can translate into a driving force for shared development, cooperation potential can be unlocked through technological connectivity, joint standard-setting and shared markets, and innovation dividends can be better delivered to humanity.

I wonder if China has a comment on this? (Similar question from CNBC)
Lin Jian: China has made clear on many occasions its firm opposition to illicit unilateral sanctions that have no basis in international law or the authorization of the UN Security Council. Economic warfare and maximum pressure provide no solution. On the contrary, they only serve to fuel tensions and lead to risk spillover, which will disrupt the global economic and financial order, and harm the legitimate rights and interests of other countries. The pressing task is to facilitate the deescalation of the situation and return to dialogue and negotiation as soon as possible. China will do everything necessary to firmly safeguard its rights and interests.
AFP: U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration on Monday moved to impose a fee of more than US$100,000 on employers hiring foreign workers through the highly skilled H-1B visa program. And given that around 12 percent of H-1B holders in 2025 were from China, do you have a comment on this?
Lin Jian: I have no comment on the U.S. visa policy.
Bloomberg: Following on the developments with the U.S. sanctions relating to Iran, we saw that there have been new sanctions on entities, individuals and vessels, including on some Chinese firms. Is China willing to change some of its behaviors and interactions with Iran to comply with U.S. demands? If so, what kind of actions is China considering to take?
Lin Jian: China’s cooperation with Iran is conducted within the framework of international law, thus should not be disrupted. China is closely following the developments, and will do everything necessary to firmly safeguard its rights and interests.
CNBC: The U.S. said that it would give countries a timeline on when to shut down the actions that it has identified. We’re wondering if China has received any sort of timeline or has any plans to address the China-based entities and individuals named in the Treasury announcement?
Lin Jian: We are closely following the developments, and will do everything necessary to firmly safeguard our rights and interests.

====================================================================================================

Gaza's cancer patients are running out of time for treatment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:00:56 UTC
19:00:56 KST

Breadcrumb
Between the tent and the cancer ward: Gaza's patients wait for a treatment that may never come
Karima Abu Al-Saud lies motionless on an iron bed inside the Gaza Cancer Centre at Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, receiving the second of three chemotherapy doses she takes over three days every 21 days, since her cancer diagnosis in October 2025.
The 60-year-old mother of eight, four sons and four daughters, breathes with great difficulty, her frail body barely moving as she turns her face from side to side, hoping to ease the pain that keeps intensifying.
Her voice fades to nothing under the weight of the pain until her movements, her gaze, and her head settle in one position, as though she were breathing her last, only her index finger occasionally lifting, a gesture toward God, asking for relief, as if to say she has no one left but Him.
Time passes slowly under the medical protocol prescribed for Karima, while a nurse checks on her periodically in the patients' hall to make sure the chemotherapy dose is being administered properly through to the end.
In front of this scene stands her eldest daughter, 36-year-old Mayada, herself a mother of three, watching her mother's every movement.
With each groan from her mother, the daughter winces, turns away to hide her tears, then returns to hold her mother's hands, offering words and prayers.
Gaza's 'compound hell'
Mayada describes her mother's condition: cancer in the bone of the lower spine's left side, which later spread to the lungs, after her chance for treatment abroad was delayed since diagnosis, despite having received a referral for treatment outside Gaza.
She has accompanied her mother since the diagnosis, through every treatment available, unable to imagine losing her given the disease's progression and the lack of both adequate local treatment and permission to leave for care abroad.
"My mother's life is a compound hell," Mayada tells The New Arab.
"Unprecedented weakness and wasting, constant pain throughout her body, complete loss of appetite, inability to move, sometimes total loss of movement so she cannot walk, and screaming from pain that never stops, without us being able to ease it. Even strong painkillers don't work," she adds.
"My mother takes a dose over three days every 21 days," she adds. "After each dose, she remains in near-total physical collapse for at least two weeks, as if absent from the world except for her breathing. Just as she begins to recover, for a week or less, the next dose comes due."
Mayada lives in a tent after being displaced from Rafah in May 2024, like her mother and the rest of the family, who are also displaced in tents in Al-Mawasi, Khan Younis. They live in conditions that the healthy could barely endure, she says, let alone a cancer patient who needs proper medical, environmental, and living conditions and specialised care.
Mayada describes interrupted access to the medicines and painkillers her mother needs, unavailable in hospitals or commercial pharmacies.
"Medicine shortage has been a constant crisis since her diagnosis," she says.
"Some days a type is available; other days it isn't, so she survives on incomplete medication, which worsens her condition. Our only hope of not losing my mother is getting her treatment outside Gaza, at specialised cancer centres, so she might survive longer and not be denied her right to treatment and life," she explains.
"Staying in Gaza means a pre-written death sentence for my mother. The doctor treating her case from the beginning was shocked to learn that she had not left Gaza for treatment, especially since her case is classified as extremely urgent. He recommended urgent transfer, as her condition keeps deteriorating and there is no local capacity for precise diagnosis and treatment."
Karima spoke to The New Arab before receiving her chemotherapy dose, while still able to talk, despite severe hearing loss.
She affirmed her right to life, whether through treatment available in Gaza or permission to travel abroad for it.
"Our home was destroyed, we were displaced to Al-Mawasi, we live in worn-out tents, we've lost everything we own, and on top of all this, we're denied treatment," Karima says.
"At the height of my grief and weakness, have mercy on me; do whatever it takes to save my life."
Crying, in her most sorrowful moment, she adds: "I hope God extends my life so I can perform Hajj, that's my most important dream. I also dream of marrying off my youngest son Ali, who is over 26, but our financial situation doesn't currently allow it."
Karima receives chemotherapy, like other cancer patients, at the Gaza Cancer Centre in Khan Younis, a structure made of agricultural greenhouse arches and iron poles, covered in nylon and cloth, its interior and exterior divided by sheet metal, wood, and fabric, its floor made of tiles meant for gardens and streets.
But the space is designated only for diagnosis and treatment, with no wards for patients to stay overnight. The centre's administration has had to allocate part of two rooms inside Nasser Medical Complex's wards, in two separate buildings, for male and female cancer patients who need to stay overnight.
'I fear I won't see tomorrow'
In the men's internal medicine ward at Nasser Medical Complex, 33-year-old Basel Abu Al-Aynayn was admitted with lung cancer after his condition deteriorated and he could barely breathe, having also lost the ability to move.
He has spent more than a week seeking relief and doesn't know when he'll leave, since his health doesn't allow him to be discharged.
Basel is accustomed to coming to the hospital periodically, staying a week or more whenever his health deteriorates, living his life moving between a worn-out tent he's been displaced to since May 2024, in wretched living and medical conditions, and the hospital, whose corridors he now knows by heart.
The young man lies in bed, an oxygen tube never leaving his nose, whether in hospital or in the tent, to preserve his ability to breathe and stay alive, especially since he went without treatment from the start of the war until early this year, as it was completely unavailable in Gaza.
His face and wasted body make him look far older than his years. His journey with cancer began in 2021, when he received chemotherapy inside Gaza before being transferred to Al-Muttala Hospital (Augusta Victoria) in Jerusalem, where he received seven doses, the last in September before the war. A new dose was scheduled for October, but the war prevented it.
Basel, who worked as a taxi driver and stopped working entirely before the war, groans more than he speaks, barely able to move his weak body, helped by his brother, his wife, and relatives who come to check on him.
"Since I resumed treatment at the start of this year, there's been no improvement in my health. It's only deteriorated further, and I now spend more time in the hospital than in my tent," he tells The New Arab.
"I often lose the ability to breathe and can't be without the oxygen cylinder, and sometimes I go days unable to walk. I was supposed to leave for treatment outside Gaza before the Israeli army entered Rafah in May 2024 and occupied the Rafah crossing," he adds.
"I called the World Health Organization and was told to prepare to travel, and afterwards I was told at least twice more to prepare to travel, but it never happened."
Basel considers staying in Gaza "a sentence of quick death, not slow," his health having deteriorated unprecedentedly. Holding back tears, he adds: "I am dying daily, and I fear I won't see tomorrow."
The young man falls silent for a long time before his only daughter, four-year-old Sawsan, rushes into his arms, telling him in innocent words: "Baba, don't cry. I swear you'll live with us, my love, Baba. Please don't cry."
He wipes away his tears and kisses his only daughter, while relatives around him try to soften the scene with words of hope, wishes for healing, blessings, and wishes for a long life.
A nurse arriving to give Basel his available prescribed medicine breaks the grief filling the room, offering him more hope that he might travel soon.
He responds with an angry question: "Why does Israel prevent patients from travelling? Why must I wait three years, and my turn still hasn't come? The world is obligated to intervene to stop us from dying," he adds.
"Before the war, I was scheduled to begin radiation therapy, unavailable in Gaza, and was set to travel to Al-Muttala Hospital in Jerusalem to receive it, but that still hasn't happened."
'Nothing left but prayers'
In Al-Mawasi, Sharifa Abu Muammar believes that her 21-year-old son Yasser could die at any moment. She doesn't know if he has weeks, days or hours left with him.
The grieving mother stands over her son, who has a blood disorder, elevated haemoglobin, and adrenal insufficiency, causing developmental and neurological delay and spinal curvature.
She listens to Yasser scream at the top of his voice from pain that has robbed him of his mental capacity. She watches him breathe through a special tube, and he is unable to control his bladder or bowels due to his deteriorating condition.
Sharifa says through tears: "This is the first time I've felt my son is in truly grave danger. His health has deteriorated unprecedentedly amid limited treatment and no chance of treatment abroad. My son also has a physical disability and crawls to meet his needs."
The 51-year-old adds, still in pain, as her son continues to groan, "He used to live a life suited to his disability, in appropriate housing conditions before the war, displacement, and the destruction of our home east of Khan Younis, but things have worsened amid Israel's war. Yasser's illness also deteriorated at the same time, and any semblance of normal life vanished in the tents we're displaced in."
Her son's screams, "Ah, ah, ah," interrupt her, and she responds: "I swear I don't know what to do for you... my heart is breaking for him. His whole body is covered in sores and turning bluer by the day," she says.
"There's nothing left for us now but prayers."
Gaza's cancer drug shortage
Zaher al-Wahaidi, director of the health information centre at Gaza's Ministry of Health, describes the situation as “compounded and complicated”.
Early in the war, the Israeli army destroyed the Turkish-Palestinian Friendship Hospital, Gaza's only specialist oncology hospital.
He says Gaza now has 11,500 cancer patients, including 4,000 waiting for medical evacuation abroad. At least 1,500 cancer patients have been killed, he says, with two deaths recorded each day due to patients being denied treatment abroad and the lack of alternative medicines in Gaza.
Cancer care has also been reduced to less than 10 percent of its pre-war capacity, according to Zaher. Three temporary centres now operate across northern, central and southern Gaza, each occupying only a room or small section of an existing government hospital.
Before Israel's genocide, cancer patients had a dedicated hospital with specialist services.
He compares the limited cancer care now available with the services once provided by the destroyed specialist hospital. The Turkish-Palestinian Friendship Hospital had 180 beds and departments for diagnosis, treatment, surgery, palliative care, nutrition and psychological support. Most of these services are now either extremely limited or unavailable.
The computerised systems used for oncology care also collapsed at the start of the war. This included computers, an integrated information system and cloud servers. As a result, accurate and detailed patient data, including diagnoses and treatment plans, were lost.
"Of eight mammogram machines designated for early cancer detection, only two remain functional now," Zaher says.
"There is no MRI machine or CT scanner at all, and only a limited number of new X-ray machines, since the war destroyed all the equipment that was available at the oncology hospital, and we haven't been able to repair a single device."
He adds that Israel has not allowed medical equipment or devices to enter Gaza since the start of its war on the besieged enclave.
Medical supplies, laboratory materials, and medicines have been allowed in only very limited quantities and not in accordance with declared local needs.
Israeli occupation forces also destroyed all the equipment inside the Turkish-Palestinian Friendship Hospital. During its incursions into Gaza, the hospital was turned into a command, control and detention centre, leaving none of its former facilities or equipment intact, Zaher shares.
He says cancer patients now face several major problems: shortages of treatment protocols and painkillers, the lack of centres providing complete cancer care, fragmented medical services and being denied travel abroad for treatment, adding that 61 percent of cancer medicines and treatments are at zero stock.
This means patients are missing 61 percent of their medication needs, either completely or partially. Some receive a treatment once but cannot complete the course, while others receive it only intermittently.
"About 46 percent of the essential medicines list, comprising 593 drugs, is at zero stock," Zaher tells The New Arab.
"This includes emergency, surgical, intensive care, primary care, and chronic disease medications, for cancer, heart disease, diabetes, and blood pressure, with the percentage varying between different medicines, and the percentage of cancer medications at zero stock is among the highest."
Zaher describes the situation facing cancer patients as "a death sentence upon them". He says the most urgent need is to allow patients to travel abroad for treatment, giving them a chance of survival. Until that happens, he says chemotherapy must be allowed into Gaza without the current restrictions, along with other cancer medicines, medical supplies, equipment, laboratory materials and screening and diagnostic devices.
"Without that, we will continue counting cancer deaths daily," he says, adding that the figures only include recorded cases, while many others have never reached hospitals or received the medical examinations they needed because of the collapse of Gaza's health system.
Mohamed Solaimane is a Gaza-based journalist with bylines in regional and international outlets, focusing on humanitarian and environmental issues

Individualism and income appear to shape relationship status across 59 countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:00:26 UTC
19:00:26 KST

Whether a person remains single is linked to a combination of personal circumstances and the cultural values of the country they live in. A large study published in PLOS One found that personal traits like age and income relate to relationship status differently depending on how much a society values individualism and adaptability. These findings suggest that singlehood is shaped by broad cultural environments rather than just individual choices.
Over the past few decades, the traditional family structure has shifted in many parts of the world. In the United States, Canada, and various European and Asian nations, the population of single adults has grown steadily. Researchers want to understand the broad societal forces driving this trend. Past sociological research has mostly focused on personal characteristics, such as education levels or economic stability.
Psychologists Marta Kowal and Katarzyna Adamczyk, based at the University of Wrocław and Adam Mickiewicz University respectively, wanted to expand on this past research. They suspected that personal demographic characteristics might operate differently depending on the surrounding culture. The researchers decided to examine how national culture interacts with personal circumstances to predict relationship status.
To measure culture, the researchers relied on a framework known as the Minkov-Hofstede model. This model divides national cultures into two main spectrums. The first spectrum is individualism versus collectivism. Individualistic cultures value personal freedom, independence, and self-reliance. Collectivistic cultures prioritize tradition, strict social rules, and group loyalty.
The second cultural spectrum is flexibility versus monumentalism. Flexible cultures, often found in East Asia, value adaptability, humility, self-control, and long-term goals like acquiring a good education. Monumentalist cultures, which the model associates with regions like Latin America and the Arab world, value an unchanging and proud sense of self. Monumentalist societies encourage people to follow their impulses, seek immediate gratification, and remain invariant in their values.
To conduct the study, Kowal and Adamczyk analyzed an existing dataset from the World Values Survey. The researchers utilized a large sample of 71,169 individuals across 59 countries. The data, collected between 2017 and 2021, included detailed interviews conducted at the participants’ homes.
The researchers categorized participants based on their relationship status. People who were married or living together as married were classified as partnered. Those who were single and never married were classified as single. For the main analysis, the researchers excluded people who were divorced, widowed, or separated.
The researchers then gathered personal details for each participant, including their age, sex, hometown size, education level, income, and employment status. Next, they assigned each participant a cultural score based on their country of residence. They used established national scores for both the individualism and flexibility spectrums.
Finally, the researchers used a statistical technique that allowed them to look at data on multiple levels at once. This method let them evaluate how national cultural trends might alter the effects of personal demographics on a person’s relationship status. A secondary analysis that included divorced and widowed individuals as single yielded the exact same statistical patterns.
The analysis revealed several consistent patterns across all countries. People were more likely to be single if they were younger, male, and living in larger towns. Higher education levels, lower income, and unemployment were also associated with a greater likelihood of being single.
These demographic associations align with expectations from past sociological research. Younger people are still in the phase of searching for a partner. Educational expansion delays entry into the workforce, which often pushes back the timeline for marriage. A lack of economic stability, characterized by unemployment or low income, can discourage people from committing to serious relationships.
The sex and location differences also matched established patterns. Women often face more social pressure to marry, which may make them less likely to remain single compared to men. Living in larger urban areas often correlates with a lower adherence to traditional family values, creating environments where singlehood is more socially accepted.
National culture also played a direct role in predicting relationship status. People living in highly individualistic countries were more likely to be single. Individualism grants people the freedom to behave according to their own beliefs, making a single lifestyle an easier path to choose.
People in less flexible, or more monumentalist, countries were also more likely to be single. Because monumentalist cultures encourage people to follow their immediate impulses and desires rather than prioritizing long-term goals, they may promote short-term dating over settling down into a long-term partnership.
The study uncovered notable interactions between personal traits and cultural values. In more individualistic countries, the link between being single and having a lower income or being unemployed was much stronger. Individualistic societies expect young people to become self-reliant and secure their own financial resources before starting a family. If a person lacks those resources in an individualistic culture, they are highly likely to remain single.
The connection between being male and being single was also stronger in individualistic nations. The researchers proposed that individualistic cultures emphasize independence. This cultural emphasis aligns with the traditional social expectation that men should be self-reliant, potentially making singlehood an expected path for men in those societies.
In monumentalist countries, older age was more strongly associated with singlehood than it was in flexible countries. Monumentalist cultures encourage people to live authentically according to their personal desires rather than conforming to societal expectations. Since older adults tend to conform less to social pressures as they age, they may be more inclined to live independently in societies that celebrate personal authenticity.
The researchers noted a few limitations to their work. The data used in the analysis was observational, meaning it cannot prove cause and effect. While lower income and unemployment predict a higher likelihood of singlehood, it is also possible that living alone leads to different financial outcomes. The relationship between these factors could go in both directions.
The analysis also grouped all single and never-married people into one unified category. Single individuals are a highly diverse group with different dating histories and personal desires. Some people actively choose to remain single, while others are involuntarily single.
Future research could expand on these findings by tracking people over time to observe how their relationship status evolves. Researchers could also look at other cultural dimensions to see how the freedom to choose new social groups affects the likelihood of finding a partner.
The study, “Sociodemographic and cultural factors are related to singlehood rates: A multilevel analysis across 59 countries from the World Values Survey,” was authored by Marta Kowal and Katarzyna Adamczyk.

China’s J-16s face off against Egypt’s Rafales in combat drills as Iran war rumbles on
PLA pilots test strategic reach in 6,000km mission as Middle East conflict pushes Cairo and Beijing closer
Chinese fighter jets have conducted combat training with their Egyptian counterparts in a joint exercise following a major Chinese air force deployment to the Middle East.
The aircraft flew more than 6,000km (3,730 miles) over nine hours to reach Egypt, crossing four countries, according to a report by state broadcaster CCTV. However, it did not specify which four countries the PLA Air Force aircraft flew over, or whether their route approached Iran or any Persian Gulf nations.
“Through cross-border deployment and rapid loading and unloading operations, the exercise tested the air force’s capabilities in long-range force projection, rapid deployment and integrated operations,” CCTV reported.
During the flight, the J-16s conducted aerial refuelling from YU-20 tankers before landing at an airbase in Egypt on August 21, the report said.
The PLA Air Force then unloaded supplies, sorted equipment and coordinated briefings ready for training missions within a single day, according to the report.
“The joint exercises have provided a valuable platform for us pilots to improve our combat capabilities,” Ning Yiming, a pilot taking part in the drill, was quoted as saying.

MADE: bush terminal by NYCEDC empowers creative ecosystem on brooklyn waterfront
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:00:07 UTC
19:00:07 KST

Along Brooklyn’s Sunset Park waterfront, MADE: Bush Terminal is home to a growing community of artisans, designers, and industrial pioneers shaping the future of New York City’s creative economy. To support these urban makers, New York City Economic Development Corporation (NYCEDC)revitalized the historic public building after decades of restricted access, creating productive workspaces designed to fuel local innovation alongside economic benchmarks – including a projected 165 permanent jobs and 2.6 billion USD in economic impact over 30 years. Designed by nARCHITECTS, the MADE (Manufacturers, Artisans, Designers, and Entrepreneurs) campus provides 140,000 square feet of manufacturing space and 30,000 square feet of public event programming. Public Records, a multifaceted music venue that originated in Gowanus, Brooklyn will program the ground floor as a music driven community space. The MADE campus serves as a collaborative incubator where local talent, craft-based enterprises, and technical innovators work side by side, cultivating shared knowledge, sustainable practices, and long-term economic resilience.
‘At MADE: Bush Terminal, NYCEDC continues to bring together design, manufacturing, and artistic partners to expand opportunity for all New Yorkers. By activating more than 66,000 square feet at the Brooklyn Army Terminal and MADE: Bush Terminal, we’re strengthening a thriving industrial ecosystem that supports manufacturers, mission‑driven companies, and the local community,’ said NYCEDC Interim President and CEO Jeanny Pak, ‘cementing Sunset Park’s role as a hub for innovation, entrepreneurship, and inclusive economic growth.’
NYCEDC REVITALIZES HISTORIC BUILDING FOR ECONOMIC GROWTH
Managed by NYCEDC, the project reflects a long-term strategy to modernize historic municipal spaces into drivers of inclusive design and growth. First established in the late 19th century as the largest multi-tenant industrial campus in the United States, Bush Terminal played a pivotal role in New York’s maritime history. Today, NYCEDC brings a new chapter to the waterfront site with advances in environmental stewardship, social equity, and active local engagement. Offering adaptable spaces for emerging enterprises, the initiativeensures that industrial investment directly fosters both job creation and community-centered development.
MADE: Bush Terminal anchors a new era of urban manufacturing on the Brooklyn waterfront
MADE: BUSH TERMINAL SCALES SUNSET PARK’S CREATIVE INDUSTRY
At MADE: Bush Terminal, a curated mix of craft-based and high-tech tenants is redefining contemporary fabrication on the Brooklyn waterfront. Lighting manufacturer Stickbulb expands its presence across campus to over 27,000 square feet in Buildings A and B, consolidating its production, design studio, and showroom into a unified circular design footprint. 3D-printing hub Makelab operates alongside design studios PELLE, Aripack, and MushLume. Together, these studios combine technical expertise with bio-based material exploration to push the boundaries of modern object design.
craft-based and high-tech studios redefine contemporary fabrication at MADE: Bush Terminal
This creative momentum extends across the broader Sunset Park ecosystem, where the neighboring Brooklyn Army Terminal (BAT) hosts audiovisual pioneer Audible Difference, clean-tech B-Corp EcoLogic Solutions, logistics provider GoLocker, and cinema technology leader Otto Nemenz. Complementing this industrial mix, NYCEDC launched the BATWorks climate innovation hub alongside a new cultural partnership with Public Service. With the transformation of 1,000-capacity space into a dynamic venue for live music and large-scale art installations, the project anchors MADE as a landmark model for civic design, material circularity, and creative industry.

Chinese dad’s chemotherapy note prompts food vendor’s US$15 donation, going viral
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:00:07 UTC
19:00:07 KST

Chinese food vendor goes viral after donating US$15 to customer undergoing chemotherapy
Father praises stranger’s compassion for bringing warmth to their darkest days
A street food vendor in central China received widespread acclaim after discreetly slipping 100 yuan (US$15) into a takeaway order for a family whose child was undergoing chemotherapy.
On August 17, Wang Xianhuang, an egg pancake vendor in Hefei, Anhui province, noticed a heartfelt note attached to a food delivery order that read, “For a child undergoing chemotherapy. Please do not include shredded kelp or lettuce. Make half of it non-spicy.”
The message resonated with Wang, prompting him to reflect on the challenges the child and family were facing.
After preparing the pancake, Wang added two complimentary cups of soy milk and tucked 100 yuan in cash inside the package.
The child’s father, surnamed Zhu, was profoundly moved and subsequently shared the story online. His four-year-old son, Haolin, had been diagnosed with leukaemia in February and was currently undergoing treatment.

====================================================================================================

Why AI Watermarks and Detectors Could Backfire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

Claude now watermarks AI-generated text to comply with European Union transparency rules. OpenAI and Google add invisible fingerprints to AI-generated images. And Substack is touting a feature that scans pieces for signs of AI. Will we finally be able to tell what’s real on the Internet? My take: not even close.
In fact, AI watermarks and detectors may leave us worse off by creating a false sense of confidence in content marked as genuine.
Watermarks and detectors are gaining traction as we lose our ability to trust our senses online. Look up the Will Smith eating spaghetti test, and you’ll see just how far AI has come. A 2023 AI-generated video shows the actor slurping spaghetti, face distorted, in a way that breaks physics. By 2025, AI was producing lifelike renditions. Deepfakes are so good that experts recommend families develop secret codewords to identify one another.
“But I know a fake when I see it,” someone might say.
Unfortunately, research consistently shows that you do not. This can feel especially hard to accept given the abundance of AI slop rocketing around the Internet. You may even start to think you can sniff out offending content. It might work, for a little bit. It almost never lasts. Any signal that becomes discernible is one a sophisticated actor will find ways to avoid.
We’ve seen this story before. During the earliest days of the Internet, visual polish at least told you something. Major institutions had the resources needed to produce well-designed websites. Janky-looking sites, on the other hand, screamed “scam!” Information experts directed Internet users to dwell on features such as design, broken links, and typos. But when the Internet changed, the advice didn’t.
A study I led, published in 2022, found that 96% of America’s leading colleges and universities offered outdated advice on how to evaluate online information—long after platforms like Wix, Squarespace, and Photoshop made it easier for bad actors to create fake but convincing-looking websites. Inexpensive software made slick graphics ubiquitous. Educators, however, continued to instruct Internet users to search for visual clues like a game of Where’s Waldo?
The most dangerous legacy of this aesthetic fixation is the inverse illusion: the cognitive tendency to believe that if the presence of a signal proves one thing, its absence proves the opposite. Yes, a site with misspellings that claims to show aliens still isn’t legit. But a beautiful site with a dot-org domain can also be harmful. In 2019, our research group found that nearly half of hate groups had dot-org domains. Bad actors know how to adopt the trappings of credibility.
The same is true with AI. Even if visible flaws sometimes linger, their absence doesn’t mean content is genuine. Yet, too often, experts offer surface-level clues to identifying AI-generated content. This is why in the lead-up to the 2024 elections, Stanford Professor Sam Wineburg and I warned about public officials who advised citizens to pay attention to lighting, strange shadows, or other visual cues to identify deepfakes, even after AI content stopped making these errors. Many 2026 guides to spotting AI content mislead readers with the same poor advice.
Which brings us to AI watermarks and detectors. These approaches, based on hidden signals in content, promise that while we can’t always spot the signs, their algorithms can.
I’m not a software engineer. Yet I was able to easily strip metadata from some AI-generated images just by screenshotting them. Anthropic confirms that file metadata can be “stripped through format conversion, re-saving, screenshots, or other means.” Watermarks like SynthID are stronger and can persist after screenshots. But I was able to use a free online tool to remove a SynthID watermark.
Google admits that the accuracy of detecting watermarked AI text is “greatly reduced” when users thoroughly rewrite what they generate, and that it “is not designed to directly stop motivated adversaries from causing harm.” More broadly, open-weight AI models that can run locally, outside platform terms and conditions, guarantee the spread of unmarked content.
Third-party detectors, too, have a spotty track record. I’ve regularly run AI-generated text through detectors that said it was human and vice versa. Many studies of text, image, and audio detectors find that they don’t work very consistently, and yet, their findings are used as the basis for public accusations. Every detector must confront an arms race with humanizer tools and other workarounds motivated actors find.
I would argue that the biggest problem for detectors and watermarks remains the inverse illusion. Just because content lacks a watermark doesn’t mean it wasn’t produced or edited with AI. As Anthropic notes: “lack of a detected mark doesn’t mean the content wasn’t AI-generated or processed.” Deferring judgment to AI detectors leaves us vulnerable to bad actors who know how to launder content and make it pass muster.
This is a confusing time. Many of us are, understandably, uncertain. In one recent pilot, our research group showed 117 students a confident chatbot answer about local history with hallucinated facts. Half said they weren’t sure if it was true. One student said AI is sometimes right and sometimes wrong and “you never know which is which.”
But just because we can’t trust our eyes or place full faith in detectors doesn’t mean we can’t trust anything. Rather than hunt for visual clues or outsource judgment to detectors and watermarks, we can turn to reputation and context. It’s easy to fake content. It’s much harder to fake a good reputation that’s validated by credible sources.
The next time you see unfamiliar content online, resist the urge to ask, “Does this look like AI?” or run the content through a detector. Instead, ask yourself, “Do I trust where this information is coming from?” Open a new tab and check if reputable people and organizations confirm what you’re seeing.
In an era of dwindling trust, we should not fork over ours to cheap signals or cheap software.

Summer Is Ending With a 'Blood Moon' Lunar Eclipse. Here's What To Know.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

It’s not often that 3.6 billion people—or 44.4% of the world’s population—look at the same thing at the same time. And it’s not often that something comes along that’s worth the attention of all those billions. But that will happen on the evening of Aug. 27 when much of the world will be able to witness a blood moon lunar eclipse, during which 96% of the face of the full moon will fall into Earth’s shadow, glowing a deep orange-red in the process.
Lunar eclipses occur during a full moon, when the Earth is positioned between the sun and the moon, blocking all or most of the solar light that otherwise bathes the lunar surface. On average, lunar eclipses occur two to three times per year, though total lunar eclipses, when the moon is entirely shadowed, make up only 29% of those events. The autumnal color the moon takes on is due to a trick of the Earth’s atmosphere. Not all of the sunlight that would otherwise be striking the moon during an eclipse is blocked by the Earth; some of it leaks around the periphery of the planet and manages to reach the moon. That light streams through the Earth’s atmosphere during its passage to the moon, and some of the wavelengths of visible light—particularly the blue—are absorbed and scattered. What’s left is principally the red spectrum which partially lights the moon. All total lunar eclipses result in blood moons.
In theory, a lunar eclipse ought to occur once a month. On every orbit around the Earth on its 27.3-day journey, after all, the moon will always pass through a point at which the planet sits between it and the sun. But the plane of the moon’s orbit around the Earth is tilted about five degrees compared to the Earth’s orbit around the sun. That means that on some passages behind the Earth the moon avoids the shadow, soaring above or ducking below the planet.
How long will the lunar eclipse last?
An eclipse of the moon plays out slowly. The one that will begin on the evening of Aug. 27 and continue into the early hours of Aug. 28 will last a total of five hours and 38 minutes. Even the most dedicated eclipse chaser, however, may not be able to take it all in. Depending on where in the world an observer is—and this eclipse will be visible in Europe, Africa, North and South America, and western Asia—the moon may set before the eclipse is done or rise after it’s already begun. That will be the case in the Americas, where observers will see an eclipsed moon come up in the skies. Finding a flat area with few buildings and a clean sight line may be necessary to witness the eclipse, since in many places the moon will be low in the sky, close to the horizon. In the U.S., the eclipse will begin at 9:23 p.m. ET on Aug. 27, and end at 3:01 ET the next day.
There are three phases of any lunar eclipse—the penumbral, partial, and total or maximum. The penumbral phase occurs first, when the moon moves into the faint, outer reaches of the Earth’s umbra, or shadow. The partial phase comes next, when the true, darker shadow of the Earth begins to cover the lunar disk. The total or maximum phase is when only a small portion—or none at all—of the moon remains unshadowed. For the upcoming eclipse, the penumbral phase will take one hour and ten minutes, the partial phase one hour and 39 minutes, and the maximum phase, when the moon will be 96% obscured, will also take one hour and 39 minutes. That maximum shadow will occur at 12:12 a.m. ET. The eclipse will then return to the partial and penumbral phases before the moon soars on and leaves the Earth’s shadow behind.
What is an 'eclipse season'?
This eclipse occurs in a busy time for the skies. On Aug. 12, just over two weeks before the lunar eclipse is set to occur, there was a total eclipse of the sun, visible in Spain, Portugal, Iceland, Greenland, and Siberia. There is actually such a thing as an eclipse season, a month-long stretch occurring twice a year—in the summer and winter—when the moon passes the point in its five-degree orbit that the Earth, moon, and sun align in a way to make both types of eclipses possible.
If you fancy eclipses, you’re well advised to take this one in while you can. The next total lunar eclipse will not be until Dec. 31, 2027 to Jan. 1, 2028. New Years Eve fireworks will be going off that night, but they will be nothing compared to the sky show the Earth, the sun, and the moon will serve up.

Border Wall Construction Threatens 6,000 Years of History on Private Lands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Outrage has exploded over border infrastructure that recently began tearing up pristine desert landscapes in Big Bend National Park. But there’s a quieter battle taking place on private lands in Texas, where the US border wall is set to cut across some of North America's richest archaeological sites, digging up ancient indigenous artifacts and fracturing millennia-old rock art in its path.
The US Department of Homeland Security and Customs and Border Protection awarded billions of dollars in contracts this year toward the construction of a wall and other barriers in West Texas along a remote 500-plus-mile (800-plus-kilometer) riverfront expanse of the US-Mexico border that includes Big Bend National Park and other idyllic parklands.
Bipartisan backlash against border wall construction in the national park was swift, ultimately prompting DHS to scuttle plans for a 30-foot steel bollard wall, instead replacing it with miles of riverside vehicle barriers and 200-plus miles of road construction. Bulldozers began clearing along the Rio Grande corridor near Santa Elena Canyon on August 6.
Construction has since been paused in the park in response to lawsuits. But the agency is still planning to construct the wall, as well as a web of road construction, over mountains and across canyons outside the national park. That includes private property that ranchers and other landowners say have archeological sites worth protecting, too. And they’re concerned that construction of the wall will bifurcate their own land and damage archeological sites, many of which have yet to be fully studied.
Archeologist Bryon Schroeder has been digging on rancher Jeff Fort’s property for two years. Schroeder runs Sul Ross University’s Center for Big Bend Studies, a research program dedicated to studying the cultural, historical, and archeological legacy of the region. He removes 4 inches (10 centimeters) of sediment at a time, and his meticulous digs have uncovered pottery and melted adobe slick building material from as early as the year AD 800. He’s found turquoise, too, and marine shells, both signs of trade outside the region. Evidence shows the site is related to Paquimé, an UNESCO World Heritage site that’s 200 miles away in Mexico.
Schroeder’s dig site, Canta Recio, is directly in the path of the proposed wall. Some of it is set to be bulldozed over. If the wall is built, other parts of the site will also become effectively inaccessible.
Schroeder likens Canta Recio to how Egyptians set up shop along the Nile, surmising the site was settled four or five times between 800 and 1400 by groups who were likely drawn to fertile land afforded by routine floods. Of course, those floods also mean that groups were eventually forced to move on when the Rio Grande overtopped its banks, only for another group to eventually settle the area once the silt firmed up. A settlement, a flood, an exit, on repeat.
“There's some bigger, cooler sites up the river that are just insane,” Schroeder said. “They have so much pottery, they have Mesoamerican copper bells, they have turquoise. They have all sorts of crazy stuff.”
The paradox facing Schroeder and other archeologists: They can't fully measure what's at risk because many of the archeological sites exist on private ranches and have never been studied.
That means construction may erase history before anyone gets to record it. A Customs and Border Protection spokesperson told WIRED that the agency is conducting environmental and cultural reviews to minimize impacts and balance operational needs with responsible land stewardship.
But previous studies haven’t stopped historically important sites from being sentenced to destruction. A 30-foot bollard wall is set to go right through the Polvo site, in Redford, Texas, which is home to a prehistoric village complete with burial ground dating back to the 1300s. The same site also has evidence of a Spanish mission that was built in the 1600s. Eagle Nest Canyon in Langtry, one of the most significant and intensively studied archeological sites in all of Texas, is also slated to see some form of barrier erected through it. That site includes the southernmost bison jump site in the US, where Native Americans hunted the animals en masse by funneling them over a cliff.
Patrick Zuberbueler, a rancher 350 miles downriver in Comstock, Texas, population 268, spent his youth picnicking in the shadows of 6,000-year-old rock art, with some displays up to 50 feet tall and hundreds of feet wide, across his family’s property. The government took some of that land by eminent domain in the 1960s and 1970s, forming the Amistad Reservoir and Seminole Canyon State Park, but he and his family still hold onto thousands of acres.
As a child, Zuberbueler would catch minnows in a stream running through Painted Shelter, a limestone rock shelter on his family’s property. To him, it was “a place we’d go picnicking.” To archeologist and rock art expert Carolyn Boyd, it’s “one of the most important archeological sites in the region.”
Painted Shelter has three distinct styles of rock art, painted between 6,000 and 1,000 years ago. Rock artworks encode stories and cosmologies, and are “libraries of human knowledge,” says Boyd, a research professor at Texas State University in San Marcos who founded Shumla Archaeological Research and Education Center in 1998.
Painted Shelter is also right in the path of border construction.
“A vehicle barrier going in just immediately above it will destroy the stream, and it will potentially destroy the paintings themselves,” says Boyd, one of the nation’s leading scholars on rock art.
Vibration from construction could potentially cause the limestone to spall, or sheet off, she says, leaving the rocky canvas in tatters. She knows of 12 other rock art sites across the region that are also at risk from construction, while another 79 will become inaccessible.
The region around the Zuberbueler ranch, known as the Lower Pecos Canyonlands Archeological District, was designated as a National Historic Landmark on January 13, 2021, under the first Trump administration. Federal law dictates that agencies “to the maximum extent possible undertake such planning and actions as may be necessary to minimize harm” to National Historic Landmarks. But with the National Historic Preservation Act one of dozens of laws waived by the Department of Homeland Security in its pursuit of a border wall, those requirements to minimize harm are off the table.
For Zuberbueler, pushing back against the border barrier isn’t just about the archaeology his land holds. It’s about the legacy of his great-grandfather, who started working the land in 1898.
“The ranch continues to shrink and shrink and shrink, and you can't effectively ranch something that way,” Zuberbueler says. “They're hurting our livelihood as producers.”
Boyd, who has dedicated four decades to unearthing the history behind the region’s rock art, says she feels like she’s living a nightmare. “Maybe it’s wishful thinking,” she says, but she hopes she can get the government to understand the significance of the region’s archeology and revise its plans to rely on technology to patrol the area rather than physical infrastructure.
But time is seemingly running short to make that case. Several miles of steel bollards lay in piles at staging areas, and several temporary workforce housing “man camps” have cropped up on newly cleared land across the region. Locals say wall contractors have already bulldozed private property before they were legally allowed to, damaging irrigation systems and clearing vegetation. But some locals aren’t ready to give up. And there are signs of resistance to development on private lands elsewhere, including suits filed earlier this month by residents in San Ygnacio, which sits about 275 miles further south of the Big Bend region.
“It's almost unfathomable to even put it into context, the different ways that this can be detrimental to us,” Zuberbueler said about the border construction. “We're not going to go down without a fight.”

Kyiv • UNN

"Based on the analysis of the data, damage to a MiG-29 fighter jet at the ‘Millerovo’ airfield in Russia’s Rostov region on August 24, 2026, was confirmed," the General Staff stated.

Iran-linked Swiss oil trader hit by US sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
09:59:21 UTC
18:59:21 KST

Iran-linked Swiss oil trader hit by US sanctions
The Trump administration has extended sanctions against the sprawling network of Iranian oil trader Hossein Shamkhani, targeting his Wellbred group of commodities businesses as part of a wide-ranging set of measures intended to isolate Iran.
The Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control has sanctioned Singapore-based Wellbred Capital, United Arab Emirates-based Wellbred Trading FZCO and Switzerland-based Wellbred Trading, according to a notice on Monday. It also named a French cooking oil refinery described as being owned by Wellbred, La Nivernaise de Raffinage SAS.
+ Iran war: Switzerland expects bumper tax from oil traders
“Shamkhani built Wellbred as a company outside the network’s Iranian business, though Shamkhani is ultimately responsible for Wellbred’s operation,” the Treasury said in a statement.
Washington has already sanctioned Shamkhani, the son of late senior Iranian security official Ali Shamkhani, and other companies in his network.
The Singapore-based Wellbred entity did not immediately respond to calls and emails requesting comment. The UAE and Swiss-based companies also did not immediately respond to queries outside normal business hours.
Washington unveiled sanctions against dozens of entities on Monday, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent saying the US was focusing on five of Iran’s “most vital lifelines,” including digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping.
Bessent also threatened to sanction a major financial institution over Iran ties by the end of this week but didn’t name the target.

Kremlin rebukes Finland's Stubb over support for long-range Ukrainian strikes
MOSCOW, Aug 25 - The Kremlin said on Tuesday that remarks by Finnish President Alexander Stubb approving of Ukrainian strikes on Russian territory showed that he, along with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, belonged to the "party of war."
Stubb has backed Ukraine's long-range strikes deep inside Russia, saying that such attacks, including on civilian logistics centres, increase the cost of Moscow's war effort and could help bring it to the negotiating table.
Asked about Stubb's comments, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said they had come as a surprise and showed that the Finnish leader, like Britain's Burnham, wanted the war in Ukraine to continue.
Peskov also accused Stubb and other Western leaders of misleading their own voters by claiming that it was possible for Russia to be strategically defeated. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

EU posts $25.4B trade deficit in Q2, 1st time since 2023
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
09:58:59 UTC
18:58:59 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
The EU recorded a trade deficit of €21.8 billion ($25.4 billion) in the second quarter of 2026, as non-EU goods imports exceeded exports, official data showed on Tuesday.
 
According to Eurostat, goods imports from non-EU countries reached €701.8 billion, while exports stood at €680 billion during the April-June period.
 
This marks the bloc's first trade deficit since the second quarter of 2023, ending a period of positive trade balances.
 
The trade deficit was driven primarily by an expanding energy deficit, which grew to €101.1 billion in the second quarter from €71.3 billion in the previous quarter.
 
Deficits also widened in raw materials, reaching €9.4 billion, and in other manufactured goods, which rose to €9.1 billion.
 
Meanwhile, trade surpluses declined in key sectors, as machinery and vehicle surpluses fell to €23.2 billion, and other goods dropped to €9.1 billion.
Conversely, chemical surpluses expanded to €54.0 billion, while food and drink surpluses grew to €11.5 billion.
 
Quarter-on-quarter, EU exports increased 5.4% or €34.9 billion, while imports surged 9.9% or €63.4 billion.
The growth halted a continuous decline in trade since mid-2025 that was previously driven by global tariff tensions.

Vietnam targets universal electronic health records by 2030
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
17:58:35 CST
18:58:35 KST

HANOI, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- Vietnam aims to provide electronic health records and lifelong health management for 100 percent of its population by 2030, local daily Suc Khoe&Doi Song reported Tuesday.
It is one of the goals set out in the national target program on culture, society, rural development, and ethnic minority and mountainous areas for the 2026-2030 period, which was recently approved by Vietnam's 16th National Assembly.
The program, with a budget of over 808.5 trillion Vietnamese dong (about 31.1 billion U.S. dollars), also aims to ensure that 100 percent of local centers for disease control are capable of testing for pathogens, antigens and antibodies of dangerous infectious diseases, as well as testing clean water quality and school sanitation conditions in accordance with Ministry of Health regulations. ■

Filipino surgeons perform Philippine 1st telesurgery in China's Shanghai
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
17:58:12 CST
18:58:12 KST

MANILA, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- Two Philippine surgeons performed the country's first telesurgery on Tuesday in China's Shanghai by operating a surgical robot on a 53-year-old Filipino patient in Quezon City, the Philippines, according to local media reports.
The procedure was carried out at the Urology Center of the Philippines, using high-speed internet and robotic technology for real-time coordination between Shanghai and Manila. The surgeons operated from Shanghai, with a local team on standby at the Quezon City site, according to GMA News.
The surgery marked a new step in China-Philippines medical cooperation, following previous collaborations in liver transplants, physician training, and cloud-based medical platforms.
The Philippines, an archipelago with unevenly distributed medical resources, could benefit from remote surgery as a new option for patients in remote areas. ■
