Data centers going off-grid does not make them good neighbors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:44:09 UTC
01:44:09 KST

As a forest of pitchforks approaches the US’ data centers, “big tech” can turn to a time-tested strategy: hiding. As in, behind the meter. That phrase refers to onsite power generation that can offer backup for data centers or, at the extreme, let them bypass the electricity grid completely.
The latter seems increasingly attractive because of yearslong wait times for a grid hookup, now compounded by growing general opposition to data centers. When Texas Governor Greg Abbott unexpectedly paused grid connections for data centers in the state earlier this month, shares of traditional power plant operators took a hit, but stocks bounced for companies that make the engines and turbines for generating power separately. As if to punctuate this, it emerged that Amazon.com Inc has begun work on a giant data-center campus in West Texas hosting up to 7.65 gigawatts of gas-fueled power, more than the entire generating capacity of some states.
However, going off-grid comes at a steep cost and could actually make the hyperscalers bigger targets, not smaller ones.
Just like hospitals or even houses, data centers routinely install some backup power to keep running if the grid falters. That is different from going off-grid altogether. Amazon’s GW Ranch project, for example, is described as a “private grid,” albeit one that is the size of a city.
The benefit of going it alone is that companies avoid waiting perhaps four years or more for the local utility to connect them, with onsite generation up and running in something more like 18 months — a significant advantage in the accelerating AI arms race. Self-powering also offers a rebuttal to criticism that data centers are raising utility bills for their neighbors.
It is a beguiling argument, but half-baked.
Maddening as the power grid can be, it has three advantages: It is the cheapest source of electricity; it is not perfect, but still remarkably reliable; and it already exists. There is a reason hyperscalers previously tried to cut deals to hive off some of that valuable grid for themselves (thereby helping to fuel the backlash against data centers).
Going off-grid means building your own; that means obtaining not just the generators, but all the associated equipment, too, much of which is also backlogged. You also have to install more than you need to replicate the grid’s big selling point — redundancy — because your turbines can also go down. That reduces utilization, raising unit costs further, which can then be compounded if your data center eventually does hook up to the regular grid.
Hyperscalers are not known for their sensitivity to energy costs, so maybe none of these inefficiencies matter to them. If the US is truly engaged in the opening stages of a battle for artificial intelligence (AI) supremacy with existential consequences, why not reach for the quickest, if imperfect, solutions? If there was a war on, you would not complain if an ammo plant was running on diesel engines.
Therein lies part of the wider problem. Most Americans do not view data centers as essential defense assets, but rather as unsightly, resource-hogging nuisances that enrich the super wealthy and make a “product” that could possibly put them out of a job. Despite AI’s potential, and real tax windfalls for some localities that host data centers, they have an image problem that has festered and inevitably jumped from opinion polls to statehouses. Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro is the latest of his peers to reverse course and impose strict constraints on data centers.
Hyperscalers fumbled the important selling point that, done right, the extra load that data centers put on the grid could actually reduce bills by spreading the network’s fixed costs across more kilowatt-hours. Withdrawing from the grid would kick away that pitch completely as well as magnify the disconnect between these AI factories and the local communities in which they land.
The pollution aspect is also important. There is already a legal battle over gas turbines installed without an air permit to power a Memphis, Tennessee, data center — with the warm and fuzzy name of Colossus — owned by xAI, a unit of SpaceX. The Sierra Club and Public Citizen contend that another data center project, in San Antonio, Texas, is bypassing regulatory obligations for significant sources of pollution and have signaled their intent to file suit. Given the sheer scale of the mostly gas-fired onsite capacity now being planned, such as for Amazon’s project, data centers run the risk of becoming the next Keystone XL.
There are other routes to solving AI’s power quandary, which involve a mixture of demand response, batteries and, yes, behind-the-meter generation — but in the context of also being active participants on the grid. Retreating to islands, and letting everyone around cope with the consequences, is not going to fly. Rather, developers must work harder to demonstrate benefits they can offer to the communities in which they land and must integrate somehow. Becoming a good member of society does not begin with retreating from it.
Liam Denning is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering energy. A former banker, he edited the Wall Street Journal’s “Heard on the Street” column and wrote the Financial Times’ “Lex” column. Humble balloon gets green makeover
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:44:06 UTC
01:44:06 KST

A global symbol of parties and celebrations but an environmental headache, the humble balloon is undergoing a green revolution thanks to British researchers.
Researchers at Imperial College London say they have developed the first fully biodegradable balloon and hope to bring it to market within two years.
“So there was hundreds of trials. We had many, many failures,” said Juliana Cumming, a doctorate student at the university and co-creator of the “Bioloon,” a 100 percent biodegradable balloon.
Photo: AFP
In a university laboratory, the 29-year-old proudly showed a flask containing a precious yellow liquid.
Once solidified, it becomes a soft, elastic material with a texture comparable to that of a conventional balloon.
However, there is one crucial difference — it breaks down completely within nine months unlike traditional balloons, Cumming said.
The Bioloon is the result of a public-private partnership launched by Charlotte Melia, an events entrepreneur, who describes herself as environmentally minded.
“I was a party planner for over 10 years and ... I was very sustainably focused. The final stumbling block for me was the balloon waste,” she said.
“We were putting out thousands of party balloons every single week,” she said, but they were only there “for a matter of hours simply to be popped and thrown in the trash.”
The final straw came when she realized “balloons were non-biodegradable” even though the packaging said they would say break up “at the rate of an oak leaf.”
Convinced that a sustainable alternative was possible, Melia decided with an associate to put up about 30,000 (US$41,000) to part fund Cumming’s doctoral research.
The environmental impact of traditional balloons, which despite their advertising do not degrade, is largely unknown to the general public.
However, a number of studies have documented the dangers posed by balloons once they end up in nature, particularly for marine life and birds.
A 2019 study by the University of Tasmania, published in Scientific Reports, found balloons were “the highest-risk plastic debris item” for seabirds, carrying a mortality risk 32 times higher than ingesting hard plastics.
Imperial College’s chemical engineering department estimates that between 20 and 25 billion balloons are purchased worldwide every year.
Cumming spent three years developing her formula. The starting point is the same as for an ordinary balloon: natural latex derived from the sap of the rubber tree, native to the Amazon and has changed little since the balloon was invented in 1824.
“In order to turn the natural latex into something that we refer to as rubber it goes through this process called sulphur vulcanization,” she said.
That involves adding “sulphur accelerators, antioxidants, and activators into the material” which “prevents the biodegradation of balloons” and also leaks “toxic chemicals into the environment.”
It was this stage of the manufacturing process which became the focus of Cumming’s research. “Our balloon is still made with natural latex, but we blend it with another biodegradable polymer and we don’t add any of these additives that are used in traditional balloons,” she said.
“So this retains the biodegradability,” she added, declining to reveal further details of the patented process.
According to the creators, the Bioloon breaks down regardless of where it ends up.
The researchers “tested it in soil, seawater and deionized water. It degraded in all of those conditions ... and we estimate that it would biodegrade within about nine months,” she said.
Importantly for all those planning a shindig, the balloon inflates as easily as a conventional one.
For Melia, the technology’s potential extends far beyond party decorations, and could be adapted for everyday and medical products, including household gloves, surgical gloves, latex clothing and condoms.

Chinese professor describes gig work as form of ‘welfare’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:44:02 UTC
01:44:02 KST

The term “flexible employment” has gone viral in China after a prominent economics professor described gig work as a form of “welfare,” drawing widespread public anger and highlighting deep anxieties over job insecurity.
Zhang Dandan (張丹丹), a professor of economics and deputy dean at Peking University’s National School of Development, made the remarks during a discussion on social protection for gig workers, on the popular financial show Let’s Talk (張丹丹) last week.
She said that from the perspective of labor economics, “flexibility itself is a form of welfare.”
Photo: Reuters
While regular employees trade schedule flexibility for pensions and other benefits, flexible workers enjoy greater control over their time at the cost of weaker social protections, Zhang said.
The comments triggered a fierce backlash over the weekend, with social media users accusing Zhang of being oblivious to the harsh realities of the gig economy.
Zhang did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.
The controversy has struck a nerve for many in China, where a cooling economy has made secure, full-time employment harder to find.
The think tank China New Employment Forms Research Center estimates the number of flexible workers — those without permanent full-time contracts — would rise to 320 million this year from 280 million last year.
That represents about 44 percent of China’s urban workforce and is roughly equivalent to the entire population of the US.
The rise of gig jobs in China, where employers are not mandated to make social insurance contributions, heightens long-term risks for the nation’s already strained welfare and pension systems, some industry experts have said.
Prominent nationalist commentator Hu Xijin (胡錫進), a former editor at the state-backed Global Times newspaper, called Zhang’s remarks “shocking” and “unacceptable.”
“She has paid the price for her reputation for speaking this way, and the responsibility lies with her,” Hu wrote on his Weibo account, adding that she should “respond to public opinion, explain where necessary, and apologize where appropriate.”
Despite the backlash, some social media users pointed out that Zhang’s academic career had focused largely on documenting the struggles of gig workers and advocating for their social security.
Zhang last year said that on-demand workers made up about 31 percent of the workforce in China’s manufacturing sector.
During peak seasons, that proportion can rise to as high as 80 percent for large manufacturers with more than 10,000 workers, she said.
Nevertheless, Zhang’s framing of “flexibility” as a benefit was seen as insensitive.
“Such comments from experts are no less than rubbing salt into the wounds of those without job security,” one Weibo user wrote.
Another user pointed out the relentless pressure faced by delivery drivers and couriers: “Every day, they are racing against the platform’s algorithm at all costs, without rest ... [flexible work] is precisely the most unavoidable of choices, not a preference.”

Disaster resilience begins in the community
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:44:02 UTC
01:44:02 KST

Climate change has progressed far more rapidly and with greater intensity than some thought possible. Events once thought of as once-in-a-century occurrences — urban flooding caused by torrential rain, powerful typhoons and severe droughts — have become increasingly common, while earthquakes can compound disaster risks in an aging society.
Emergency personnel and public servants know all too well the limits of what can be achieved at disaster sites. When extreme natural disasters strike simultaneously, government emergency-response resources are inevitably stretched to capacity.
Government assistance is the final line of defense, but what often makes a difference in a disaster is the ability of the public to protect themselves and the capacity of communities to assist each other in the early stages of a disaster.
To confront extreme weather, we must overturn the traditional view of disaster preparedness as something passively received, and instead incorporate it into our personal and collective approach to risk management.
Traditional disaster-preparedness campaigns tend to treat disasters as separate categories, but under extreme weather conditions, such events often occur in sequence. A sudden downpour following a drought could trigger landslides, while a typhoon after an earthquake could result in the prolonged loss of water, electricity and communications.
People need more than a rigid manual. They need the ability to continually assess risks in their surroundings, learn to interpret hazard maps and other data, and make decisive choices at critical moments about whether to shelter in place or evacuate.
Household-level resilience also needs a shift in mindset. Just as we understand the importance of risk management and asset allocation in financial planning, emergency kits and stored food should not be seen as unnecessary expenses. They are resilience assets that protect families against extreme weather. That means maintaining at least one week’s worth of essential supplies, a backup power source, backup communications and backups of important documents. By making investing in personal safety a normal part of everyday life, we can buy ourselves time for rescue when essential lifelines fail.
Building up local mutual aid capacity is also critical. When disaster strikes, disrupted transportation and communications can prevent authorities from immediately reaching every corner of a community. At such times, a community’s social capital can become its lifeline.
A community with an established mutual assistance network and knowledge of where vulnerable residents live would recover far more effectively from a disaster than an isolated and disconnected neighborhood. Bottom-up, collective resilience is the strongest support for a government’s emergency-response capacity.
We must also acknowledge that during extreme weather events, there is no such thing as a zero-risk environment. The government cannot build flood-control infrastructure that ignores physical limits, nor can it deploy an unlimited number of search-and-rescue personnel.
When the public develops a mature understanding of risk and takes responsibility for protecting themselves, the government can concentrate its most valuable emergency resources on the areas in greatest danger.
Extreme weather is our new reality. We cannot control when torrential rain will fall or the next earthquake will hit, but we can control how prepared we are.
Starting today, check your household emergency kit and familiarize yourself with evacuation routes. That is one of the most worthwhile forms of risk insurance we can buy for ourselves and our families.
Ethan Chen is an associate technical specialist.

Although the government has budgeted more than NT$40 billion (US$1.26 billion) to improve pedestrian safety and walking infrastructure, pedestrian fatalities remain high and sidewalks are still inadequate, members of a political alliance said yesterday.
Taipei City Council candidates from Taiwan Go Go, a political alliance comprising members of the New Power Party (NPP), Taiwan Obasang Political Equality Party, Taiwan Statebuilding Party, Green Party Taiwan and independents, highlighted the urgency of the issue as they shared their transportation policy proposals in a news conference in Taipei.
NPP candidate Chen Chi-ying (陳峙穎) said that 354 pedestrians died in traffic accidents last year.
Photo: Tu Chien-jung, Taipei Times
The government has enacted the Pedestrian Traffic Safety Facilities Act (行人交通安全設施條例) and allocated NT$40 billion for pedestrian infrastructure improvements from 2024 through next year, but only 21.1 percent of roads nationwide have sidewalks, Chen said.
Fewer than 40 percent of roads in urban areas have sidewalks, he added.
From 2022 to 2024, an average of 103km of sidewalks were installed per year. At this rate, if the government wanted to install sidewalks on all urban area roads, their construction would not be completed until 2038.
About 40 percent of the sidewalks are narrower than the legally required minimum width of 1.5m, he said.
Chen also released the results of a survey of school zones, which compared data from the National Land Management Agency’s Pedestrian Safety Geographic Information System with information on 3,250 elementary and junior-high schools nationwide.
The survey found that only 31 percent of roads within 150m of school entrances have sidewalks, while the figure drops to just 24.3 percent within 500m. A total of 1,047 schools have no sidewalks around them, he said.
“Taiwan Power Co has estimated that approximately 8,000 utility poles in Taipei are installed on sidewalks. The Pedestrian Traffic Safety Facilities Act stipulates that public utility facilities can be relocated from the sidewalks, and public utility enterprises refusing to do so could face penalties. However, the Taipei City Government only said that identifying the utility poles to be removed would be the city’s top priority,” Chen said, adding that the city should set the timeline of gradually increasing the availability of sidewalks, particularly in school zones.
A survey conducted by the Jing Chuan Child Safety Foundation among 22 elementary and junior-high schools in the six special municipalities also showed that 66 percent of the schools have problems with sidewalks, including inadequate sidewalk width, discontinuity and gaps in sidewalk network.
Meanwhile, all schools in non-urban areas in the survey have problems with sidewalks, and 70 percent of the designated school commute routes lack sidewalks, with children walking or biking to schools having to share roads with motorcycles and cars, the foundation said.
The foundation also cited data from the Ministry of Transportation and Communications, saying that 36,406 children younger than 12 were injured or killed in traffic accidents in the past three years, and 3,580 were pedestrians.
A total of 2,405 children were killed or injured in traffic accidents in the six special municipalities, accounting for 67 percent of all child pedestrian casualties nationwide, it said.
The alliance urged the government to earmark traffic fines for transportation safety, abolish mandatory two-stage left turns, improve bus drivers’ working conditions and tighten vehicle safety requirements.

Taiwan has an opportunity to become a global innovation hub for precision health by taking advantage of its strengths in biotechnology and information and communications technology, an academic said at an annual biotech meeting in Taipei yesterday.
Wong Chi-huey (翁啟惠), a professor at Scripps Research in California and a distinguished research fellow at Academia Sinica’s genomics research center, made the remarks during a speech at the opening of the three-day Bio Taiwan Committee meeting.
Wong, a committee member and former president of Academia Sinica, said global medical spending is rising faster than economic growth as populations age.
Photo: CNA
Wong said global medical spending was about US$10.6 trillion in 2018, accounting for 10.9 percent of global GDP, based on statistics.
It is projected to reach US$15 trillion by 2030, when it is expected to reach 12.1 percent of GDP, expanding demand for biomedical innovation focused on prevention and precision health, he said.
Taiwan, with its unique National Health Insurance (NHI) data and strong semiconductor and tech sectors, is well positioned to use artificial intelligence (AI) and other technologies to become a global innovation hub for precision health, Wong said.
He outlined four priorities for ushering in this new era: The first is to integrate NHI, human biobank and genomic data into an AI learning platform while keeping the data within institutions. The second is to using Taiwan’s technological strengths to develop biomedical chips and smart healthcare computing.
The other priorities are to cultivate talent with expertise in biomedicine and AI, and to strengthen international cooperation by participating in large-scale global research and development projects, he said.
Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) and National Science and Technology Council Minister Wu Cheng-wen (吳誠文) attended the event organized by the BTC, a national advisory body established by the Executive Yuan in 2005 to help shape biotechnology policy and guide the strategic development of Taiwan's biomedical industry.
Taiwan’s biotech industry attracted NT$55.08 billion (US$1.73 billion) in investment last year and generated NT$805 billion in revenue, demonstrating its potential for driving economic growth, Cho said.
He said the government wants to revise and accelerate policies supporting biotechnology and medical technology to help the industry reach new heights and build a broader group of “national champions.”
The premier said the government has been investing more in biotechnology through its Ten AI Initiatives Promotion Plan (2025-2028), with the sector playing a leading role in applying AI to healthcare.
Cho said the government wants to make health information generated through AI-enabled services more widely available for noncommercial academic research.
Meanwhile, Wu said the Executive Yuan’s National Development Fund approved a 10-year, NT$10 billion investment program for Taiwan’s biomedical industry to promote the development of the biotechnology and pharmaceutical sectors.
Wu said the government would continue promoting healthcare for older people, home-based medical care and remote healthcare, and aims to combine Taiwan’s strengths in semiconductors and AI hardware with its healthcare, pharmaceutical and medical device sectors to build a “smart biotech national team.”

The drill takes place roughly once every two years.
Photo: AP

US Marine Corps Forces Pacific and US Forces Korea did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Those exercises ended about a week early on Friday last week.
The US has sent a wide range of military hardware and personnel to support the conflict against Iran. Most recently, the US has sent its lone aircraft carrier in the Asia-Pacific region, the USS George Washington.
Despite the deployments, the US had maintained its schedule of training in the Asia-Pacific region up until Trump’s intervention.
The Marine Corps spokesperson said the Ssangyong exercise was not scrapped indefinitely.
“While there may be some timing-related constraints for this year’s Ssangyong Exercise, the ROK and US Marine Corps are continuing close consultations regarding the future resumption of the exercise,” the person said at a briefing.

TASA rockets conduct test flights despite heavy rain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:43:57 UTC
01:43:57 KST

The Taiwan Space Agency (TASA) yesterday announced that two research rockets, SST3 and FARCX-1, completed test flights despite heavy rain at the short-term research rocket launch site in Pingtung County’s Syuhai Village (旭海).
SST3 is the largest solid-propellant sounding rocket launched in Taiwan by an academic team, while FARCX-1 is Taiwan’s first liquid-propellant sounding rocket independently developed and flight-tested by students, TASA said.
The tests came two days after TASA launched its first domestically developed sounding rocket, Maraho, on Saturday.
Photo courtesy of the Taiwan Space Agency via CNA
SST3 is 3.5m long and reached an altitude of 8.3km, TASA said.
The 33-member mission team includes the Advanced Rocket Research Center (ARRC), National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University’s Institute of Space Systems Engineering and, Aerospace Systems and Aerodynamics Research Labs, and National Cheng Kung University’s Department of Mechanical Engineering, and Yang Ming Chiao Tung University’s Formosan Fox student team.
The rocket uses a Pioneer-50K RNX solid-fuel propulsion system and reached its maximum altitude 40 seconds after launch. Although its parachute failed to deploy, and the rocket was not recovered, communications were successfully maintained during key stages of the flight.
Wei Shih-hsin (魏世昕), an assistant professor at the institute, said SST3 builds on the development of SSTO, which reached 1km in 2024, and SSTT, which targeted 3km last year.
For the new rocket, the team increased the target altitude to 9km and verified its propulsion system and structural strength, he said, adding that the team hope to provide more standardized propulsion systems for the future Rocket Taiwan Cup.
FARCX-1 uses an independently developed liquid propellant system, with ARRC responsible for designing, manufacturing and ground-testing the engine.
The rocket uses highly concentrated hydrogen peroxide as an oxidizer and kerosene as fuel. During the initial test, its propulsion system operated for three seconds, and the rocket reached an altitude of 532m.
Liquid rocket technology has a high technical threshold, and the first flight test provided valuable data, Wei said, adding that the team would use system performance analysis to increase the rocket’s energy level and extend its range.

Reinvest AI dividends in Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:43:55 UTC
01:43:55 KST

President William Lai (賴清德) has announced a NT$10,000 cash handout to every citizen to share the economic dividends generated by the artificial intelligence (AI) boom. Significant precedent has been built up over the past few years of ruling and opposition parties supporting such cash handouts from budget surpluses, making the practice seem set to become a new norm. However, some have suggested that the funds should be used on projects such as a renewable-energy transition and environmental conservation, given the enormous amounts of water and electricity needed to meet AI industry demands.
Consider the Taiwanese humpback dolphin, the only endemic subspecies of cetacean in Taiwan. It has attracted attention because of a land reclamation project at the Port of Taichung that could affect the dolphins’ habitat.
Under the combined pressures of deteriorating marine environments and new development projects, the dolphin’s population has fallen sharply. An early estimate based on surveys conducted from 2002 to 2004 put the population at 99, while Taiwanese government monitoring estimates put the population at about 48 over the past few years.
Taiwan’s conservation policies have failed to keep pace with the decline of the dolphin’s population. Government and business developments around their habitats have not been accompanied by sufficient measures to offset the ecological damage.
Much of the enormous power demands for companies in the AI supply chain comes from energy facilities along the west coast, placing additional pressure on marine ecosystems. Compared with a system in place for logging, funding for ecological compensation for west coast developments remain woefully inadequate. The government should embrace an initial population recovery target of 100 dolphins by 2030 proposed by the Taiwanese White Dolphin Advisory Panel, and channel AI dividends into ecological conservation along the west coast.
The same principle should apply to conservation of the endangered eastern grass owl near the Southern Taiwan Science Park.
Where endangered species are at stake, the only responsible approach is to first invest in population recovery and then proceed cautiously with development. That is what it means to truly look after Taiwan.
Another key issue is climate justice. AI development depends heavily on electricity. Extending the operating lives of Taiwan’s aging nuclear power plants would not help meet the stringent standards of international supply chains. For example, the RE100 initiative precludes nuclear power. Meanwhile, small modular reactors are expensive and could not be brought online quickly enough. Expanding renewable energy therefore remains an overriding priority.
There is a serious disconnect between Taiwan’s energy transition and how much electricity people use daily. Household users consuming more than 700 kilowatt-hours of electricity per month could save money by installing renewable-energy systems rather than purchasing electricity from the grid.
Rooftop solar gardens for household use, community renewable-energy projects that share revenues with residents and agricultural companies that can meet RE100 certification could help return the benefits of renewable energy to local communities. If the government were to allocate budget surpluses to a comprehensive and inclusive green energy program, it could address public concerns and build a broader consensus in support of a green-energy transition.
Protecting endangered species can help create sustainable economies within socioecological systems, while realizing climate justice provides a foundation for urban, rural and industrial development. Investing AI dividends in ecological restoration and decentralized renewable energy would generate far-reaching, long-term benefits, far beyond what could be achieved through a one-off cash payment.
As the ruling and opposition parties debate how best to distribute budget surpluses and AI dividends, they should not forget that Taiwan’s environment, ecosystems and energy transition are in critical need of support.

The crime of losing faith in the CCP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:43:53 UTC
01:43:53 KST

Hong Kong’s latest national security verdict is disturbing not simply because two veteran democracy activists have been convicted of inciting subversion. Its greater significance lies in the reasoning used to convict them. Read the judgement carefully, as it establishes a consequential principle: Peacefully persuading people that the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) should cease ruling China can itself be an act of subversion.
Former Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China chairman Lee Cheuk-yan (李卓人) and former vice chairwoman Chow Hang-tung (鄒幸彤) were on Friday convicted over the alliance’s longstanding call to “end one-party dictatorship.” Western coverage has understandably portrayed the verdict as another example of the territory’s shrinking political freedoms under Hong Kong’s National Security Law. However, the court’s reasoning deserves closer attention.
The judgement begins with an assurance: The defendants were not being tried because of their political views or beliefs. Nor was the case about democracy, the June 4, 1989, Tiananmen Square Massacre or criticism of the Chinese central government, it says. The court would simply examine the law and evidence and determine whether the prosecution had proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
The court ruled that the CCP leadership is an integral element of the “fundamental system” established by the Chinese constitution. The CCP’s leadership as the ruling party is constitutionally entrenched, with “no possibility for Western-style party alternation,” it says. Therefore, overthrowing or undermining CCP leadership amounts to overthrowing or undermining China’s fundamental system of governance itself.
The alliance did not advocate for replacing the CCP through armed uprising. Indeed, the court expressly acknowledged that it had “not used or advocated violence or the threat of violence.” Nor had Lee and Chow proposed a specific method or timetable for achieving their objective.
Their offense ultimately rested on something more fundamental: They continued advocating an end to one-party rule.
The judgement goes further. “Undermining” a political system, the court held, need not involve violence. It can include “sowing discord, creating division, causing others to lose confidence in the system.”
Yet causing people to lose confidence in those who govern them is an ordinary function of democratic politics. Opposition parties try to persuade voters that governments have failed. Journalists expose abuses that diminish public trust. Activists challenge institutions. Nevertheless, the court found that Lee and Chow intended to cause people to “lose confidence in the CCP,” thereby undermining the fundamental system.
The implications are profound. The CCP cannot be peacefully replaced through political competition, yet advocating that it should cease to rule can put a person in prison. The ruling party is therefore protected not only from losing power, but from the very idea that it should be possible for it to lose power.
However, perhaps the most unsettling aspect of the verdict lies deeper still.
The alliance was not campaigning in Beijing or Shanghai. It was a Hong Kong organization operating in Hong Kong and addressing primarily Hong Kongers. The court itself acknowledged that its target audience was mainly people within Hong Kong.
That distinction goes to the heart of the “one country, two systems” framework. Hong Kong has its own constitutional document, the Basic Law. Yet the court held that although the Chinese constitution does not apply in its entirety in Hong Kong, provisions including CCP leadership under Article 1 are directly applicable in the territory.
The consequence is extraordinary. A Hong Kong organization advocating political change from Hong Kong can be convicted because the political change it advocates is incompatible with the constitutional entrenchment of CCP rule in China — even though the organization neither used nor advocated the use of violence.
This is therefore about more than the limits of free speech under the National Security Law. It raises a fundamental question about “one country, two systems” framework itself. If China’s constitutional entrenchment of CCP rule can be applied in Hong Kong to determine which political ideas Hong Kongers may lawfully advocate, where exactly does one system end and the other begin?
The implications for Taiwan are clear. Beijing has long presented “one country, two systems” as a framework capable of preserving a society’s distinct way of life after unification. Hong Kong was supposed to demonstrate that promise.
The verdict demonstrates something rather different: When the interests of “one country” collide with the freedoms promised under the “two systems” formula, it is increasingly difficult to see where the second system begins — or whether it still exists at all.
John Cheng is a retired businessman from Hong Kong now living in Taiwan.

Qingqing: My friends have been sharing lots of exhibition photos lately. Every picture looks like it came from a movie.
Huahua: Many exhibitions today are very creative. Besides looking at the displays, you can also interact with them and take photos.
Qingqing: No wonder people say visiting an exhibition is like going on a little journey.
Huahua: Some exhibitions even use lights, music, and digital effects to make you feel as if you’ve stepped into a painting.
Qingqing: And since they’re indoors, you don’t have to worry about the summer heat.
Huahua: After the exhibition, grabbing a drink nearby is a perfect way to spend the afternoon.
Qingqing: It sounds like I’ve found another great way to stay cool this summer.
Huahua: Exactly. In Taiwan, exhibitions let you enjoy the air conditioning, take great photos, and have fun—all in one trip.

With AI, our imperfect minds make us insecure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:43:51 UTC
01:43:51 KST

Two faces that appeared on my Instagram feed in the past few months gave me pause. One belonged to John Travolta at Cannes, France. The other to Carla Bruni on a date night with her husband, former French president Nicolas Sarkozy. Both looked recognizably themselves, yet, they also looked oddly unfamiliar. Their looks have provoked speculation about cosmetic enhancement, although never acknowledged by them. Bruni has previously denied having had work done.
In any case the feeling lasted only a second: a flicker of unease, as though I were looking at people who had become approximations of themselves.
There is a name for that sensation. In a 1970 article, the Japanese robotics professor Masahiro Mori described what he called the “uncanny valley.” He found that robots that were designed to look as human as possible often provoked discomfort in people. That was a surprise, since the benefit of humanoid robots was supposed to be that we humans would trust them more.
Illustration: Yusha
What scares us about a robot that almost passes as human? One explanation might be that we sense danger when encountering something we cannot categorize easily as human or not. Another is that the features that seem “off,” such as glossy skin or frozen expressions, resemble signs of disease or death.
For a humanoid robot, triggering the uncanny valley sensation means failure. However, what does it signify when a human provokes it? In 1956, the German-Austrian philosopher Gunther Anders published a collection of essays entitled The Obsolescence of the Human. Anders said that technological progress would push humans to develop a novel form of self-contempt. Faced with the perfection of mass-produced goods, humans would come to regret their “bodily clumsiness” and “corporeal imprecision.” They would grow ashamed of being merely the result of the “blind and uncalculated, highly archaic process of procreation” rather than of careful design.
Anders wrote:
“Each day out of machines arise,
ever more beautiful machines.
Only we remain malformed,
only we’re born obsolete.”
However, here comes the crux: Anders predicted that the intimidated humans would not find the strength to rebel against the objects they feel humiliated by. On the contrary, they would aspire to resemble them. They would want to become less like people, and more like a product: Something standardized, optimized and yes, literally “put together.”
I am wondering whether we have come to live in Anders’ dystopia. With prices tumbling, there is a boom in surgical cosmetic procedures across the globe and across demographics. Often the goal does not seem to be to “correct” nature’s mistakes, or to look natural — just slightly better by adopting the logic of product design, such as symmetry or recognizability. This is what the contoured faces and Botox lips associated with Kim Kardashian, or the sharply angular chins sought by “looksmaxxers,” deliver.
However, Anders matters today for a reason other than making sense of contemporary beauty ideals. The human’s inferiority complex toward profit-making products that he described might no longer be limited to our bodies. In the age of artificial intelligence (AI), it is spreading to the mind. I can surely feel the shame Anders described when comparing my small, moody and heat-sensitive brain to the relentless and always available computing power of AI. No wonder then that four years after the public launch of ChatGPT, the use of AI is ever expanding — just like cosmetic procedures.
It is a vicious cycle: The better AI gets and the better it gets at imitating humans, just minus our flaws, the more we would perceive our minds as defective. The more we would be tempted not only to use AI, but to talk, sing and behave like technology in a quest to resemble our unfailing inventions.
This is the self-reinforcing motor of human self-alienation in an age of technological excellence. A study released last year by the renowned German Max Planck Institute for Human Development evaluating 360,000 YouTube videos and 772,000 podcasts found that after the release of ChatGPT, people started to use words preferred by the AI chatbot such as “delve,” “boast” and “meticulous” far more often — even in their spoken language.
Thus, it is no longer just the face remade by cosmetic procedure. It is the text message from a date that sounds oddly staccato. The tender love ballad that you have been listening to for a week on repeat until you realize that it was created by a program that never experienced a bad breakup. Your former work colleague who used to answer e-mails in one-liners and now publishes three polished essays a week on Substack.
The uncanny valley sensation appears wherever we begin to doubt the humanity of what stands before us.
That doubt, that eeriness about whether what we see, read and hear is really human accompanies us everywhere these days. That persistent suspicion is, perhaps, becoming the defining condition of our life entering the second quarter of the 21st century. Technology manages to imitate us ever more convincingly, and we humans cannot resist approximating our glorious technological inventions. As humans and technology are moving into the same hybrid gray space, the uncanny valley is the space that we inhabit.
Yet we must not strive to eliminate that lingering feeling of unease. On the contrary, we need to learn to cultivate it. As long as something in us, perhaps the crooked timber of our humanity, recoils from that world, there is hope. Recognizing our own self-alienation is to begin resisting it.
Joseph de Weck is an associate fellow with the German Council on Foreign Relations and writes for Guardian Europe from Zurich and Paris.

TRANSPORTATION
Starlux baggage fees change
Taiwanese carrier Starlux Airlines is adjusting its excess baggage fees starting Tuesday next week, with the highest fee set at US$280 per piece, the airline announced yesterday. The new fees would vary by destination and apply to passengers whose tickets are issued or reissued on or after Tuesday next week, the airline said in a statement. Destinations would be split into three regions, with the first covering Asia, excluding Southern Asia and Taiwan, as well as Guam. The second region covers Canada, Southern Asia, Oceania, the Middle East and the western US. The third region covers the rest of the US, Europe, Africa, and Central and South America. Starlux said the adjustment was made with reference to industry standards and was necessary, as its flight network continues to expand and the number of transfer passengers increases. Passengers can pay in advance for excess baggage online up to three hours before departure and receive a 20 percent discount, the airline said. Passengers who do not pay in advance would be charged for excess baggage, including additional pieces, overweight baggage and oversized baggage, it said.
DIPLOMACY
Quake donations surge
Donations raised through a dedicated bank account set up by the government to help people affected by a magnitude 7.1 earthquake that struck Japan’s Kumamoto Prefecture late last month had surpassed NT$300 million (US$9.42 million) as of yesterday. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a news release that the designated Mega International Commercial Bank account (021-09-01-7741), which was set up on Aug. 1, would continue to accept public donations until Monday next week. Meanwhile, the government and its Japanese counterparts are still discussing how the funds would be used to assist post-disaster relief efforts in Kumamoto after the one-month donation period ends, the ministry said, adding that more details would be announced later. In addition to the fundraising campaign, the government has already donated NT$5 million to support Japan’s reconstruction efforts following the earthquake, it said.

Taiwan phases out AT-3 trainer after decades of service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:43:51 UTC
01:43:51 KST

The air force’s AT-3 trainer aircraft has completed its final flight-training missions and been officially replaced by the Brave Eagle advanced jet trainer (AJT), a source familiar with the matter said yesterday.
The AT-3 has been one of the air force’s trainer aircraft since it entered service in 1984. It was jointly developed by the Aero Industry Development Center, the predecessor of Aerospace Industrial Development Corp (AIDC), and US company Northrop.
Under the government’s indigenous defense program, AIDC later developed the AJT to gradually replace the aging AT-3, which could also be adapted for wartime missions, including light attack and ground-attack operations.
Photo: CNA
The final flight-training missions were completed late last month, the source said.
An official decommissioning ceremony is to be held at a later date.
The air force held a handover ceremony for the Thunder Tigers aerobatic team — which previously flew the AT-3 — at its Gangshan Air Base in Kaohsiung in August last year, after Brave Eagle AJTs equipped with smoke generators were delivered to replace the team’s previous aircraft.
Meanwhile, Latin American multimedia news portal Zona Militar has reported that Paraguay is in talks with Taiwan to acquire jet aircraft, including F-5s and AT-3s, as part of efforts to rebuild its jet combat capability. The South American country is expected to acquire 10 to 15 of the aircraft starting next year.
Paraguay and Taiwan maintain close and friendly relations, and all military cooperation and exchanges are conducted in line with the government’s overall foreign policy, said an air force official who asked to remain anonymous.
The official declined to comment on the report.

A public survey on food safety related to the Central Union Oil Corp (CUOC) soybean oil scandal released yesterday showed that 61 percent of the respondents have no confidence in the government’s food safety inspection mechanism and 63 percent are against allowing sales of processed food products containing less than 20 percent of CUOC’s problem oil.
CUOC, which was jointly established by Taisun Enterprise Co (泰山企業), Fwusow Industry Co (福壽實業) and Formosa Oilseed Processing Co (福懋油脂), was ultimately found to have seven noncompliant batches of soybean oil; the first was reported to regulators on June 30.
Yen Yung-shen (顏永森), the Grassroots Influence Foundation’s convenor of polling, said the foundation commissioned TVBS Poll Center to conduct a computer-assisted telephone interviewing survey from Aug. 7 to 13.
Photo: CNA
It collected a total of 1,147 responses from people aged 18 or older, with a margin of error of 2.9 percentage points, Yen said.
The survey showed 69 percent of the respondents were worried that they would consume the benzopyrene-tainted cooking oil when eating out, while 26 percent were not concerned.
Fifty-two percent of respondents said they were unsatisfied with the government’s response speed in conducting inspections, seizures and removal of products, while 29 percent were satisfied; and 63 percent were against allowing sales of oil products containing less than 20 percent of CUOC’s problem oil, while 21 percent supported the policy, the survey showed.
Regarding the government’s food safety management ability, 61 percent of the respondents have no confidence in the inspection mechanism, while 30 percent were confident; and 54 percent were unsatisfied with the government’s handling of the scandal, while 33 percent were satisfied.
Asked if they agree that heavy penalties and fines should be imposed on CUOC and its responsible managers, 87 percent of the respondents agreed, while only 4 percent disagreed.
The survey also showed that 43 percent of the respondents did not think Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) needs to resign over this scandal, while 41 percent thought he should, and 16 percent had no opinion.
The survey showed that people’s attitudes toward food safety do not entirely align with their political party affiliation, Former Health Promotion Administration director-general Chiou Shu-ti (邱淑媞) said.
“Even for people with obvious political stances, their body is honest,” she said, adding that even supporters of the ruling party were concerned about the possibility of consuming contaminated oil, showing that food safety is a livelihood issue transcending political lines.
The survey shows that about 70 percent of people are concerned about consuming contaminated oil when eating out — an anxiety shared across political parties, National Taipei University Department of Public Administration and Policy professor Liu Jia-wei (劉嘉薇) said.
Meanwhile, 63 percent do not support allowing oil products containing less than 20 percent of the tainted oil on store shelves, indicating that food safety concerns have not subsided following the incident, so the government should re-evaluate its decisions, she said.
The poll showed that 73 percent agree with a “zero-detection” policy for carcinogens, so the government should adopt the strictest standards for carcinogens in food products to alleviate public concerns at the source, the foundation said.
While 87 percent agreed that the companies and responsible people should face severe penalties, it also suggested the government should uphold the principle of strict enforcement, conduct speedy trials, and impose heavy penalties to deter companies not reporting abnormalities, and restoring public trust in food safety and the rule of law, it said.

China’s latest meme is a complete load of bull
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:43:43 UTC
01:43:43 KST

Frustrated stock investors in China are finding dark humor from a crude, low-budget film that has become a box office hit.
Niu Lai (牛來), which translates as “Here Comes the Bull,” is an 86-minute animation about a newborn calf that follows a skylark into an abstract dream sequence. In it, the calf, Niu Lai, encounters a mysterious cobra, befriends a young leopard and fights against a pack of wolves. He learns life lessons from his mother who sacrifices herself, so her son has a chance to escape the predators. When Niu Lai wakes up, he finds the strength to stand up and live a full life.
The film grossed just 7,700 yuan (US$1,145) in the first 10 days after its release on Aug. 5, but online discussions of how bad it is, especially the “hand-crafted” animation in the era of artificial intelligence (AI), has turned it into a meme not just for young audiences, but for retail investors. It has now generated more than 25 million yuan at the box office, the biggest dark horse — er, wrong species — of this summer’s movie season.
It was good timing. Having just emerged from a nasty wipeout last month, individual investors are turning the young bull’s personal growth story into a reflection of the brutal reality of being preyed on in China’s US$15 trillion stock market. They tend to chase after momentum stocks, and last month, this investment style had its worst drawdown in history.
The parallels came naturally. The mysterious cobra is perceived to be the shape-shifting K-line chart that millions of mom-and-pop investors use to read market psychology. However, just like Niu Lai, who gets bitten by the snake and becomes scared of it, over-reliance on technical analyses has not panned out, causing many to lose faith in their validity.
Over the last decade, good candlestick patterns, which many believe foretell upward market trends, are followed by negative 20-day returns 55 percent of the time, data compiled by Bloomberg Opinion showed. Clusters of strong technical indicators and poor returns tend to overlap with negative macro backdrops. Examples are 2022’s COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns, or in 2023, when China’s reopening failed to revive the economy, and in late 2024 after Beijing did not undertake the massive stimulus it had vaguely promised.
The young leopard, whom Niu Lai befriends, is uncannily called Bao La (豹拉). Its name can be translated as a sharp spike up. The brave Bao La tries to fend off a pack of wolves with little success — just like the many dead-cat bounces that Chinese traders are all too familiar with.
Niu Lai’s name is eerily called out many times during the movie, as the herd panics over predators and migrates across arid land with little food or water, hoping to get to a safer landing. Is this not the experience of a typical retail trader? There is no slow and steady bull; the benchmark CSI 300 Index is a perpetual manifestation of booms and busts, with less-informed investors caught out by brokerage hype. By comparison, average Americans are faring much better. They have come to rule the market, notching impressive gains by buying the dip.
With the aid of AI, the Internet is creating parodies with clever word plays. My favorite is a video that borrows from a scene in the movie, in which Niu Lai comes to his mother crying after tripping over a big stone. “Silly child, that’s semiconductors. Even dogs won’t touch them,” the mother says.
The benchmark index of Shanghai’s STAR board, which hosts chip companies that the exchange claims to align with “national strategies,” is down as much as 30 percent from its late June peak.
To be sure, the animation is poor quality, but watching the movie through an investor’s lens, it is full of symbolism and dark humor that bring knowing laughter. Here Comes the Bull is an ironic name in a nation that is perpetually waiting for one. It has become a meme for good reason.
Shuli Ren is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Asian markets. A former investment banker, she was a markets reporter for Barron’s. She is a CFA charterholder. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

These conflicts are demonstrating that a less conventionally powerful state, by leveraging asymmetric capabilities, can impose major costs on an aggressor and fundamentally reshape the outcome of conflict. Taiwan is not only drawing lessons from those conflicts, but also translating them into practice. Far from seeking to match China ship for ship, missile for missile or aircraft for aircraft, Taiwan needs to make Chinese aggression so costly, problematic and uncertain that Beijing is deterred from launching an attack. Taiwan cannot become a bigger wolf than China, but it can ensure that

Work harassment survivor fights for right to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:43:42 UTC
01:43:42 KST

Kept in the dark after reporting her boss for harassment, South Korean advocate Baek Song-yi is now campaigning for survivors’ right to know how their bullies were disciplined.
Baek, 40, experienced first-hand a troubling paradigm in South Korea’s workplace harassment response, with victims often expected to keep silent while employers have no clear legal duty to tell them how their cases ended.
At her former company, a US firm with offices overseas, Baek said she was verbally harassed by her boss, an older man.
Photo: AFP
When she reported him, the company asked her to accept a confidentiality agreement warning she could be fired for disclosing information discussed during the process.
“I was just so stunned,” Baek said, adding that she had believed her employer encouraged victims to come forward.
Baek refused to accept the agreement and the investigation went ahead anyway, ultimately upholding her complaint.
The company still declined to disclose what disciplinary action had been taken, citing the need to “align with a privacy protection law” in South Korea, Baek said.
An investigator told her only that the harasser would be “monitored.”
Baek, who has since left the company, never learned whether her request to bar him from the firm’s South Korean office had been granted.
‘NO CLOSURE’
“I just felt like victims are left with no closure, no sense of justice and no way of knowing,” she said.
She is now campaigning for legislation asimilar to California’s Silenced No More Act, which restricts non-disclosure agreements in workplace harassment cases, and for a clear legal right for victims to be informed of disciplinary measures.
South Korea introduced a workplace anti-bullying law seven years ago, but critics say it fails to guarantee adequate protections.
A study last year by workplace abuse support group Gapjil 119 found that just 15.3 percent of victims reported harassment.
Nearly half of respondents said they believed action would change nothing, and about one-third feared career repercussions.
Experts say the law requires employers to act against confirmed harassers, but stops there, often leaving victims in the dark while shielding perpetrators and their reputation.
“Employers have full discretion over whether to disclose disciplinary action, as there is no provision requiring them to inform the victim,” labor attorney Kim Yu-kyung said.
A woman identified only by her surname Yoo spent about 10 months pursuing a complaint, only to face a Kafkaesque process to learn how it ended.
Her former employer, a South Korean firm, cited “privacy concerns,” saying only that action had been taken under “company rules.”
The Ministry of Employment and Labor, which upheld her complaint, later intervened, allowing Yoo to inspect the company rules — but only in person, without taking any photos or making notes.
Yoo discovered that the rules contained no provisions on workplace harassment, she said.
She was then told that her harasser had merely been asked to submit a written account of what happened.
Yoo, who quit over the harassment and waited until leaving to report it for fear of retaliation, said she suffered insomnia and panic attacks.
“I wondered what I had put myself through more than 10 months of stress and fighting for,” she said.
“It all felt a bit pointless,” she said.
RIGHT TO KNOW
In Baek’s case, she turned to Seoul’s regional labour office, hoping to find out what action had been taken.
Instead, she was told the company had complied with the law.
“There is no provision in the law requiring disclosure of what measures the perpetrator received,” a labor official said in a recorded call reviewed by Agence France-Presse.
The company was required only to ask Baek what measures she wanted before deciding what action to take, the official said.
Withholding the outcome to protect a perpetrator’s privacy is a “distorted interpretation,” labor attorney Kim said, adding that seeking victims’ views should also mean informing them of the decision.
Baek said that her former employer was “just using ambiguous law” to protect victims “in the most minimal way possible.”
“Victims should not be silenced, victims should be able to speak about their experiences” for their own safety and that of others, she said.
The labor ministry said it revised its workplace harassment guidelines last month, “recommending” employers share with victims the outcome of investigations and the basis for their conclusions.
However, it said mandating such disclosure would “require careful consideration,” weighing the involved parties’ privacy and individual rights.
Baek said she reached out to several South Korean lawmakers proposing restrictions on confidentiality agreements and a requirement that employers disclose disciplinary measures to victims.
None responded.

‘Taiwan Grapevine’: An expat time capsule from the end of martial law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:43:40 UTC
01:43:40 KST

During the Martial Law era, newspapers and magazines were strictly controlled by the government. But from 1985 to 1990 — a period that straddled the lifting of martial law in 1987 — a free monthly expat magazine emerged as one of the first published and edited by foreigners. It was also perhaps the first to express a uniquely local expatriate voice.
Taiwan Grapevine’s articles were irreverent, politically incorrect and plagued by typos. Neither editors nor writers were named in the magazine, and those bylines that appeared were obvious pseudonyms like Archibald Hellbender.
Yet the magazine achieved nationwide distribution. And while its circulation is not known, similar publications that followed on its heels printed 15,000 to 20,000 issues per month.
In concept, Taiwan Grapevine plied the route of American ad-driven community magazines. In voice, it took inspiration from alternative US newspapers like Village Voice and the bawdy, gonzo reportage found in the likes of the Bangkok Post’s legendary bar column, “Night Owl.”
One article from Jan 1989, which loosely described a visit to Taipei Adventist Hospital, opened as follows:
“I had been nursing a bad liver for some time. I had found that I couldn’t take the grind of trade reports, market surveys, public relations consultations and so forth without drinking heavily. I was desperately casting about for something to do. I probably should have known better than to enter a den of Christians, but I randomly decided to check out the Seventh-Day Adventist Hospital’s five-day quit-smoking clinic. There might be an article there, I thought.”
Photo: David Frazier
Mainly, however, Taiwan Grapevine was a vehicle for community news. Dubbing itself “a publication for the Taiwan expatriate community,” it reported on changing flight routes, holidays and festivals and the goings-on of international clubs and associations, including a number of veterans’ organizations that no longer exist. Advertising came from major expat watering holes of the day.
“There was really no other place to get information at that time in English,” said Trace Gomez, a 66-year-old American who served as Taiwan Grapevine’s final managing editor.
Describing the magazine as a “time capsule,” Gomez pointed to articles on having to apply to the phone company to hook up a modem or answering machine, the launch of Wellcome supermarkets, and the explosion of pubs and discos that accelerated during the 1980s.
“This was martial law-era news for foreigners,” he said.
GOING DIGITAL
Only around 50 issues of Taiwan Grapevine were ever published, and until recently the magazine was almost completely forgotten. I first learned of its existence around three years ago from Gomez, who showed me a large but deteriorating stack he’d kept stored in his basement.
Since then I’ve asked numerous Taiwan old-timers about it, but only a few had vague recollections.
Gomez, who built his career in manufacturing, says he inherited the magazine in late 1989 from its final editor and publisher Dennis Keagan, who died mysteriously in Thailand three years later.
Gomez had arrived in Taipei in 1987 and initially helped the magazine’s editors with layout and graphics. After taking charge, he went on to publish its final few issues before folding the publication around March 1990.
“When [Keagan] left, it fell in my lap totally,” said Gomez. “But I didn’t want to do it because I was already working full time.”
Now four decades later, Gomez — in part at my urging — has digitized the 13 issues of the magazine he can still locate and uploaded them to archive.org for all to access. He says he will continue to search for more issues and add them if possible.
‘GREATEST PUBLICATION’
The magazine was hardly Taiwan’s only English-language publication of its day. Daily newspapers of the time included the China Post and the China News. In 1970, AmCham Taipei also launched a newsletter, Taiwan Business Topics, which by the 1980s had become a magazine.
Taiwan Grapevine’s main competitor was another expatriate-run monthly, This Month in Taiwan. Founded in 1974 by an ex-military man, E. Kirk Henderson, that publication had a strong commercial focus and placed little value on original writing. According to Earl Wieman, an editor working in Taipei since the early 1970s, Henderson referred to everything except his advertisements as “non-revenue paper.”
Taiwan Grapevine set itself apart from this field with its irreverent voice and strong doses of irony. From its letters section, one can see that readers both loved and hated it.
One reader slammed an entire issue as “blatantly insulting to black people, women, and gays.” Another declared the bar column to be “gutter talk.”
But others praised the magazine. “Taiwan Grapevine is the greatest publication to ever hit the Taiwan expatriate community,” declared one reader.
Another opined, “A month without Grapevine is like a month without ketchup. Your efforts are deeply appreciated by those of us who are here by choice, who love Taiwan and its people and who dread the prospect of returning to the quagmire of reality that awaits us on the other side of the Pacific.”
‘GETTING ACQUAINTED’
One of Taiwan Grapevine’s more fascinating columns, “Getting Acquainted,” offered short biographies of long-term expats. These linked the roots of Taiwan’s foreign community to the end of World War II and — in the case of British tea merchant Frank Berger, who’d first arrived during the Japanese colonial era — even earlier.
One of these columns profiled one of ICRT’s first news readers, David G. White. A UK native, White had been present at D-Day in a spotter submarine and also fought for the British army in Burma. He first arrived in Taiwan in 1949 working for Civil Air Transport, a commercial airline that was acquired covertly by the CIA in 1950.
White eventually got into radio in 1955 when he took a job with the BBC in England. He then hopscotched the globe before returning to Taipei and ICRT in 1980 — the radio station’s second year of operation.
A column on American Ed Little offered just as much intrigue, though from a later generation. Little came to Asia as part of a US Marines Corps combat unit and fought in Vietnam from 1968 to 1969. During that tour, he “had the first seed of Buddhist dharma planted in his soul by a Bangkok prostitute.”
It was Buddhism that brought Little to Taiwan in the mid-1970s — to live as a monk at Kaohsiung’s Fo Guang Shan (佛光山寺) monastery. But he only lasted six months, complaining that there was “too much ‘Pureland’ chanting and not enough meditation.” He eventually walked out of the monastery in his orange robes, bought pants and a t-shirt in a Kaohsiung department store and started looking for work as an English teacher.
As Taiwan moved toward liberalization, the magazine also commented on the December 1986 election. An April 1987 column signed “Cyril H.B. Dilling” treated the democratic transition with a mixture of gravitas and barstool irony.
“We live in remarkable times… and are seeing elements of fundamental history played out before our very eyes,” wrote the magazine’s anonymous political columnist. Then, with eyes on the future, the column predicted that Taiwan “will find out that it is as impossible to be a little bit democratic as a little bit pregnant.” Finally, it welcomed Taiwan “on board the often leaky, sometimes badly ballasted Ship of Democracy.”
MYSTERY FOUNDER
It is perhaps impossible to know who wrote most of these articles. Even the identity of Taiwan Grapevine’s founder remains something of a mystery.
As government regulations made it difficult for foreigners to own media businesses, Gomez says the magazine operated under the aegis of publishing companies run by Taiwanese proxies.
As a result, the name of the magazine’s founder does not appear in business registration records, and he further concealed his identity by omitting a masthead. One guest editor noted that the founder, in addition to serving as managing editor, was “also the chief writer, sales executive, delivery boy and all around handyman,” but did not mention his name.
Gomez and former advertisers contacted for this article can only remember that Taiwan Grapevine’s founder was an American man named “Dave.”
Gomez remembers that “Dave” left Taiwan for Thailand around March 1989. At that time the magazine passed to Keagan, who he says wrote the bar column under the pseudonym Durdley Drinkright, before Keagan in turn gave the magazine to Gomez later that same year.
After the magazine folded in early 1990, Taiwan’s publishing landscape continued to liberalize. Later that decade, other publishing ventures sprang up that were ad-fueled and expat-targeted, including Taichung Compass, which began in 1994 and has been published continuously ever since.
According to Taichung Compass co-publisher, Courtney Donovan Smith, who is also a Taipei Times columnist, even into the late 1990s, “publishing magazines was still very much in a grey zone.”
Smith said that in those early years, his magazine was repeatedly targeted by citizen complaints, and the publishers were once called in by the police for questioning. But the magazine was cleared in every instance.
Later on, local governments “gave us positive attention because we were doing a better job than their own tourism bureaus at promoting what to do and where to go. Taichung mayor Jason Hu (胡志強) said as much, both to us personally and publicly in city council,” Smith said.
Taiwan Grapevine perhaps produced too little too early to leave such a lasting impression. But an archive can now be found online at: archive.org/details/taiwangrapevine/

Even if Taiwan and the United States take steps to better prepare for a Chinese blockade, they face a greater threat from China than analysts previously believed.” The authors

US territories hit out at Trump plan to explore deep sea mining in the Pacific
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:43:40 UTC
01:43:40 KST

A US government plan to lease out millions of hectares of seabed near the Mariana Trench for deep sea exploration has drawn opposition from US territories in the Pacific, as US President Donald Trump’s administration remains locked in a race with China for control of critical ocean minerals.
The Marine Mineral Administration, an agency under the US Department of the Interior, on Tuesday last week released a proposal to auction deep sea mining leases for 28 million hectares of seafloor off the coast of the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam.
The leases would allow companies to explore the seabed and potentially extract deposits of critical minerals — known as polymetallic nodules — that could be used in batteries, electronics and defense technologies. Many environmental groups have opposed deep sea mining, arguing that more research is needed on its effects on marine ecosystems.
Photo: AFP
The Northern Mariana Islands is a self-governing commonwealth of the US, while Guam is an unincorporated territory of the US.
Northern Marianas Governor David Apatang has said his government would approach the Trump administration’s proposal “with extreme caution.”
Apatang, while acknowledging the strategic importance of critical minerals, said it was necessary that “no activity, survey or otherwise, takes place without rigorous scientific baseline studies, complete transparency, and explicit protections for our marine resources.”
He said his administration would “thoroughly examine the proposed terms over the next 60 days to ensure that the ecological integrity of our waters and the long-term wellbeing of the [Northern Marianas] are fully safeguarded.”
The Guardian approached the Marine Mineral Administration for comment.
In an earlier statement, the agency said it had completed an environmental review of proposed commercial leases for critical minerals in the Marianas area. It said it would consider comments from the governor.
A statement from the office of the governor of Guam acknowledged the Trump administration’s focus on national security and strategic needs, but added: “National security cannot mean asking the people of the Pacific to accept environmental risks before those risks are fully understood.
“We’re unequivocally opposed to the deep sea mining efforts in this region,” Guam Lieutenant Governor Joshua Tenorio said.
“The Department of Interior is giving assurances that mining activity is not going to commence with the awarding of these licenses, [but] I think that this is a matter where we can’t really trust that because this has been rapidly evolving,” he said.
The proposed lease notice for deep sea exploration in the Marianas region came just weeks after the initiation of a leasing process for 12.4 million hectares of American Samoa’s seafloor, with plans to award contracts in November.
American Samoa Governor Nikolau Pula said his government remained opposed to deep sea mining, adding that untested extraction processes could harm the territory’s tuna industry, which fuels its economy.
On Wednesday last week, environmental groups in American Samoa and Hawaii launched legal proceedings against the US government to halt the proposed auction of seafloor permits around the islands, alleging that federal agencies failed to evaluate the destructive impact mineral extractions could have on marine ecosystems.
In a Hawaii court, Fa’asao Ameika Samoa and the Conservation Council for Hawaii warned that the extraction machinery “can destroy nearly all life in its path” and “stirs up sediments that can introduce toxic substances into the food web and smother seafloor ecosystems.”
“Even just exploring for seabed minerals introduces extremely loud noise into the marine environment that can harm marine mammals and other wildlife,” the complaint reads.
The Marine Mineral Administration was approached about the concerns over the American Samoa leasing process.

Photo: AFP
“For Ukraine, independence is not an abstract idea. We defended it against all odds,” Ukrainian Minister of Foreign Affairs Andrii Sybiha said on social media. “In times like these, nations learn how important it is to have allies by your side.”

Photo: Reuters

SCALP is the French version of the UK’s Storm Shadow missile, with both systems incorporating shared French and British technology.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the Kremlin views the plan “extremely negatively.”

Ukraine’s long-range drones have repeatedly hit facilities in Russia’s vital oil industry, causing fuel shortages, and have also engaged in a campaign against Russia’s largest online retailer, Wildberries.

Kyiv urgently needs more interceptors before winter, when Russia routinely bombards its power grid, but the demands of the Iran war and slow output of the sophisticated interceptors have left Ukraine short and vulnerable.

Israeli authorities change name of Jerusalem’s Damascus Gate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:39:33 UTC
01:39:33 KST

Breadcrumb
Israeli authorities change name of Jerusalem’s historic Damascus Gate in unprecedented move
Israeli authorities have changed the name of one of the historic gates leading to the highly revered al-Aqsa mosque in occupied East Jerusalem, triggering major concerns that this is an example of the latest efforts to change the character of the area.
Photographs of roads leading to Al-Aqsa now show signs which refer to the gate as the ‘Ancient Gate’ in Arabic, English and Hebrew.
Fakhri Abu Diab, a member of Al-Aqsa’s board of trustees, told The New Arab that the move to change the signs “is part of Israel’s plans to change the visual identity of areas with Palestinian, Arabic and Islamic symbolism in Jerusalem”.
Abu Diab noted that Israeli authorities started off with one of the most prominent and important gates in the Old City, which is sometimes referred to as “Victory Gate” – a name that emerged after the Second Intifada.
“The gate’s name also has significance in Islamic history, as it is one of the entrances to the Old City and is linked to the narrative of Salahaddin passing through this side during the recapturing of Jerusalem in 1187,” he continued.
Sources who spoke to The New Arab said that the move was clearly motivated to erase Islamic history and significance, as Sultan Suliman the Magnificent street leads to the gate, sending a message that any historical context will be removed. The sources also noted this comes as there has been a surge in Muslim tourists visiting from Turkey.
According to Abu Diab, the choice of the new name – Ancient Gate - has links to Talmudic Jewish narratives.
“These narratives claim there was a gate in this area that was once used to access what they refer to as the Temple. It passes through Silwan and heads towards the Al-Aqsa mosque, passing through what Talmudic narratives refer to as facilities associated to the Temple, such as the Silwan Spring.”
Members of Al-Aqsa’s board of trustees told The New Arab that the change in name was not merely a matter of linguistics but rather is a direct attempt to associate Israeli and Jewish narratives with the site, to allow Israelis to claim that the gate existed during the period described in those accounts, and that it was a path leading to what Israel refers to as the ‘temple’.
Israelis refer to Al-Aqsa as the Temple Mount, based on their belief that two ancient Jewish temples once stood there - the temple built by King Solomon, which was destroyed by the Babylonians, and the Second Temple, destroyed by the Romans.
Israeli extremists have called for Jewish prayer at al-Aqsa, despite this violating a long-held agreement, and some call for the destruction of the mosque and the building of a Jewish temple.
Palestinians have also raised concerns that changing the names and changing signs to make them Hebrew reinforces the Israeli narrative among tourists visiting the city, further stripping it of its heritage.
Far-right Israeli ministers regularly storm al-Aqsa.

NEW DELHI: The Bharatiya Janata Party on Monday put speculation over an alliance with the Shiromani Akali Dal to rest, saying the saffron party will contest all 117 seats in the upcoming Punjab assembly elections.BJP national general secretary (organisation) BL Santosh said the party was fully prepared for the polls and would form the government in Punjab.
